FIN.description:
Southern and western Scandinavia’s Mesolithic is a watery cosmos: Maglemosian lakes, Kongemose blade elegance, Fosna–Hensbacka coastal pioneers. Genetically Scandinavian Hunter-Gatherers (SHG) model as WHG-related with extra EHG affinity—a northern contact sea between western and eastern forager worlds. Seal, fish, and forest deer structured identity more than painted caves.

Post-glacial rebound and changing Baltic salinity forced constant environmental updating. Later overturns would come first from TRB farmers, then from Single Grave / Battle Axe steppe-rich groups—but around 8000 BCE those futures were remote.

Speech was unattested; pre-Germanic associations belong to much later Battle Axe / Nordic Bronze Age models.
FIN.summary: Scandinavian Hunter-Gatherers of wetlands and rising Baltic/North Sea shores—WHG with elevated EHG affinity—before TRB farming.
FIN.culture:
Coastal and inland rounds; dugouts and leisters enable dense wetland living. Amber animals and beads mark prestige. Territorial knowledge of seal rookeries and salmon runs is political capital.

Seal rookeries and salmon runs create defendable, memorable places; northern politics begins with knowing which skerries feed which kin.

Key sites: Maglemose wetland sites of Zealand and southern Scandinavia; Kongemose culture coastal sites; Fosna–Hensbacka pioneer sites of Norway/west Sweden; Early Scandinavian amber find contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous seal-hunters and wetland dwellers.
FIN.art:
Bone and antler leisters, amber pendants, Kongemose blade aesthetics; emerging coastal rock art in some areas. Portable amber animals glow as prestige.

Amber’s warm translucence suits a cosmology of shore light and winter dark—prestige that glows against grey water.
FIN.ideas:
Archipelago and lake mobility; eastern genetic affinity mixed into western baselines. Scandinavia as contact sea rather than cul-de-sac.

SHG as WHG-plus-east affinity makes Scandinavia a genomic harbour where Baltic conversations dock early. Maglemosian lakes and Kongemose coasts are not backwaters; they are contact seas whose ideas travel by paddle.
FIN.philosophy:
Amber and animal deposits, wetland platforms, careful burials suggest water and animal persons holding power. Many thresholds—shore, ice, forest edge—few temples.

Threshold thinking—ice edge, forest edge, tide line—likely organised taboo and story more than any single mountain sanctuary. Amber deposits and wetland platforms suggest offerings at those thresholds.
FIN.science:
Dugout canoes, fish weirs, leister design, seal-hunting logistics. Tracking rebound, Baltic salinity, and forest succession—an environmental science of rising land.

Boat repair cycles and fish-weir carpentry are continuous R&D against a moving coastline. Post-glacial rebound makes yesterday’s harbour today’s meadow—environmental literacy is mandatory.

stories.title: Paddling a Rising Sea

ALA.description:
Southern and western Scandinavia’s Mesolithic is a watery cosmos: Maglemosian lakes, Kongemose blade elegance, Fosna–Hensbacka coastal pioneers. Genetically Scandinavian Hunter-Gatherers (SHG) model as WHG-related with extra EHG affinity—a northern contact sea between western and eastern forager worlds. Seal, fish, and forest deer structured identity more than painted caves.

Post-glacial rebound and changing Baltic salinity forced constant environmental updating. Later overturns would come first from TRB farmers, then from Single Grave / Battle Axe steppe-rich groups—but around 8000 BCE those futures were remote.

Speech was unattested; pre-Germanic associations belong to much later Battle Axe / Nordic Bronze Age models.

SMR.description:
Italian Mesolithic foragers inherited Epigravettian portable traditions across a peninsula of Tyrrhenian–Adriatic contrasts and Alpine–Apennine vertical seasons. Southern refugia mattered for WHG diversity relative to northern Europe. Alpine and Apennine rock shelters kept older image places alive as memory; Mediterranean shell ornaments already hinted at maritime aesthetics.

Farming would arrive by sea (Impresso/Cardial) and largely replace this demographic layer. Historical Etruscan and Italic languages are not Mesolithic holdovers in any demonstrated sense.

Obsidian recognition from island sources foreshadowed the sea roads Impressa farmers would intensify—materials prospecting before villages.
SMR.summary: Peninsula WHG foragers after the Late Glacial—coastal and mountain rounds, early obsidian awareness—before Impressa maritime farming.
SMR.culture:
Small bands; identity local to valley and coast. North–south and sea-to-sea contrasts in foraging strategies. Exchange of shell and early obsidian foreshadows network Italy.

Tyrrhenian versus Adriatic shores teach different winds and molluscs; Italian forager society is already a peninsula of specialised coasts linked by ridge paths. Small bands still meet at passes where Alpine and Apennine seasons reverse.

Key sites: Epigravettian–Mesolithic rock shelters of the Apennines and Alps; Coastal Mesolithic camps of Liguria and southern Italy; Early Lipari obsidian find contexts in forager assemblages; Adriatic versus Tyrrhenian coastal forager facies.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous; no attested names.
SMR.art:
Engraved stones, bone tools, personal ornaments—small-scale, mobile, coast-aware. Continuity of place at painted/engraved shelters as memory rather than new atelier florescence.

Portable engraving and shell beads keep beauty light for mountain crossings; caves hold the heavier memory of older images. Obsidian flakes, when they appear, add a volcanic luxury to the portable kit.
SMR.ideas:
Peninsula as corridor of contrasts. Sea links and mountain passes structure mobility. Obsidian and shell exchange prefigure Neolithic maritime roads.

Early obsidian awareness turns volcanoes into distant ‘mines’ in the mind long before specialised workshops industrialise them. Sea roads are imagined before they are crowded with farmer boats.
SMR.philosophy:
Cave burials and ochre rites continue Paleolithic body care. Sacred geography of caves, high passes, and shoreline shrines without recoverable god names. Continuity of place over new dogma.

Passes and shoreline shrines structure pilgrimage-scale movement without temples—sacred logistics before villages. Ochre burials continue Paleolithic body care into Holocene silence.
SMR.science:
Vertical seasonal scheduling—upland game, lowland plants, marine shellfish. Early obsidian recognition as materials prospecting. Coastal navigation along indented shores.

Vertical scheduling is biometric: body fat, hide quality, and shellmeat peak on different months of the same slope. Coastal pilotage along indented shores is ordinary technical knowledge.

GRC.description:
The Iron Gates gorge and related Balkan Mesolithic communities are among Europe’s most striking forager societies: Lepenski Vir’s trapezoidal houses and sandstone fish-human sculptures fuse architecture and idol beside the Danube. Rich fisheries supported denser, more sedentary life than northern forests allowed. Genetically they form a distinctive WHG-related node used carefully in admixture models—not generic western WHG.

The gorge was a corridor of contact, not a sealed refuge. When Anatolian-related farmers approached, the Danube became a negotiation zone of genes, pots, and spouses. Languages were unknown and not Greek, Thracian, or Slavic—all far later.

Sculpture here is monumental for foragers; sacred order is riverside and bodily.
GRC.summary: Danube Iron Gates foragers—trapezoidal houses, fish-human sculpture, distinctive HG genetics—contact corridor before Anatolian-related farming.
GRC.culture:
Semi-sedentary riverside communities with house burials and curated ornaments of shell and stone. Social density exceeds typical northern bands. Contact skills matter as much as fishing skills.

House burials and sculptural investment imply longer residential commitment than northern microlith camps; Iron Gates society could stage denser ritual publics beside the catch. Ornaments of shell and stone mark persons who live by a corridor, not a refuge myth.

Key sites: Lepenski Vir; Padina, Vlasac, and related Iron Gates sites; Danube gorge terraces; Early contact horizons with Starčevo farmers.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous sculptors and house-builders of Lepenski Vir; no historical names.
GRC.art:
Sandstone fish-human sculptures, trapezoidal houses facing the water, ochre, carefully posed burials—a riverside aesthetic of fish and ancestor.

Fish-human beings are not decorative mascots—they sit at the hinge of architecture and cosmology, facing the same water that feeds the village. Trapezoidal houses are themselves sculptural statements toward the Danube.
GRC.ideas:
Gorge as contact corridor. Fisher abundance enabling architectural investment. Negotiation with incoming farmers as historical process, not mythic wipe.

Contact-corridor consciousness prepares the gorge for the farmer dialogue centuries before Cardial boats reach Iberia. Abundance of fish makes sedentism thinkable without cereals.
GRC.philosophy:
Fish-human sculptures and house burials imply river persons, ancestors, and living sharing space. Houses face water as if architecture prays downstream. Intense place cult, no scripture.

If the river is person-like, fishing ethics and burial ethics may have been one conversation. Ancestors under floors keep the living answerable to the current.
GRC.science:
Specialised sturgeon and migratory-fish harvesting with nets, spears, seasonal timing. Sedentary architecture and hearth management approach village science before farming. Dual knowledge systems collide at contact.

Migratory fish calendars are as exacting as any early farmer’s sowing schedule—and denser calories enable stone sculpture. Hearth and house engineering approach village science before the plough.

ALB.description:
The Iron Gates gorge and related Balkan Mesolithic communities are among Europe’s most striking forager societies: Lepenski Vir’s trapezoidal houses and sandstone fish-human sculptures fuse architecture and idol beside the Danube. Rich fisheries supported denser, more sedentary life than northern forests allowed. Genetically they form a distinctive WHG-related node used carefully in admixture models—not generic western WHG.

The gorge was a corridor of contact, not a sealed refuge. When Anatolian-related farmers approached, the Danube became a negotiation zone of genes, pots, and spouses. Languages were unknown and not Greek, Thracian, or Slavic—all far later.

Sculpture here is monumental for foragers; sacred order is riverside and bodily.
ALB.summary: Danube Iron Gates foragers—trapezoidal houses, fish-human sculpture, distinctive HG genetics—contact corridor before Anatolian-related farming.
ALB.culture:
Semi-sedentary riverside communities with house burials and curated ornaments of shell and stone. Social density exceeds typical northern bands. Contact skills matter as much as fishing skills.

House burials and sculptural investment imply longer residential commitment than northern microlith camps; Iron Gates society could stage denser ritual publics beside the catch. Ornaments of shell and stone mark persons who live by a corridor, not a refuge myth.

Key sites: Lepenski Vir; Padina, Vlasac, and related Iron Gates sites; Danube gorge terraces; Early contact horizons with Starčevo farmers.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous sculptors and house-builders of Lepenski Vir; no historical names.
ALB.art:
Sandstone fish-human sculptures, trapezoidal houses facing the water, ochre, carefully posed burials—a riverside aesthetic of fish and ancestor.

Fish-human beings are not decorative mascots—they sit at the hinge of architecture and cosmology, facing the same water that feeds the village. Trapezoidal houses are themselves sculptural statements toward the Danube.

Gorge as contact corridor. Fisher abundance enabling architectural investment. Negotiation with incoming farmers as historical process, not mythic wipe.

Contact-corridor consciousness prepares the gorge for the farmer dialogue centuries before Cardial boats reach Iberia. Abundance of fish makes sedentism thinkable without cereals.
ALB.philosophy:
Fish-human sculptures and house burials imply river persons, ancestors, and living sharing space. Houses face water as if architecture prays downstream. Intense place cult, no scripture.

If the river is person-like, fishing ethics and burial ethics may have been one conversation. Ancestors under floors keep the living answerable to the current.

BLR.description:
East of the early farmer line, Eastern Hunter-Gatherer–related populations of the Volga–Don–Pontic forest-steppe kept a forager political economy with Ancient North Eurasian affinity. They are not Yamnaya yet; Yamnaya forms later when EHG-related ancestry mixes with Caucasus/Lower Volga–related groups. Linguistic Indo-European status is not Mesolithic.

Art concentrates in graves: amber, animal-tooth pendants, richly furnished burials such as at Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov. Bone and antler tools carry engraved designs; pottery appears in some eastern ‘Neolithic’ forager contexts without farming—pots without ploughs.

Mobility across forest and steppe edges linked Baltic, Volga, and Pontic zones. Path knowledge across vast low-density landscapes was the core information technology.
BLR.summary: EHG forest-steppe foragers with Ancient North Eurasian affinity—amber-rich burials, optional pottery, not yet Yamnaya or Indo-European.
BLR.culture:
Hunter-fisher identity with ceramics optional. Lavish burials imply ranked persons and afterlife provisioning. Wide-ranging lithic procurement and waterway travel structure alliance more than villages.

Rich graves imply that even low-density foragers could sustain hereditary or achieved rank loud enough to dress the dead for an audience of the living. Waterway travel and wide lithic catches structure alliance more than villages do.

Key sites: Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov cemetery; Volga–Oka and related forest forager sites; Pontic steppe-edge Mesolithic camps; Eastern forager ceramic (pre-farming) contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous ranked burial persons; no historical names.
BLR.art:
Amber, tooth pendants, engraved bone, grave theatre—prestige of the body. Aesthetic power sits in burial and adornment more than settlement monuments.

Animal teeth and amber stage a body politic: who may wear the forest’s brightest trophies. Engraved bone tools carry design into the hunt kit itself.
BLR.ideas:
Genomic ‘great divide’ east of early farmers. Forager political economy at continental scale. IE speech not to be projected onto Mesolithic EHG.

Keeping IE and Yamnaya labels off this slice protects chronology—EHG is ingredient, not empire. The genomic great divide east of early farmers is already a lived political economy of the hunt.
BLR.philosophy:
Lavish burials imply afterlife provisioning—tools, ornaments, animals as companions beyond death. Waterways and forest clearings structure sacred geography. Cosmology inferred from grave theatre, not hymns.

Afterlife provisioning in graves treats death as a journey needing tools—practical metaphysics in bone and bead. Forest clearings and rivers are the sacred map.
BLR.science:
Cold-forest hunting, ice-season fishing, wide lithic procurement. Early forager pottery shows ceramic chemistry without agriculture. Path knowledge as information tech across low-density space.

Ice fishing and wide lithic logistics are survival mathematics across seasons that punish the unprepared. Forager pottery, where present, proves ceramic chemistry can travel without the plough.

Ice fishing and wide lithic logistics are survival mathematics across seasons that punish the unprepared. Forager pottery, where present, proves ceramic chemistry can travel without the plough.

AZE.description:
East of the early farmer line, Eastern Hunter-Gatherer–related populations of the Volga–Don–Pontic forest-steppe kept a forager political economy with Ancient North Eurasian affinity. They are not Yamnaya yet; Yamnaya forms later when EHG-related ancestry mixes with Caucasus/Lower Volga–related groups. Linguistic Indo-European status is not Mesolithic.

Art concentrates in graves: amber, animal-tooth pendants, richly furnished burials such as at Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov. Bone and antler tools carry engraved designs; pottery appears in some eastern ‘Neolithic’ forager contexts without farming—pots without ploughs.

Mobility across forest and steppe edges linked Baltic, Volga, and Pontic zones. Path knowledge across vast low-density landscapes was the core information technology.
AZE.summary: EHG forest-steppe foragers with Ancient North Eurasian affinity—amber-rich burials, optional pottery, not yet Yamnaya or Indo-European.
AZE.culture:
Hunter-fisher identity with ceramics optional. Lavish burials imply ranked persons and afterlife provisioning. Wide-ranging lithic procurement and waterway travel structure alliance more than villages.

Rich graves imply that even low-density foragers could sustain hereditary or achieved rank loud enough to dress the dead for an audience of the living. Waterway travel and wide lithic catches structure alliance more than villages do.

Key sites: Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov cemetery; Volga–Oka and related forest forager sites; Pontic steppe-edge Mesolithic camps; Eastern forager ceramic (pre-farming) contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous ranked burial persons; no historical names.
AZE.art:
Amber, tooth pendants, engraved bone, grave theatre—prestige of the body. Aesthetic power sits in burial and adornment more than settlement monuments.

Animal teeth and amber stage a body politic: who may wear the forest’s brightest trophies. Engraved bone tools carry design into the hunt kit itself.
AZE.ideas:
Genomic ‘great divide’ east of early farmers. Forager political economy at continental scale. IE speech not to be projected onto Mesolithic EHG.

Keeping IE and Yamnaya labels off this slice protects chronology—EHG is ingredient, not empire. The genomic great divide east of early farmers is already a lived political economy of the hunt.
AZE.philosophy:
Lavish burials imply afterlife provisioning—tools, ornaments, animals as companions beyond death. Waterways and forest clearings structure sacred geography. Cosmology inferred from grave theatre, not hymns.

Afterlife provisioning in graves treats death as a journey needing tools—practical metaphysics in bone and bead. Forest clearings and rivers are the sacred map.

periods.label: First farmers on two corridors
periods.narrative: By the mid-sixth millennium BC Anatolian-related farmers push into Europe by sea (Cardial/Impresso) and up the Danube (Starčevo–LBK). Early farmer genomes are strongly EEF; local hunter-gatherers persist as Ertebølle holdouts in the north and Narva–Comb Ware farther east. This is demic farming spread, not a pan-European ethnic conversion — and still centuries before steppe ancestry.
periods.culturesNote: Cardial, Impresso, LBK, Starčevo–Vinča + HG holdouts (Ertebølle, Narva/Comb Ware, EHG persistence).

iberia.culture:
Household and herd replaced band and seasonal round as the basic social unit. Labour focused on clearing, sowing, milking, and potting; kinship likely organised land clearance and livestock inheritance even without written law. Pioneer settlements hugged coasts and river mouths where maritime logistics and Mediterranean crops worked best.

Identity advertised itself on ceramic surfaces—shell-stamped pots as badges of belonging. Interaction with foragers ranged from exchange and intermarriage (minor early) to spatial segregation; genomes show replacement first, admixture later.

Key sites: Early Cardial sites of Catalonia and Valencia; Andalusian Early Neolithic coastal settlements; Portuguese Estremadura Early Neolithic; Cova de l’Or / related impressed-ware caves (regional exemplars).

Key people / anonymity: No named historical persons. ‘Cardial’ is an archaeological ware label, not a polity or prophet.
iberia.description:
By the mid–sixth millennium BCE, Mediterranean pioneer farmers reached Iberia by boat. Cardial/Impresso pottery—rims and bodies stamped with cockle-shell edges—marks a littoral leapfrog from Catalonia and Valencia toward Portugal’s Atlantic fringe. Villages, storage, polished axes, and domestic sheep and goat arrived as a package with people whose genomes cluster with Anatolian Neolithic–related Early European Farmers (EEF). Early farmer WHG ancestry was low; the peninsula’s forager majority was demically sidelined along the coasts first.

This was not yet a Meseta-wide farming law. Inland WHG neighbours remained, and pioneer colonisation implies planned landings and rapid coastal leaps more than slow village creep from a single hearth. Caves and open deposits still held burials; ornament stayed personal (shell, stone) rather than megalithic. The visual and social language of Iberia shifted from forager portables to household ceramics within a few centuries of contact.

Linguistically, Cardial speech is unrecoverable and should not be equated with later Basque or Iberian. Genetically, early Iberian farmers often model ~85–95% EEF—the first Holocene replacement layer that Middle Neolithic megalith builders would inherit and partly remix with returning WHG ancestry.
iberia.ancestryNote: Early Iberian farmers ≈ 85–95% EEF in published models; WHG minority.
iberia.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE farmer language(s). Not ancestral Basque or Iberian by evidence — those are later attestations.
iberia.art:
Cardial impressed ware is the signature aesthetic: cockle-edge stamps marching around rims, polished stone axes, and simple clay figurines. The forager portable world yields to the daily visual environment of the settled household. Burial mixes caves and open deposits; prestige stays small-scale until later megalithic theatre.

Compared with later plaque idols, Early Neolithic ornament is intimate—beads at the throat, stamps on the cooking pot—identity at arm’s length from the hearth.
iberia.ideas:
The transformative idea is the village package carried by sea—seed corn, livestock, clay recipes, and fixed houses. Coastal leapfrogging treats the Mediterranean and Atlantic fringe as a single maritime frontier. Farming is a littoral claim that will take generations to become peninsula-wide practice.

Pioneer risk management matters: which cove holds fresh water, which slope takes barley, which forager band must be gifted around rather than fought.
iberia.philosophy:
Domesticated plants and animals reorder the sacred: hearths, storage pits, and household burials locate fertility and ancestry inside the settlement. Shell-stamped pots may mark group identity as much as kitchen use. Cosmology stays oral; archaeology catches ritual around food, death, and the new domestic animals—not named philosophical schools.

Storage pits become moral objects; to steal grain is to wound a household’s future in a way deer theft never quite matched.
iberia.science:
Seafaring farmers moved seed, livestock, and pottery recipes across open water—maritime logistics as enabling technology. They tuned Mediterranean crops to thin coastal soils while learning Iberian rainfall and wild resources. Flint and polished-stone toolkits standardised woodworking and field clearance.

Kill-off patterns in sheep and goat bones show herders learning Iberian forage calendars within a few generations of landfall.
iberia.summary: Seafaring Anatolian-related farmers bring cereals, sheep, and shell-stamped pottery along Iberia’s Mediterranean and Atlantic littoral, largely replacing WHG ancestry.

stories.text: A farmer presses a Cardium shell into wet clay and fires a pot that will still speak, millennia later, of a maritime identity. The kitchen vessel becomes a coastal passport.
stories.title: Cockle Edges on Clay

stories.text: Boats carry sheep, seed, and potters past forager beaches in jumps, not a slow green tide. Each landing rewrites a cove’s demography before the interior even hears of cereal.
stories.title: Leapfrog Landings

stories.text: Inland, WHG bands continue deer rounds while coastal villages store grain. For a time Iberia is two economies sharing one peninsula—replacement on the shore, persistence behind the hills.
stories.title: Neighbours Still Hunt

britain.culture:
Fixed houses, herds, and cereal stores reorganised kinship around land and livestock. Timber halls and early monuments imply communal labour and feasting politics. Enclosures gathered people for rites and negotiation—soft regional institutions without kings we can name.

Timber halls and interrupted-ditch enclosures concentrate labour debts and feast obligations; Neolithic society learns to schedule people as carefully as seed.

Key sites: Early Neolithic houses and halls (e.g. Irish rectangular house horizons); Southern British causewayed enclosures (Windmill Hill tradition); Early long barrows of Wessex and the Cotswolds; Carinated Bowl pottery assemblages.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous pioneer farmers; no attested leaders.
britain.description:
Farming reached Britain after the continental Early Neolithic was already mature. When established, Neolithic Britons were strongly Anatolian farmer–related (EEF), a demic replacement of Mesolithic WHG that aDNA makes unusually stark. Pottery, polished axes, cereals, cattle, and eventually earthen long barrows arrived as a continental-derived package adapted to island stone and timber. Ireland’s secure house-and-cereal horizons slightly lag some British footprints but join the same Atlantic farmer conversation.

Causewayed-enclosure thinking—gathering, feasting, boundary—began to organise regional identity even before the great stone theatres of the later Neolithic. WHG ancestry survived higher at some Atlantic edges than in pioneer cores, but the overall mode was replacement.

This farmer gene pool would itself be largely overturned in the Beaker age (~2500 BCE). Early Neolithic speech was unknown and non-IE in any evidenced sense; later Celtic languages are not continuous with it by default.
britain.ancestryNote: Earliest farming Britain: EEF-led; WHG higher at Atlantic edges than in pioneer cores.
britain.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE. The later Celtic languages are not this Neolithic speech.

ancestryCline.label: Core pioneer → Atlantic edge
ancestryCline.note: WHG% higher where farmers meet residual foragers; EEF highest in early pioneer packages.

britain.art:
Carinated bowls, polished axes, and early chambered tombs / long barrows sketch a new visual package after millennia of forager portables. Art is still mostly functional and funerary; Orkney–Wessex stone theatre peaks later.

Long barrows and early chambers are architecture-as-sculpture: white chalk spoil and dark timber façades announce lineage before stone circles mature.
britain.ideas: The transformative idea is demic farming: cereals, cattle, and fixed houses arrive with people who largely replace Mesolithic ancestry. Causewayed-enclosure thinking—gathering, feasting, boundary—begins to organise regional identity. Ireland’s secure house-and-cereal horizons slightly lag Britain’s earliest footprints but join the same Atlantic farmer conversation.
britain.philosophy:
Ancestors move underground into long mounds and early chambers; fertility and lineage attach to monuments and herds. Ritual is deposition, animal offering, and communal gathering—the shift from mobile forager ethics to landed, heritable place.

Putting ancestors under long mounds invents a moral geography of ‘our dead under our hill’ that forager camps rarely made permanent.
britain.science:
Imported crops meet Atlantic clay and chalk; farmers learn what thrives. Forest clearance, timber halls, and early axe-stone quarrying (foreshadowing Langdale) are landscape science. Seacraft underwrites colonisation—boats as enabling technology.

Soil and rainfall lessons are harsh tutors; failed clearances and successful cattle herds both leave pollen and isotope signatures.
britain.summary: Continental-derived farming reaches Britain and Ireland with strongly EEF genomes—the first major replacement of insular WHG—before later megalith florescence.

stories.text: Boats bring not only seed but lowing animals to island shores. The soundscape of Britain changes from deer and gull to herd and dog within generations.
stories.title: Cattle on the Beach

stories.text: Mesolithic WHG lineages that survived Doggerland’s drowning largely do not survive the farmers’ fields—a genomic silence sharper than any battle poem.
stories.title: The Interrupted Hunt

stories.text: Communities dig interrupted ditches and feast on cattle. The enclosure is temporary city and treaty ground—politics before stone circles.

france.culture:
Two ceramic-and-house traditions meant two social dialects of farming meeting in Gaul. Household and enclosure began to replace pure seasonal round. Burial rites diverged—Cardial caves and open deposits versus LBK cemetery rows—encoding different ideas of person and kin.

Where Cardial and LBK spheres approach, households may have recognised strangers by pot and house form before by speech—material dialect as social sorting.

Key sites: Mediterranean Cardial sites of Provence/Languedoc; LBK-related settlements of Alsace / Paris Basin northeast; Early Alpine jadeitite axe findspots in Gaul; Loess-terrace Early Neolithic villages.

Key people / anonymity: No named persons; ‘Cardial’ and ‘LBK’ are archaeological packages.
france.description:
Early Neolithic France was Europe’s hinge where maritime pioneer farming and the Danube corridor almost touched. Cardial impressed ware lit southern and western coasts while LBK-related banded pottery and longhouses entered the northeast. Both streams were EEF-rich demic spreads that replaced most local hunter-gatherer ancestry, with WHG admixture rising through the Middle Neolithic.

West-of-Rhine communities often mixed more local HG ancestry into farmer lives than some eastern LBK extremes—an idea of coexistence written in genomes as much as pots. Settlement chose loess, river terraces, and coastal enclaves rather than a uniform carpet.

Farmer languages are unknown; Gaulish Celtic appears only in the Iron Age record millennia later.
france.linguisticNote: Unknown farmer languages; Gaulish Celtic is ~4000+ years later.
france.ancestryNote: Early farmers ~EEF; WHG admixture increases through Middle Neolithic.
france.art:
Shell-stamp littoral ware versus Danubian linear pottery: rival visual languages. Early figurines and polished axes travel with both streams; Alpine axe stone already sketches future megalith routes.

Rival ceramic languages make Early Neolithic Gaul a visual borderland; axes of Alpine greenstone already glint as shared prestige across that border.
france.ideas:
Hinge geography: sea pioneers and loess colonists almost meet. Coexistence and admixture west of the Rhine complicate any simple replacement cartoon. Settlement ecology—loess, terrace, coast—selects where farming sticks.

Hinge geography trains communities in pluralism: farming arrives twice, with different house morals and burial grammars.
france.philosophy: Household and enclosure begin to replace pure seasonal round as sacred centres. Burial rites diverge by tradition—Cardial caves and open deposits versus LBK cemetery rows—encoding different ideas of person and kin. Cosmology remains oral; archaeology catches practice at the grave and the hearth.
france.science: Farmers transplant Near Eastern crops into Atlantic and continental climates, learning frost, rainfall, and soil the hard way. Longhouse carpentry and Cardial kiln-less pottery are parallel technical schools. Early exchange of Alpine axe stone already sketches the routes later megalith builders will intensify.
france.summary: France as hinge: Mediterranean Cardial along the littoral and Danubian LBK influence in the northeast—two EEF streams replacing most WHG.

stories.text: A shell-stamped bowl from the sea and a banded LBK pot from the loess can lie a few valleys apart. France learns farming in stereo.
stories.title: Two Potteries Meet

central.culture:
Longhouse villages invent agrarian social architecture: aDNA often supports patrilocal kinship, cattle wealth, and rapid fission-colonisation. Cemeteries stage gendered tool kits. Crisis centuries reveal massacre and ritualised processing of bodies as dark limits of community.

Patrilocal signals in aDNA, if read cautiously, align with longhouse politics where in-marrying women joined cattle-rich timber lineages—and where late massacres show how brittle that order could become.

Key sites: Bylany and classic Bohemian/Moravian LBK settlements; Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten massacre sites; Herxheim ritual enclosure; Loess-belt longhouse villages of the Rhine–Danube corridors.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous villagers and victims of late LBK massacres; no royal names.
central.description:
The Linear Pottery Culture (LBK, ~5500–4900 BCE) is the textbook Central European Early Neolithic: vast timber longhouses, banded pottery, shoe-last adzes, and rapid colonisation of loess. Genomes are strongly Anatolian farmer–related; initial hunter-gatherer admixture is limited and rises later. Eastern and western LBK diverge in HG ancestry—same pottery brand, different genetic histories.

Spondylus shell ornaments from the Mediterranean show prestige chains hundreds of kilometres long. Late LBK violence—massacres at Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten—and Herxheim’s ritual deposits show belonging turning violently exclusive. This world is not ‘Celtic’ or ‘Germanic’; those labels belong to much later ages.

Language is unknown and widely assumed non-IE under steppe-IE models.
central.ancestryNote: Early LBK cores often >85% EEF; WHG rises later in Mid–Late Neolithic.
central.linguisticNote: Unknown; widely assumed non-IE under steppe-IE models.

ancestryCline.label: LBK core → northern contact
ancestryCline.note: WHG higher toward northern/forest contact; EEF highest in loess LBK heartland.

central.art: Banded pottery—incised linear and spiral motifs on fine ware—and vast timber longhouses define the central European look. Clay figurines, shoe-last adzes, and Spondylus shell ornaments from the Mediterranean are prestige art inside an otherwise agrarian aesthetic. Cemeteries stage bodies with gendered tool kits as social portraiture.
central.ideas: The longhouse village invents a new social architecture: patrilocal kinship (aDNA), cattle wealth, and rapid colonisation of loess. Eastern and western LBK diverge in hunter-gatherer ancestry—same pottery brand, different genetic histories. Late LBK massacres (Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten) and Herxheim’s ritual deposits show ideas of belonging turning violently exclusive.
central.philosophy:
Row-grave cemeteries and household practice locate ancestors beside the living; fertility attaches to cattle and grain. Herxheim’s skull-cap rites imply a dark theology of processing the dead—or the stranger—as ritual theatre. Communal and bodily, not textual.

Herxheim and the massacre pits force a hard inference: Neolithic sacred order could include the ritualised unmaking of persons.
central.science:
Emmer, einkorn, barley, pulses, and cattle on loess with geographic consistency. Longhouse joinery across generations. Pottery, flint mines, and Spondylus logistics as early systems science.

Loess agronomy’s geographic consistency is itself a technology transfer success story—package knowledge moving with people.
central.summary: Classic Central European Early Neolithic: longhouses, Linearbandkeramik pottery, loess pioneer farming—strongly EEF, not Celtic or Germanic.

scandinavia.culture:
Shell middens double as ancestral places—refuse that is also memory. Marine mammal hunting and oyster seasons structure prestige and diet. Contact with LBK/TRB south is wary and porous.

Ertebølle communities can adopt pots and still refuse villages; identity is chosen package by package at the farmer contact zone. Shell middens remain the public monuments of a people who will not yet surrender the sea.

Key sites: Ertebølle and Bjørnsholm-type shell middens; Danish straits coastal forager settlements; Earliest TRB farming footholds in southern Scandinavia; Pointed-base pottery type assemblages.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous Ertebølle fishers and earliest TRB pioneers.
scandinavia.description:
In the later Mesolithic / earliest Neolithic contact centuries, Ertebølle communities of Danish and south Swedish coasts remained demographic majority: thick shell middens, seal and fish economies, and pointed-base pottery among Europe’s earliest northern ceramics—pottery without full farming. They negotiated exchange and occasional violence with southern farmers while defending coastal lifeways.

Genetics show SHG/WHG holdouts beside rising EEF as earliest Funnelbeaker (TRB) farming appears in the south. The first Holocene turnover is beginning, not finished. ‘Becoming Neolithic’ here is delayed, chosen, and uneven—not automatic.

Language shift likely accompanies farming eventually; details unknowable and not Old Norse.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Ertebølle holdout still strong; earliest TRB farmers only beginning the first Holocene turnover.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Language shift likely with farming; details unknowable. Not Old Norse.

ancestryCline.label: Forager coast → earliest TRB farms
ancestryCline.note: SHG/WHG dominate Ertebølle coasts; EEF rises where earliest Funnelbeaker farming sticks.

scandinavia.art:
Pointed-base Ertebølle pottery, bone combs, antler tools, marine mammal motifs—last-forager style at the edge of the farmer world.

Pointed-base pottery looks awkward beside LBK bowls yet perfect for beach sands—form following forager use. Bone combs and antler gear keep an aquatic body aesthetic beside the new clay.
scandinavia.ideas:
Ceramics for seal fat and fish, not yet a full Neolithic package. Identity can adopt clay without adopting the plough. Negotiation replaces inevitability.

Delayed Neolithisation is an intellectual stance: the south’s ‘progress’ is optional when the sea still feeds you. Exchange with farmers can enrich a forager toolkit without rewriting forager law.
scandinavia.philosophy:
Marine animals remain central spirit partners even as pots enter daily life. Middens as ancestral monuments of shell. Worldview resists grain-and-cattle sacred order until TRB centuries deepen.

Middens as ancestor hills keep forager sacredness legible even as clay enters the ritual kit. Marine animals remain partners in a moral world grain has not yet conquered.
scandinavia.science:
Peak coastal ecology expertise: oysters, seals, fish, wild plants timed to Baltic seasons. Early ceramics require tempering and firing knowledge at the farmer contact zone. Boat craft still underwrites economy.

Oyster and seal seasonality remain sharper sciences than early cereal trials on thin northern soils. Ceramic firing is borrowed or invented at the contact edge without importing the full agro-package.
scandinavia.summary: Ertebølle coastal foragers keep SHG ways and invent northern pottery while earliest Funnelbeaker farming only begins the first Holocene turnover.

italy.culture:
Villages redefine land as fields and pastures; forager edges persist in mountains. Household shrines and figurines locate the sacred in domestic space. Obsidian specialists and sailors stitch islands to coasts.

Sailors, potters, and herders form the Early Neolithic public; mountain foragers remain neighbours whose knowledge of passes still matters to anyone moving flocks. Household burials and figurines locate belonging inside the settlement rather than the seasonal camp.

Key sites: Impressed Ware coastal settlements of Apulia and Sicily; Tyrrhenian Early Neolithic villages; Lipari and related obsidian workshops; Adriatic Impressa sites facing the Balkan shore.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous maritime pioneers and obsidian knappers.
italy.description:
Impressed and Cardial-related wares announce farmer aesthetics across southern and central coasts. Italy becomes a launch corridor for Mediterranean Neolithisation—Adriatic and Tyrrhenian leapfrogs toward France and Iberia. Strong EEF signal replaces most forager ancestry; inland uptake varies. Village pottery and obsidian blades from island sources redefine daily visual life.

This farmer substrate will later be overlain by Bronze Age steppe-related ancestry and, historically, by Italic and Etruscan languages—none of which equal Impressa speech.

Sea links make the peninsula a network node, not a cul-de-sac.

Inland Apennine valleys took up farming more unevenly than the coasts, so for generations Italy held a patchwork of cereal villages, herding uplands, and residual hunting edges. That mosaic matters for later history: the peninsula’s farmer substrate is coastal-rooted, maritime-connected, and never a single uniform countryside in the earliest centuries.
italy.linguisticNote: Unknown Impresso-related farmer speech — not Latin, not Etruscan, and not recoverable from later Italic.
italy.ancestryNote: Early Italian Impresso farmers are EEF-dominated in published models; WHG is a minority that rises later.
italy.art:
Impressed and painted-band wares, clay figurines, gleaming obsidian blades—village pottery replaces forager portables as the daily visual environment.

Impressed surfaces and figurines make the house a small museum of belonging; obsidian’s gloss adds a volcanic luxury to everyday cutting. Village pottery replaces forager portables as the daily visual environment.
italy.ideas:
Italy as Neolithisation corridor. Maritime leapfrog as planned demic strategy. Farming as coastal claim with mountain lag.

Launch-corridor thinking treats Italy as a node on Mediterranean routes—success measured in landfalls farther west as much as in local fields. Adriatic and Tyrrhenian leapfrogs are planned demography, not accident.
italy.philosophy:
Domestic shrines, figurines, and burial under or near houses. Fertility of crops and herds structures ritual calendars. Practised covenants with land and dead—no philosophy schools.

Burial near houses folds the dead into domestic fertility; the sacred is under the floor and beside the grain. No philosophy schools—only practised covenants with land, herd, and ancestor.
italy.science:
Island obsidian specialised production and distribution as measurable early industry. Crop tuning from Po fringe to Sicily. Boat-building and coastal pilotage enable Impressa expansion.

Obsidian sourcing (Lipari and kin) is archaeology’s proof that sailors already ran mental maps of island vents with commercial precision. Crop tuning from Sicily to the Po fringe is agronomic R&D under one maritime brand.
italy.summary: Maritime Impressed Ware farming along Italian coasts—EEF demic replacement and launch corridor toward France and Iberia.

balkans.culture:
Tell living stacks generations—the past literally underfoot. Household cults centre figurines; ritual pits and house burnings suggest cyclical renewal. Craft and farming specialisation grow with settlement scale.

Tell neighbours stack obligations vertically: rebuilding on ancestors’ rubble is both practical and moral continuity. Figurine-rich households make ritual labour a daily chore, not a rare pilgrimage.

Key sites: Starčevo type sites; Körös and Criș settlement zones of the Carpathian Basin edge; Early Vinča tell settlements; Iron Gates contact-period mixed horizons.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous tell villagers and figurine makers.
balkans.description:
The Balkans are the demic bridge from Anatolia into Europe—farming’s first European idea factory. Starčevo–Körös–Criș and early Vinča tell settlements carry Anatolian-related farmers who mix more visibly with distinctive local HG (Iron Gates) than some early western LBK groups. Painted and fine polished pottery, anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figurines, and stamp seals fill villages with a crowded visual theology of clay bodies.

From here Cardial and LBK streams will diverge, carrying Balkan-tempered farmer culture west and north. Village life, storage, and cattle reorganise kinship and labour.

Languages are unknown Starčevo/Vinča-related speech; Ancient Greek is still far future and unrelated by attestation.
balkans.linguisticNote: Unknown Starčevo/Vinča-related languages. Ancient Greek is still far in the future and unrelated by attestation.
balkans.ancestryNote: EEF majority + elevated local HG vs early LBK extremes.
balkans.art:
Earth-toned Starčevo wares; early Vinča darkening and sophisticating surfaces; dense figurine worlds; stamp seals. Houses accumulate art as stratified memory.

Figurine crowds and stamp seals fill domestic space with watching clay—art as constant company, not festival rarity. Starčevo earth tones and early Vinča polish chart a rising craft ambition.
balkans.ideas:
Balkans as bridge and splitter of Neolithic streams. Elevated HG admixture as regional signature. Tells as vertical archives of belonging.

As the splitter of Cardial and LBK streams, the Balkans invent Europe’s two Neolithic accents from one Anatolian-related root. Elevated local HG admixture is a regional signature, not a footnote.
balkans.philosophy:
Figurines—often female, sometimes ambiguous—point to household cults of fertility, protection, or ancestor presence without proving a single ‘mother goddess’ church. House burnings and ritual pits suggest cyclical renewal rites for buildings as well as people.

House-burning rites, where present, suggest buildings have life-cycles demanding funerary attention. Female and ambiguous figurines invite fertility and protection readings without proving a single goddess church.
balkans.science:
Refining the Neolithic package for European latitudes—crops, animals, mudbrick/wattle housing. Early copper ornaments as metallurgical curiosity beside stone. Pottery kilns and tell drainage as settlement engineering.

Mudbrick, wattle, and early copper trinkets show materials science diversifying faster than political centralisation. Tell drainage and kiln craft are settlement engineering at growing scale.
balkans.summary: Europe’s first farming corridor—Anatolian-related tell villages, figurines, and elevated local HG admixture versus some western LBK extremes.

eastern.culture:
Plural frontier: forager burial richness continues; farmer rites bring figurines and painted ceramics at the contact fringe. River routes (Dniester, Dnieper, Bug) are logistics backbone.

Frontier etiquette—gift, raid, marriage, avoidance—matters more than any single ‘Neolithic conversion’ sermon along the Dniester–Bug line. Forager burial richness and farmer fringe figurines can coexist for centuries.

Key sites: Comb Ware forest zone sites; Precucuteni / early Trypillia fringe settlements; Dniester–Bug river corridor contact sites; Pontic steppe forager camps contemporary with farmer fringe.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous frontier foragers and fringe farmers.
eastern.description:
While true farming paints pottery farther west, many forest-steppe groups remain forager-derived. Eastern forager ceramics (Comb Ware and related) keep comb-and-pit decoration as a forest aesthetic. On the western fringe, early Trypillia/Precucuteni painted wares begin to appear—farmer colour advancing into the forest-steppe. Two visual systems face each other across the divide.

‘Neolithic’ here often means pots, not crops—an idea that confuses later textbooks. Pontic and forest foragers coexist with approaching Balkan–Carpathian farmers for centuries. Exchange and occasional admixture happen without immediate lifestyle collapse. Pre-Yamnaya ancestry keeps EHG and CHG-related components separable; farmer fringe only on the southwest edge.

Languages are an unknown mix—not Slavic (medieval) and not yet clearly IE.
eastern.ancestryNote: Pre-Yamnaya: EHG + CHG-related kept separate (not yet fused as WSH). Farmer fringe only on the southwest edge.
eastern.linguisticNote: Unknown mix; not Slavic (medieval) and not yet clearly IE.

ancestryCline.label: Forest-steppe HG → farmer fringe
ancestryCline.note: EHG (+ some CHG-related) east of the Neolithic divide; EEF rises on Bug–Dniester contact — not WSH yet.

eastern.art: While true farming paints pottery farther west, eastern forager ceramics (Comb Ware, related) keep comb-and-pit decoration as a forest aesthetic. On the western fringe, early Trypillia/Precucuteni painted wares begin to appear—farmer colour advancing into the forest-steppe. Two visual systems face each other across the divide.
eastern.ideas:
Pots ≠ ploughs. Long coexistence without pan-eastern replacement. Rivers as contact infrastructure.

Textbook ‘Neolithic’ fails here; the east teaches that ceramic fashion and farming demography can travel on different clocks. EHG and CHG-related ancestries remain separable ingredients beside a thin EEF fringe.
eastern.philosophy:
Worldviews pluralise along the frontier—no single conversion narrative. Ancestors and animals remain central on the forager side; figurines enter at the farmer edge.

Plural sacred media on one frontier mean children could grow up hearing more than one answer to who owns the dead. Animals and ancestors still dominate forager ethics while painted pots arrive as new sacred surfaces.
eastern.science:
Forager ecological expertise persists; farmer fringe tests crops on chernozem and forest-steppe soils. Ceramic temper/firing styles mark technical schools on both sides.

Chernozem trials at the farmer fringe are high-stakes agronomy; forager fire knowledge still outperforms early ploughs in many seasons. River logistics on Dniester, Dnieper, and Bug move both ideas and spouses.
eastern.summary: East of the Neolithic genomic divide: EHG foragers and Comb Ware aesthetics meet only a western Cucuteni–Trypillia farmer fringe—not pan-eastern EEF replacement.

DEU.name: LBK pioneer villages
DEU.summary: Classic Central European Early Neolithic: longhouses, Linearbandkeramik pottery, loess pioneer farming—strongly EEF, not Celtic or Germanic.
DEU.conflicts: Expansion into forager landscapes; limited early conflict archaeologically visible as pioneer frontier.
DEU.literature: Still pre-literate in Europe. Story survives as ritual architecture and ceramic style: foundation deposits, house-burning rites, and the first farming songs we cannot hear — only the pots and longhouses that staged them. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.
DEU.art: Banded pottery—incised linear and spiral motifs on fine ware—and vast timber longhouses define the central European look. Clay figurines, shoe-last adzes, and Spondylus shell ornaments from the Mediterranean are prestige art inside an otherwise agrarian aesthetic. Cemeteries stage bodies with gendered tool kits as social portraiture.
DEU.religion: LBK farmers practiced domestic and enclosure ritual: foundation deposits, cattle offerings, and cemetery rows. Ancestor care and fertility rites are inferred; named gods are not.
DEU.ideas: The longhouse village invents a new social architecture: patrilocal kinship (aDNA), cattle wealth, and rapid colonisation of loess. Eastern and western LBK diverge in hunter-gatherer ancestry—same pottery brand, different genetic histories. Late LBK massacres (Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten) and Herxheim’s ritual deposits show ideas of belonging turning violently exclusive.
DEU.philosophy:
Row-grave cemeteries and household practice locate ancestors beside the living; fertility attaches to cattle and grain. Herxheim’s skull-cap rites imply a dark theology of processing the dead—or the stranger—as ritual theatre. Communal and bodily, not textual.

Herxheim and the massacre pits force a hard inference: Neolithic sacred order could include the ritualised unmaking of persons.
DEU.science:
Emmer, einkorn, barley, pulses, and cattle on loess with geographic consistency. Longhouse joinery across generations. Pottery, flint mines, and Spondylus logistics as early systems science.

Loess agronomy’s geographic consistency is itself a technology transfer success story—package knowledge moving with people.
DEU.culture:
Longhouse villages invent agrarian social architecture: aDNA often supports patrilocal kinship, cattle wealth, and rapid fission-colonisation. Cemeteries stage gendered tool kits. Crisis centuries reveal massacre and ritualised processing of bodies as dark limits of community.

Patrilocal signals in aDNA, if read cautiously, align with longhouse politics where in-marrying women joined cattle-rich timber lineages—and where late massacres show how brittle that order could become.

Key sites: Bylany and classic Bohemian/Moravian LBK settlements; Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten massacre sites; Herxheim ritual enclosure; Loess-belt longhouse villages of the Rhine–Danube corridors.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous villagers and victims of late LBK massacres; no royal names.
DEU.description:
The Linear Pottery Culture (LBK, ~5500–4900 BCE) is the textbook Central European Early Neolithic: vast timber longhouses, banded pottery, shoe-last adzes, and rapid colonisation of loess. Genomes are strongly Anatolian farmer–related; initial hunter-gatherer admixture is limited and rises later. Eastern and western LBK diverge in HG ancestry—same pottery brand, different genetic histories.

Spondylus shell ornaments from the Mediterranean show prestige chains hundreds of kilometres long. Late LBK violence—massacres at Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten—and Herxheim’s ritual deposits show belonging turning violently exclusive. This world is not ‘Celtic’ or ‘Germanic’; those labels belong to much later ages.

Language is unknown and widely assumed non-IE under steppe-IE models.

ESP.name: Cardial Iberia
ESP.summary: Seafaring Anatolian-related farmers bring cereals, sheep, and shell-stamped pottery along Iberia’s Mediterranean and Atlantic littoral, largely replacing WHG ancestry.
ESP.conflicts: Rapid coastal advance; WHG substrate remains minority.
ESP.literature: Still pre-literate in Europe. Story survives as ritual architecture and ceramic style: foundation deposits, house-burning rites, and the first farming songs we cannot hear — only the pots and longhouses that staged them. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art:
Cardial impressed ware is the signature aesthetic: cockle-edge stamps marching around rims, polished stone axes, and simple clay figurines. The forager portable world yields to the daily visual environment of the settled household. Burial mixes caves and open deposits; prestige stays small-scale until later megalithic theatre.

Compared with later plaque idols, Early Neolithic ornament is intimate—beads at the throat, stamps on the cooking pot—identity at arm’s length from the hearth.
ESP.religion: Cardial communities combine cave/open-air ritual with early megalithic experiments. Burial and ceramic deposits mark ancestor and place cults.
ESP.ideas:
The transformative idea is the village package carried by sea—seed corn, livestock, clay recipes, and fixed houses. Coastal leapfrogging treats the Mediterranean and Atlantic fringe as a single maritime frontier. Farming is a littoral claim that will take generations to become peninsula-wide practice.

Pioneer risk management matters: which cove holds fresh water, which slope takes barley, which forager band must be gifted around rather than fought.
ESP.philosophy:
Domesticated plants and animals reorder the sacred: hearths, storage pits, and household burials locate fertility and ancestry inside the settlement. Shell-stamped pots may mark group identity as much as kitchen use. Cosmology stays oral; archaeology catches ritual around food, death, and the new domestic animals—not named philosophical schools.

Storage pits become moral objects; to steal grain is to wound a household’s future in a way deer theft never quite matched.
ESP.science:
Seafaring farmers moved seed, livestock, and pottery recipes across open water—maritime logistics as enabling technology. They tuned Mediterranean crops to thin coastal soils while learning Iberian rainfall and wild resources. Flint and polished-stone toolkits standardised woodworking and field clearance.

Kill-off patterns in sheep and goat bones show herders learning Iberian forage calendars within a few generations of landfall.
ESP.culture:
Household and herd replaced band and seasonal round as the basic social unit. Labour focused on clearing, sowing, milking, and potting; kinship likely organised land clearance and livestock inheritance even without written law. Pioneer settlements hugged coasts and river mouths where maritime logistics and Mediterranean crops worked best.

Identity advertised itself on ceramic surfaces—shell-stamped pots as badges of belonging. Interaction with foragers ranged from exchange and intermarriage (minor early) to spatial segregation; genomes show replacement first, admixture later.

Key sites: Early Cardial sites of Catalonia and Valencia; Andalusian Early Neolithic coastal settlements; Portuguese Estremadura Early Neolithic; Cova de l’Or / related impressed-ware caves (regional exemplars).

Key people / anonymity: No named historical persons. ‘Cardial’ is an archaeological ware label, not a polity or prophet.
ESP.description:
By the mid–sixth millennium BCE, Mediterranean pioneer farmers reached Iberia by boat. Cardial/Impresso pottery—rims and bodies stamped with cockle-shell edges—marks a littoral leapfrog from Catalonia and Valencia toward Portugal’s Atlantic fringe. Villages, storage, polished axes, and domestic sheep and goat arrived as a package with people whose genomes cluster with Anatolian Neolithic–related Early European Farmers (EEF). Early farmer WHG ancestry was low; the peninsula’s forager majority was demically sidelined along the coasts first.

This was not yet a Meseta-wide farming law. Inland WHG neighbours remained, and pioneer colonisation implies planned landings and rapid coastal leaps more than slow village creep from a single hearth. Caves and open deposits still held burials; ornament stayed personal (shell, stone) rather than megalithic. The visual and social language of Iberia shifted from forager portables to household ceramics within a few centuries of contact.

Linguistically, Cardial speech is unrecoverable and should not be equated with later Basque or Iberian. Genetically, early Iberian farmers often model ~85–95% EEF—the first Holocene replacement layer that Middle Neolithic megalith builders would inherit and partly remix with returning WHG ancestry.

stories.title: Leapfrog Landings

stories.text: Inland, WHG bands continue deer rounds while coastal villages store grain. For a time Iberia is two economies sharing one peninsula—replacement on the shore, persistence behind the hills.

ITA.name: Impresso Italy
ITA.summary: Maritime Impressed Ware farming along Italian coasts—EEF demic replacement and launch corridor toward France and Iberia.
ITA.conflicts: Coastal farmer expansion vs inland foragers.
ITA.literature: Still pre-literate in Europe. Story survives as ritual architecture and ceramic style: foundation deposits, house-burning rites, and the first farming songs we cannot hear — only the pots and longhouses that staged them. Italian cities teach prestige: from Roman monumentality to Renaissance brand management of beauty.
ITA.art:
Impressed and painted-band wares, clay figurines, gleaming obsidian blades—village pottery replaces forager portables as the daily visual environment.

Impressed surfaces and figurines make the house a small museum of belonging; obsidian’s gloss adds a volcanic luxury to everyday cutting. Village pottery replaces forager portables as the daily visual environment.
ITA.religion: Impresso/Cardial Italy: household figurines, cave rites, and emerging formal cemeteries — agrarian ritual without written pantheons.
ITA.ideas:
Italy as Neolithisation corridor. Maritime leapfrog as planned demic strategy. Farming as coastal claim with mountain lag.

Launch-corridor thinking treats Italy as a node on Mediterranean routes—success measured in landfalls farther west as much as in local fields. Adriatic and Tyrrhenian leapfrogs are planned demography, not accident.
ITA.philosophy:
Domestic shrines, figurines, and burial under or near houses. Fertility of crops and herds structures ritual calendars. Practised covenants with land and dead—no philosophy schools.

Burial near houses folds the dead into domestic fertility; the sacred is under the floor and beside the grain. No philosophy schools—only practised covenants with land, herd, and ancestor.
ITA.science:
Island obsidian specialised production and distribution as measurable early industry. Crop tuning from Po fringe to Sicily. Boat-building and coastal pilotage enable Impressa expansion.

Obsidian sourcing (Lipari and kin) is archaeology’s proof that sailors already ran mental maps of island vents with commercial precision. Crop tuning from Sicily to the Po fringe is agronomic R&D under one maritime brand.
ITA.culture:
Villages redefine land as fields and pastures; forager edges persist in mountains. Household shrines and figurines locate the sacred in domestic space. Obsidian specialists and sailors stitch islands to coasts.

Sailors, potters, and herders form the Early Neolithic public; mountain foragers remain neighbours whose knowledge of passes still matters to anyone moving flocks. Household burials and figurines locate belonging inside the settlement rather than the seasonal camp.

Key sites: Impressed Ware coastal settlements of Apulia and Sicily; Tyrrhenian Early Neolithic villages; Lipari and related obsidian workshops; Adriatic Impressa sites facing the Balkan shore.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous maritime pioneers and obsidian knappers.
ITA.description:
Impressed and Cardial-related wares announce farmer aesthetics across southern and central coasts. Italy becomes a launch corridor for Mediterranean Neolithisation—Adriatic and Tyrrhenian leapfrogs toward France and Iberia. Strong EEF signal replaces most forager ancestry; inland uptake varies. Village pottery and obsidian blades from island sources redefine daily visual life.

This farmer substrate will later be overlain by Bronze Age steppe-related ancestry and, historically, by Italic and Etruscan languages—none of which equal Impressa speech.

Sea links make the peninsula a network node, not a cul-de-sac.

Inland Apennine valleys took up farming more unevenly than the coasts, so for generations Italy held a patchwork of cereal villages, herding uplands, and residual hunting edges. That mosaic matters for later history: the peninsula’s farmer substrate is coastal-rooted, maritime-connected, and never a single uniform countryside in the earliest centuries.

GRC.name: Early Greek Neolithic
GRC.summary: Europe’s first farming corridor—Anatolian-related tell villages, figurines, and elevated local HG admixture versus some western LBK extremes.
GRC.conflicts: Corridor from Anatolia; local HG admixture varies.
GRC.literature: Still pre-literate in Europe. Story survives as ritual architecture and ceramic style: foundation deposits, house-burning rites, and the first farming songs we cannot hear — only the pots and longhouses that staged them. Greek language and forms remain a reusable antiquity — quarried by every later age for prestige.
GRC.art:
Earth-toned Starčevo wares; early Vinča darkening and sophisticating surfaces; dense figurine worlds; stamp seals. Houses accumulate art as stratified memory.

Figurine crowds and stamp seals fill domestic space with watching clay—art as constant company, not festival rarity. Starčevo earth tones and early Vinča polish chart a rising craft ambition.
GRC.religion: Early Greek Neolithic villages use figurines, hearth/house deposits, and cemetery rites. Later Olympian names must not be read back into this phase.
GRC.ideas:
Balkans as bridge and splitter of Neolithic streams. Elevated HG admixture as regional signature. Tells as vertical archives of belonging.

As the splitter of Cardial and LBK streams, the Balkans invent Europe’s two Neolithic accents from one Anatolian-related root. Elevated local HG admixture is a regional signature, not a footnote.
GRC.philosophy:
Figurines—often female, sometimes ambiguous—point to household cults of fertility, protection, or ancestor presence without proving a single ‘mother goddess’ church. House burnings and ritual pits suggest cyclical renewal rites for buildings as well as people.

House-burning rites, where present, suggest buildings have life-cycles demanding funerary attention. Female and ambiguous figurines invite fertility and protection readings without proving a single goddess church.
GRC.science:
Refining the Neolithic package for European latitudes—crops, animals, mudbrick/wattle housing. Early copper ornaments as metallurgical curiosity beside stone. Pottery kilns and tell drainage as settlement engineering.

Mudbrick, wattle, and early copper trinkets show materials science diversifying faster than political centralisation. Tell drainage and kiln craft are settlement engineering at growing scale.
GRC.culture:
Tell living stacks generations—the past literally underfoot. Household cults centre figurines; ritual pits and house burnings suggest cyclical renewal. Craft and farming specialisation grow with settlement scale.

Tell neighbours stack obligations vertically: rebuilding on ancestors’ rubble is both practical and moral continuity. Figurine-rich households make ritual labour a daily chore, not a rare pilgrimage.

Key sites: Starčevo type sites; Körös and Criș settlement zones of the Carpathian Basin edge; Early Vinča tell settlements; Iron Gates contact-period mixed horizons.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous tell villagers and figurine makers.
GRC.description:
The Balkans are the demic bridge from Anatolia into Europe—farming’s first European idea factory. Starčevo–Körös–Criș and early Vinča tell settlements carry Anatolian-related farmers who mix more visibly with distinctive local HG (Iron Gates) than some early western LBK groups. Painted and fine polished pottery, anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figurines, and stamp seals fill villages with a crowded visual theology of clay bodies.

From here Cardial and LBK streams will diverge, carrying Balkan-tempered farmer culture west and north. Village life, storage, and cattle reorganise kinship and labour.

Languages are unknown Starčevo/Vinča-related speech; Ancient Greek is still far future and unrelated by attestation.

DNK.name: Ertebølle vs earliest TRB
DNK.summary: Ertebølle coastal foragers keep SHG ways and invent northern pottery while earliest Funnelbeaker farming only begins the first Holocene turnover.
DNK.conflicts: Classic contact frontier before farmer dominance.
DNK.literature: Still pre-literate in Europe. Story survives as ritual architecture and ceramic style: foundation deposits, house-burning rites, and the first farming songs we cannot hear — only the pots and longhouses that staged them. Danish gatekeeping of the Baltic Sound makes culture a toll-booth as well as a stage.
DNK.art:
Pointed-base Ertebølle pottery, bone combs, antler tools, marine mammal motifs—last-forager style at the edge of the farmer world.

Pointed-base pottery looks awkward beside LBK bowls yet perfect for beach sands—form following forager use. Bone combs and antler gear keep an aquatic body aesthetic beside the new clay.
DNK.religion: Ertebølle holdouts keep forager burial/wetland rites beside earliest TRB farmer ceremonies — two ritual regimes in contact, not one creed.
DNK.ideas:
Ceramics for seal fat and fish, not yet a full Neolithic package. Identity can adopt clay without adopting the plough. Negotiation replaces inevitability.

Delayed Neolithisation is an intellectual stance: the south’s ‘progress’ is optional when the sea still feeds you. Exchange with farmers can enrich a forager toolkit without rewriting forager law.
DNK.philosophy:
Marine animals remain central spirit partners even as pots enter daily life. Middens as ancestral monuments of shell. Worldview resists grain-and-cattle sacred order until TRB centuries deepen.

Middens as ancestor hills keep forager sacredness legible even as clay enters the ritual kit. Marine animals remain partners in a moral world grain has not yet conquered.
DNK.science:
Peak coastal ecology expertise: oysters, seals, fish, wild plants timed to Baltic seasons. Early ceramics require tempering and firing knowledge at the farmer contact zone. Boat craft still underwrites economy.

Oyster and seal seasonality remain sharper sciences than early cereal trials on thin northern soils. Ceramic firing is borrowed or invented at the contact edge without importing the full agro-package.
DNK.culture:
Shell middens double as ancestral places—refuse that is also memory. Marine mammal hunting and oyster seasons structure prestige and diet. Contact with LBK/TRB south is wary and porous.

Ertebølle communities can adopt pots and still refuse villages; identity is chosen package by package at the farmer contact zone. Shell middens remain the public monuments of a people who will not yet surrender the sea.

Key sites: Ertebølle and Bjørnsholm-type shell middens; Danish straits coastal forager settlements; Earliest TRB farming footholds in southern Scandinavia; Pointed-base pottery type assemblages.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous Ertebølle fishers and earliest TRB pioneers.
DNK.description:
In the later Mesolithic / earliest Neolithic contact centuries, Ertebølle communities of Danish and south Swedish coasts remained demographic majority: thick shell middens, seal and fish economies, and pointed-base pottery among Europe’s earliest northern ceramics—pottery without full farming. They negotiated exchange and occasional violence with southern farmers while defending coastal lifeways.

Genetics show SHG/WHG holdouts beside rising EEF as earliest Funnelbeaker (TRB) farming appears in the south. The first Holocene turnover is beginning, not finished. ‘Becoming Neolithic’ here is delayed, chosen, and uneven—not automatic.

Language shift likely accompanies farming eventually; details unknowable and not Old Norse.

GBR.name: Earliest Neolithic arrival
GBR.summary: Continental-derived farming reaches Britain and Ireland with strongly EEF genomes—the first major replacement of insular WHG—before later megalith florescence.
GBR.conflicts: First major replacement of Mesolithic WHG.
GBR.literature: Still pre-literate in Europe. Story survives as ritual architecture and ceramic style: foundation deposits, house-burning rites, and the first farming songs we cannot hear — only the pots and longhouses that staged them. Insular voices and North Sea contact give this place a distinctive accent in the wider European chorus.
GBR.art:
Carinated bowls, polished axes, and early chambered tombs / long barrows sketch a new visual package after millennia of forager portables. Art is still mostly functional and funerary; Orkney–Wessex stone theatre peaks later.

Long barrows and early chambers are architecture-as-sculpture: white chalk spoil and dark timber façades announce lineage before stone circles mature.
GBR.religion: Earliest Neolithic Britain imports chambered-tomb and causewayed-enclosure rites: collective burial, feasting debris, and seasonal gathering places.
GBR.ideas: The transformative idea is demic farming: cereals, cattle, and fixed houses arrive with people who largely replace Mesolithic ancestry. Causewayed-enclosure thinking—gathering, feasting, boundary—begins to organise regional identity. Ireland’s secure house-and-cereal horizons slightly lag Britain’s earliest footprints but join the same Atlantic farmer conversation.
GBR.philosophy:
Ancestors move underground into long mounds and early chambers; fertility and lineage attach to monuments and herds. Ritual is deposition, animal offering, and communal gathering—the shift from mobile forager ethics to landed, heritable place.

Putting ancestors under long mounds invents a moral geography of ‘our dead under our hill’ that forager camps rarely made permanent.
GBR.science:
Imported crops meet Atlantic clay and chalk; farmers learn what thrives. Forest clearance, timber halls, and early axe-stone quarrying (foreshadowing Langdale) are landscape science. Seacraft underwrites colonisation—boats as enabling technology.

Soil and rainfall lessons are harsh tutors; failed clearances and successful cattle herds both leave pollen and isotope signatures.
GBR.culture:
Fixed houses, herds, and cereal stores reorganised kinship around land and livestock. Timber halls and early monuments imply communal labour and feasting politics. Enclosures gathered people for rites and negotiation—soft regional institutions without kings we can name.

Timber halls and interrupted-ditch enclosures concentrate labour debts and feast obligations; Neolithic society learns to schedule people as carefully as seed.

Key sites: Early Neolithic houses and halls (e.g. Irish rectangular house horizons); Southern British causewayed enclosures (Windmill Hill tradition); Early long barrows of Wessex and the Cotswolds; Carinated Bowl pottery assemblages.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous pioneer farmers; no attested leaders.
GBR.description:
Farming reached Britain after the continental Early Neolithic was already mature. When established, Neolithic Britons were strongly Anatolian farmer–related (EEF), a demic replacement of Mesolithic WHG that aDNA makes unusually stark. Pottery, polished axes, cereals, cattle, and eventually earthen long barrows arrived as a continental-derived package adapted to island stone and timber. Ireland’s secure house-and-cereal horizons slightly lag some British footprints but join the same Atlantic farmer conversation.

Causewayed-enclosure thinking—gathering, feasting, boundary—began to organise regional identity even before the great stone theatres of the later Neolithic. WHG ancestry survived higher at some Atlantic edges than in pioneer cores, but the overall mode was replacement.

This farmer gene pool would itself be largely overturned in the Beaker age (~2500 BCE). Early Neolithic speech was unknown and non-IE in any evidenced sense; later Celtic languages are not continuous with it by default.

UKR.name: Bug–Dniester / farmer fringe
UKR.summary: East of the Neolithic genomic divide: EHG foragers and Comb Ware aesthetics meet only a western Cucuteni–Trypillia farmer fringe—not pan-eastern EEF replacement.
UKR.literature: Still pre-literate in Europe. Story survives as ritual architecture and ceramic style: foundation deposits, house-burning rites, and the first farming songs we cannot hear — only the pots and longhouses that staged them. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: While true farming paints pottery farther west, eastern forager ceramics (Comb Ware, related) keep comb-and-pit decoration as a forest aesthetic. On the western fringe, early Trypillia/Precucuteni painted wares begin to appear—farmer colour advancing into the forest-steppe. Two visual systems face each other across the divide.
UKR.religion: Bug–Dniester / farmer-fringe ritual mixes forager burial habits with incoming agrarian figurines and domestic deposits along the contact zone.
UKR.ideas:
Pots ≠ ploughs. Long coexistence without pan-eastern replacement. Rivers as contact infrastructure.

Textbook ‘Neolithic’ fails here; the east teaches that ceramic fashion and farming demography can travel on different clocks. EHG and CHG-related ancestries remain separable ingredients beside a thin EEF fringe.
UKR.philosophy:
Worldviews pluralise along the frontier—no single conversion narrative. Ancestors and animals remain central on the forager side; figurines enter at the farmer edge.

Plural sacred media on one frontier mean children could grow up hearing more than one answer to who owns the dead. Animals and ancestors still dominate forager ethics while painted pots arrive as new sacred surfaces.
UKR.science:
Forager ecological expertise persists; farmer fringe tests crops on chernozem and forest-steppe soils. Ceramic temper/firing styles mark technical schools on both sides.

Chernozem trials at the farmer fringe are high-stakes agronomy; forager fire knowledge still outperforms early ploughs in many seasons. River logistics on Dniester, Dnieper, and Bug move both ideas and spouses.
UKR.culture:
Plural frontier: forager burial richness continues; farmer rites bring figurines and painted ceramics at the contact fringe. River routes (Dniester, Dnieper, Bug) are logistics backbone.

Frontier etiquette—gift, raid, marriage, avoidance—matters more than any single ‘Neolithic conversion’ sermon along the Dniester–Bug line. Forager burial richness and farmer fringe figurines can coexist for centuries.

Key sites: Comb Ware forest zone sites; Precucuteni / early Trypillia fringe settlements; Dniester–Bug river corridor contact sites; Pontic steppe forager camps contemporary with farmer fringe.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous frontier foragers and fringe farmers.
UKR.description:
While true farming paints pottery farther west, many forest-steppe groups remain forager-derived. Eastern forager ceramics (Comb Ware and related) keep comb-and-pit decoration as a forest aesthetic. On the western fringe, early Trypillia/Precucuteni painted wares begin to appear—farmer colour advancing into the forest-steppe. Two visual systems face each other across the divide.

‘Neolithic’ here often means pots, not crops—an idea that confuses later textbooks. Pontic and forest foragers coexist with approaching Balkan–Carpathian farmers for centuries. Exchange and occasional admixture happen without immediate lifestyle collapse. Pre-Yamnaya ancestry keeps EHG and CHG-related components separable; farmer fringe only on the southwest edge.

Languages are an unknown mix—not Slavic (medieval) and not yet clearly IE.
