PRT.description:
By the mid–sixth millennium BCE, Mediterranean pioneer farmers reached Iberia by boat. Cardial/Impresso pottery—rims and bodies stamped with cockle-shell edges—marks a littoral leapfrog from Catalonia and Valencia toward Portugal’s Atlantic fringe. Villages, storage, polished axes, and domestic sheep and goat arrived as a package with people whose genomes cluster with Anatolian Neolithic–related Early European Farmers (EEF). Early farmer WHG ancestry was low; the peninsula’s forager majority was demically sidelined along the coasts first.

This was not yet a Meseta-wide farming law. Inland WHG neighbours remained, and pioneer colonisation implies planned landings and rapid coastal leaps more than slow village creep from a single hearth. Caves and open deposits still held burials; ornament stayed personal (shell, stone) rather than megalithic. The visual and social language of Iberia shifted from forager portables to household ceramics within a few centuries of contact.

Linguistically, Cardial speech is unrecoverable and should not be equated with later Basque or Iberian. Genetically, early Iberian farmers often model ~85–95% EEF—the first Holocene replacement layer that Middle Neolithic megalith builders would inherit and partly remix with returning WHG ancestry.
PRT.summary: Seafaring Anatolian-related farmers bring cereals, sheep, and shell-stamped pottery along Iberia’s Mediterranean and Atlantic littoral, largely replacing WHG ancestry.
PRT.culture:
Household and herd replaced band and seasonal round as the basic social unit. Labour focused on clearing, sowing, milking, and potting; kinship likely organised land clearance and livestock inheritance even without written law. Pioneer settlements hugged coasts and river mouths where maritime logistics and Mediterranean crops worked best.

Identity advertised itself on ceramic surfaces—shell-stamped pots as badges of belonging. Interaction with foragers ranged from exchange and intermarriage (minor early) to spatial segregation; genomes show replacement first, admixture later.

Key sites: Early Cardial sites of Catalonia and Valencia; Andalusian Early Neolithic coastal settlements; Portuguese Estremadura Early Neolithic; Cova de l’Or / related impressed-ware caves (regional exemplars).

Key people / anonymity: No named historical persons. ‘Cardial’ is an archaeological ware label, not a polity or prophet.
PRT.art:
Cardial impressed ware is the signature aesthetic: cockle-edge stamps marching around rims, polished stone axes, and simple clay figurines. The forager portable world yields to the daily visual environment of the settled household. Burial mixes caves and open deposits; prestige stays small-scale until later megalithic theatre.

Compared with later plaque idols, Early Neolithic ornament is intimate—beads at the throat, stamps on the cooking pot—identity at arm’s length from the hearth.
PRT.ideas:
The transformative idea is the village package carried by sea—seed corn, livestock, clay recipes, and fixed houses. Coastal leapfrogging treats the Mediterranean and Atlantic fringe as a single maritime frontier. Farming is a littoral claim that will take generations to become peninsula-wide practice.

Pioneer risk management matters: which cove holds fresh water, which slope takes barley, which forager band must be gifted around rather than fought.
PRT.philosophy:
Domesticated plants and animals reorder the sacred: hearths, storage pits, and household burials locate fertility and ancestry inside the settlement. Shell-stamped pots may mark group identity as much as kitchen use. Cosmology stays oral; archaeology catches ritual around food, death, and the new domestic animals—not named philosophical schools.

Storage pits become moral objects; to steal grain is to wound a household’s future in a way deer theft never quite matched.
PRT.science:
Seafaring farmers moved seed, livestock, and pottery recipes across open water—maritime logistics as enabling technology. They tuned Mediterranean crops to thin coastal soils while learning Iberian rainfall and wild resources. Flint and polished-stone toolkits standardised woodworking and field clearance.

Kill-off patterns in sheep and goat bones show herders learning Iberian forage calendars within a few generations of landfall.

IMN.description:
Farming reached Britain after the continental Early Neolithic was already mature. When established, Neolithic Britons were strongly Anatolian farmer–related (EEF), a demic replacement of Mesolithic WHG that aDNA makes unusually stark. Pottery, polished axes, cereals, cattle, and eventually earthen long barrows arrived as a continental-derived package adapted to island stone and timber. Ireland’s secure house-and-cereal horizons slightly lag some British footprints but join the same Atlantic farmer conversation.

Causewayed-enclosure thinking—gathering, feasting, boundary—began to organise regional identity even before the great stone theatres of the later Neolithic. WHG ancestry survived higher at some Atlantic edges than in pioneer cores, but the overall mode was replacement.

This farmer gene pool would itself be largely overturned in the Beaker age (~2500 BCE). Early Neolithic speech was unknown and non-IE in any evidenced sense; later Celtic languages are not continuous with it by default.
IMN.summary: Continental-derived farming reaches Britain and Ireland with strongly EEF genomes—the first major replacement of insular WHG—before later megalith florescence.
IMN.culture:
Fixed houses, herds, and cereal stores reorganised kinship around land and livestock. Timber halls and early monuments imply communal labour and feasting politics. Enclosures gathered people for rites and negotiation—soft regional institutions without kings we can name.

Timber halls and interrupted-ditch enclosures concentrate labour debts and feast obligations; Neolithic society learns to schedule people as carefully as seed.

Key sites: Early Neolithic houses and halls (e.g. Irish rectangular house horizons); Southern British causewayed enclosures (Windmill Hill tradition); Early long barrows of Wessex and the Cotswolds; Carinated Bowl pottery assemblages.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous pioneer farmers; no attested leaders.
IMN.art:
Carinated bowls, polished axes, and early chambered tombs / long barrows sketch a new visual package after millennia of forager portables. Art is still mostly functional and funerary; Orkney–Wessex stone theatre peaks later.

Long barrows and early chambers are architecture-as-sculpture: white chalk spoil and dark timber façades announce lineage before stone circles mature.

Demic farming: cereals, cattle, and houses arrive with people. Causewayed enclosures invent periodic assembly as political technology. Island soils and rainfall force rapid local adaptation of an imported package.

FRA.description:
Early Neolithic France was Europe’s hinge where maritime pioneer farming and the Danube corridor almost touched. Cardial impressed ware lit southern and western coasts while LBK-related banded pottery and longhouses entered the northeast. Both streams were EEF-rich demic spreads that replaced most local hunter-gatherer ancestry, with WHG admixture rising through the Middle Neolithic.

West-of-Rhine communities often mixed more local HG ancestry into farmer lives than some eastern LBK extremes—an idea of coexistence written in genomes as much as pots. Settlement chose loess, river terraces, and coastal enclaves rather than a uniform carpet.

Farmer languages are unknown; Gaulish Celtic appears only in the Iron Age record millennia later.
FRA.summary: France as hinge: Mediterranean Cardial along the littoral and Danubian LBK influence in the northeast—two EEF streams replacing most WHG.
FRA.culture:
Two ceramic-and-house traditions meant two social dialects of farming meeting in Gaul. Household and enclosure began to replace pure seasonal round. Burial rites diverged—Cardial caves and open deposits versus LBK cemetery rows—encoding different ideas of person and kin.

Where Cardial and LBK spheres approach, households may have recognised strangers by pot and house form before by speech—material dialect as social sorting.

Key sites: Mediterranean Cardial sites of Provence/Languedoc; LBK-related settlements of Alsace / Paris Basin northeast; Early Alpine jadeitite axe findspots in Gaul; Loess-terrace Early Neolithic villages.

Key people / anonymity: No named persons; ‘Cardial’ and ‘LBK’ are archaeological packages.
FRA.art:
Shell-stamp littoral ware versus Danubian linear pottery: rival visual languages. Early figurines and polished axes travel with both streams; Alpine axe stone already sketches future megalith routes.

Rival ceramic languages make Early Neolithic Gaul a visual borderland; axes of Alpine greenstone already glint as shared prestige across that border.
FRA.ideas:
Hinge geography: sea pioneers and loess colonists almost meet. Coexistence and admixture west of the Rhine complicate any simple replacement cartoon. Settlement ecology—loess, terrace, coast—selects where farming sticks.

Hinge geography trains communities in pluralism: farming arrives twice, with different house morals and burial grammars.
FRA.philosophy:
Sacred centres shift toward household and enclosure. Divergent burial traditions encode plural farmer ethics. Cosmology remains oral; archaeology catches practice at grave and hearth.

Cemetery rows versus cave deposits are two answers to ‘where do persons go,’ practised a few valleys apart.
FRA.science:
Near Eastern crops meet Atlantic and continental climates. Longhouse carpentry and Cardial pottery are parallel technical schools. Early Alpine axe exchange is logistical science.

Crop package stress-tests against frost and Atlantic rain produce regional winners among cereals and pulses within centuries.

POL.description:
The Linear Pottery Culture (LBK, ~5500–4900 BCE) is the textbook Central European Early Neolithic: vast timber longhouses, banded pottery, shoe-last adzes, and rapid colonisation of loess. Genomes are strongly Anatolian farmer–related; initial hunter-gatherer admixture is limited and rises later. Eastern and western LBK diverge in HG ancestry—same pottery brand, different genetic histories.

Spondylus shell ornaments from the Mediterranean show prestige chains hundreds of kilometres long. Late LBK violence—massacres at Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten—and Herxheim’s ritual deposits show belonging turning violently exclusive. This world is not ‘Celtic’ or ‘Germanic’; those labels belong to much later ages.

Language is unknown and widely assumed non-IE under steppe-IE models.
POL.summary: Classic Central European Early Neolithic: longhouses, Linearbandkeramik pottery, loess pioneer farming—strongly EEF, not Celtic or Germanic.
POL.culture:
Longhouse villages invent agrarian social architecture: aDNA often supports patrilocal kinship, cattle wealth, and rapid fission-colonisation. Cemeteries stage gendered tool kits. Crisis centuries reveal massacre and ritualised processing of bodies as dark limits of community.

Patrilocal signals in aDNA, if read cautiously, align with longhouse politics where in-marrying women joined cattle-rich timber lineages—and where late massacres show how brittle that order could become.

Key sites: Bylany and classic Bohemian/Moravian LBK settlements; Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten massacre sites; Herxheim ritual enclosure; Loess-belt longhouse villages of the Rhine–Danube corridors.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous villagers and victims of late LBK massacres; no royal names.
POL.art:
Incised linear and spiral fine ware, clay figurines, shoe-last adzes, Spondylus ornaments—prestige art inside an agrarian aesthetic. Longhouses themselves are landscape sculpture in timber.

Spiral-banded fine ware and Spondylus shine are farmer bling: beauty that proves connection to distant seas and careful kilns.
POL.ideas:
Pioneer farming on loess as a transferable package. Pottery ‘brand’ can mask divergent genetic histories. Late violence shows ideas of us/them hardening.

The same pottery brand across genetically divergent east/west LBK warns against equating ceramic identity with blood identity.
POL.philosophy:
Row-grave cemeteries and household practice locate ancestors beside the living; fertility attaches to cattle and grain. Herxheim’s skull-cap rites imply a dark theology of processing the dead—or the stranger—as ritual theatre. Communal and bodily, not textual.

Herxheim and the massacre pits force a hard inference: Neolithic sacred order could include the ritualised unmaking of persons.
POL.science:
Emmer, einkorn, barley, pulses, and cattle on loess with geographic consistency. Longhouse joinery across generations. Pottery, flint mines, and Spondylus logistics as early systems science.

Loess agronomy’s geographic consistency is itself a technology transfer success story—package knowledge moving with people.

NOR.description:
In the later Mesolithic / earliest Neolithic contact centuries, Ertebølle communities of Danish and south Swedish coasts remained demographic majority: thick shell middens, seal and fish economies, and pointed-base pottery among Europe’s earliest northern ceramics—pottery without full farming. They negotiated exchange and occasional violence with southern farmers while defending coastal lifeways.

Genetics show SHG/WHG holdouts beside rising EEF as earliest Funnelbeaker (TRB) farming appears in the south. The first Holocene turnover is beginning, not finished. ‘Becoming Neolithic’ here is delayed, chosen, and uneven—not automatic.

Language shift likely accompanies farming eventually; details unknowable and not Old Norse.
NOR.summary: Ertebølle coastal foragers keep SHG ways and invent northern pottery while earliest Funnelbeaker farming only begins the first Holocene turnover.
NOR.culture:
Shell middens double as ancestral places—refuse that is also memory. Marine mammal hunting and oyster seasons structure prestige and diet. Contact with LBK/TRB south is wary and porous.

Ertebølle communities can adopt pots and still refuse villages; identity is chosen package by package at the farmer contact zone. Shell middens remain the public monuments of a people who will not yet surrender the sea.

Key sites: Ertebølle and Bjørnsholm-type shell middens; Danish straits coastal forager settlements; Earliest TRB farming footholds in southern Scandinavia; Pointed-base pottery type assemblages.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous Ertebølle fishers and earliest TRB pioneers.
NOR.art:
Pointed-base Ertebølle pottery, bone combs, antler tools, marine mammal motifs—last-forager style at the edge of the farmer world.

SMR.description:
Impressed and Cardial-related wares announce farmer aesthetics across southern and central coasts. Italy becomes a launch corridor for Mediterranean Neolithisation—Adriatic and Tyrrhenian leapfrogs toward France and Iberia. Strong EEF signal replaces most forager ancestry; inland uptake varies. Village pottery and obsidian blades from island sources redefine daily visual life.

This farmer substrate will later be overlain by Bronze Age steppe-related ancestry and, historically, by Italic and Etruscan languages—none of which equal Impressa speech.

Sea links make the peninsula a network node, not a cul-de-sac.

Inland Apennine valleys took up farming more unevenly than the coasts, so for generations Italy held a patchwork of cereal villages, herding uplands, and residual hunting edges. That mosaic matters for later history: the peninsula’s farmer substrate is coastal-rooted, maritime-connected, and never a single uniform countryside in the earliest centuries.
SMR.summary: Maritime Impressed Ware farming along Italian coasts—EEF demic replacement and launch corridor toward France and Iberia.
SMR.culture:
Villages redefine land as fields and pastures; forager edges persist in mountains. Household shrines and figurines locate the sacred in domestic space. Obsidian specialists and sailors stitch islands to coasts.

Sailors, potters, and herders form the Early Neolithic public; mountain foragers remain neighbours whose knowledge of passes still matters to anyone moving flocks. Household burials and figurines locate belonging inside the settlement rather than the seasonal camp.

Key sites: Impressed Ware coastal settlements of Apulia and Sicily; Tyrrhenian Early Neolithic villages; Lipari and related obsidian workshops; Adriatic Impressa sites facing the Balkan shore.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous maritime pioneers and obsidian knappers.
SMR.art:
Impressed and painted-band wares, clay figurines, gleaming obsidian blades—village pottery replaces forager portables as the daily visual environment.

Impressed surfaces and figurines make the house a small museum of belonging; obsidian’s gloss adds a volcanic luxury to everyday cutting. Village pottery replaces forager portables as the daily visual environment.
SMR.ideas:
Italy as Neolithisation corridor. Maritime leapfrog as planned demic strategy. Farming as coastal claim with mountain lag.

Launch-corridor thinking treats Italy as a node on Mediterranean routes—success measured in landfalls farther west as much as in local fields. Adriatic and Tyrrhenian leapfrogs are planned demography, not accident.
SMR.philosophy:
Domestic shrines, figurines, and burial under or near houses. Fertility of crops and herds structures ritual calendars. Practised covenants with land and dead—no philosophy schools.

Burial near houses folds the dead into domestic fertility; the sacred is under the floor and beside the grain. No philosophy schools—only practised covenants with land, herd, and ancestor.
SMR.science:
Island obsidian specialised production and distribution as measurable early industry. Crop tuning from Po fringe to Sicily. Boat-building and coastal pilotage enable Impressa expansion.

Obsidian sourcing (Lipari and kin) is archaeology’s proof that sailors already ran mental maps of island vents with commercial precision. Crop tuning from Sicily to the Po fringe is agronomic R&D under one maritime brand.

BGR.description:
The Balkans are the demic bridge from Anatolia into Europe—farming’s first European idea factory. Starčevo–Körös–Criș and early Vinča tell settlements carry Anatolian-related farmers who mix more visibly with distinctive local HG (Iron Gates) than some early western LBK groups. Painted and fine polished pottery, anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figurines, and stamp seals fill villages with a crowded visual theology of clay bodies.

From here Cardial and LBK streams will diverge, carrying Balkan-tempered farmer culture west and north. Village life, storage, and cattle reorganise kinship and labour.

Languages are unknown Starčevo/Vinča-related speech; Ancient Greek is still far future and unrelated by attestation.
BGR.summary: Europe’s first farming corridor—Anatolian-related tell villages, figurines, and elevated local HG admixture versus some western LBK extremes.
BGR.culture:
Tell living stacks generations—the past literally underfoot. Household cults centre figurines; ritual pits and house burnings suggest cyclical renewal. Craft and farming specialisation grow with settlement scale.

Tell neighbours stack obligations vertically: rebuilding on ancestors’ rubble is both practical and moral continuity. Figurine-rich households make ritual labour a daily chore, not a rare pilgrimage.

Key sites: Starčevo type sites; Körös and Criș settlement zones of the Carpathian Basin edge; Early Vinča tell settlements; Iron Gates contact-period mixed horizons.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous tell villagers and figurine makers.
BGR.art:
Earth-toned Starčevo wares; early Vinča darkening and sophisticating surfaces; dense figurine worlds; stamp seals. Houses accumulate art as stratified memory.

Figurine crowds and stamp seals fill domestic space with watching clay—art as constant company, not festival rarity. Starčevo earth tones and early Vinča polish chart a rising craft ambition.
BGR.ideas:
Balkans as bridge and splitter of Neolithic streams. Elevated HG admixture as regional signature. Tells as vertical archives of belonging.

As the splitter of Cardial and LBK streams, the Balkans invent Europe’s two Neolithic accents from one Anatolian-related root. Elevated local HG admixture is a regional signature, not a footnote.
BGR.philosophy:
Figurines—often female, sometimes ambiguous—point to household cults of fertility, protection, or ancestor presence without proving a single ‘mother goddess’ church. House burnings and ritual pits suggest cyclical renewal rites for buildings as well as people.

House-burning rites, where present, suggest buildings have life-cycles demanding funerary attention. Female and ambiguous figurines invite fertility and protection readings without proving a single goddess church.
BGR.science:
Refining the Neolithic package for European latitudes—crops, animals, mudbrick/wattle housing. Early copper ornaments as metallurgical curiosity beside stone. Pottery kilns and tell drainage as settlement engineering.

Mudbrick, wattle, and early copper trinkets show materials science diversifying faster than political centralisation. Tell drainage and kiln craft are settlement engineering at growing scale.

BLR.description:
While true farming paints pottery farther west, many forest-steppe groups remain forager-derived. Eastern forager ceramics (Comb Ware and related) keep comb-and-pit decoration as a forest aesthetic. On the western fringe, early Trypillia/Precucuteni painted wares begin to appear—farmer colour advancing into the forest-steppe. Two visual systems face each other across the divide.

‘Neolithic’ here often means pots, not crops—an idea that confuses later textbooks. Pontic and forest foragers coexist with approaching Balkan–Carpathian farmers for centuries. Exchange and occasional admixture happen without immediate lifestyle collapse. Pre-Yamnaya ancestry keeps EHG and CHG-related components separable; farmer fringe only on the southwest edge.

Languages are an unknown mix—not Slavic (medieval) and not yet clearly IE.
BLR.summary: East of the Neolithic genomic divide: EHG foragers and Comb Ware aesthetics meet only a western Cucuteni–Trypillia farmer fringe—not pan-eastern EEF replacement.
BLR.culture:
Plural frontier: forager burial richness continues; farmer rites bring figurines and painted ceramics at the contact fringe. River routes (Dniester, Dnieper, Bug) are logistics backbone.

Frontier etiquette—gift, raid, marriage, avoidance—matters more than any single ‘Neolithic conversion’ sermon along the Dniester–Bug line. Forager burial richness and farmer fringe figurines can coexist for centuries.

Key sites: Comb Ware forest zone sites; Precucuteni / early Trypillia fringe settlements; Dniester–Bug river corridor contact sites; Pontic steppe forager camps contemporary with farmer fringe.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous frontier foragers and fringe farmers.
BLR.art:
Comb-and-pit forager ceramics versus early painted Trypillia/Precucuteni on the fringe—two schools facing across the genomic divide.

Comb impressions versus painted spirals are rival modernities visible in sherd bags from the same river systems. Neither side yet owns the whole forest-steppe.
BLR.ideas:
Pots ≠ ploughs. Long coexistence without pan-eastern replacement. Rivers as contact infrastructure.

Textbook ‘Neolithic’ fails here; the east teaches that ceramic fashion and farming demography can travel on different clocks. EHG and CHG-related ancestries remain separable ingredients beside a thin EEF fringe.
BLR.philosophy:
Worldviews pluralise along the frontier—no single conversion narrative. Ancestors and animals remain central on the forager side; figurines enter at the farmer edge.

Plural sacred media on one frontier mean children could grow up hearing more than one answer to who owns the dead. Animals and ancestors still dominate forager ethics while painted pots arrive as new sacred surfaces.
BLR.science:
Forager ecological expertise persists; farmer fringe tests crops on chernozem and forest-steppe soils. Ceramic temper/firing styles mark technical schools on both sides.

Chernozem trials at the farmer fringe are high-stakes agronomy; forager fire knowledge still outperforms early ploughs in many seasons. River logistics on Dniester, Dnieper, and Bug move both ideas and spouses.

stories.title: Two Pots on One River

stories.title: Farming’s Thin Edge

While true farming paints pottery farther west, many forest-steppe groups remain forager-derived. Eastern forager ceramics (Comb Ware and related) keep comb-and-pit decoration as a forest aesthetic. On the western fringe, early Trypillia/Precucuteni painted wares begin to appear—farmer colour advancing into the forest-steppe. Two visual systems face each other across the divide.

‘Neolithic’ here often means pots, not crops—an idea that confuses later textbooks. Pontic and forest foragers coexist with approaching Balkan–Carpathian farmers for centuries. Exchange and occasional admixture happen without immediate lifestyle collapse. Pre-Yamnaya ancestry keeps EHG and CHG-related components separable; farmer fringe only on the southwest edge.

Languages are an unknown mix—not Slavic (medieval) and not yet clearly IE.

TUR.description:
While true farming paints pottery farther west, many forest-steppe groups remain forager-derived. Eastern forager ceramics (Comb Ware and related) keep comb-and-pit decoration as a forest aesthetic. On the western fringe, early Trypillia/Precucuteni painted wares begin to appear—farmer colour advancing into the forest-steppe. Two visual systems face each other across the divide.

‘Neolithic’ here often means pots, not crops—an idea that confuses later textbooks. Pontic and forest foragers coexist with approaching Balkan–Carpathian farmers for centuries. Exchange and occasional admixture happen without immediate lifestyle collapse. Pre-Yamnaya ancestry keeps EHG and CHG-related components separable; farmer fringe only on the southwest edge.

Languages are an unknown mix—not Slavic (medieval) and not yet clearly IE.
TUR.summary: East of the Neolithic genomic divide: EHG foragers and Comb Ware aesthetics meet only a western Cucuteni–Trypillia farmer fringe—not pan-eastern EEF replacement.
TUR.culture:
Plural frontier: forager burial richness continues; farmer rites bring figurines and painted ceramics at the contact fringe. River routes (Dniester, Dnieper, Bug) are logistics backbone.

Frontier etiquette—gift, raid, marriage, avoidance—matters more than any single ‘Neolithic conversion’ sermon along the Dniester–Bug line. Forager burial richness and farmer fringe figurines can coexist for centuries.

Key sites: Comb Ware forest zone sites; Precucuteni / early Trypillia fringe settlements; Dniester–Bug river corridor contact sites; Pontic steppe forager camps contemporary with farmer fringe.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous frontier foragers and fringe farmers.
TUR.art:
Comb-and-pit forager ceramics versus early painted Trypillia/Precucuteni on the fringe—two schools facing across the genomic divide.

Comb impressions versus painted spirals are rival modernities visible in sherd bags from the same river systems. Neither side yet owns the whole forest-steppe.
TUR.ideas:
Pots ≠ ploughs. Long coexistence without pan-eastern replacement. Rivers as contact infrastructure.

Textbook ‘Neolithic’ fails here; the east teaches that ceramic fashion and farming demography can travel on different clocks. EHG and CHG-related ancestries remain separable ingredients beside a thin EEF fringe.
TUR.philosophy:
Worldviews pluralise along the frontier—no single conversion narrative. Ancestors and animals remain central on the forager side; figurines enter at the farmer edge.

Plural sacred media on one frontier mean children could grow up hearing more than one answer to who owns the dead. Animals and ancestors still dominate forager ethics while painted pots arrive as new sacred surfaces.
TUR.science:
Forager ecological expertise persists; farmer fringe tests crops on chernozem and forest-steppe soils. Ceramic temper/firing styles mark technical schools on both sides.

Chernozem trials at the farmer fringe are high-stakes agronomy; forager fire knowledge still outperforms early ploughs in many seasons. River logistics on Dniester, Dnieper, and Bug move both ideas and spouses.

periods.label: Megaliths densify farmer Europe
periods.narrative: Near 3800 BC farmer societies thicken: Atlantic passage graves, Chasséen and Michelsberg inland, Funnelbeaker (TRB) across the north European plain, Cucuteni–Trypillia mega-settlements on the east. WHG ancestry has climbed inside many farmer groups — higher on Atlantic and northern façades — while Pitted Ware and Narva foragers still fringe the coasts. Steppe pastoralists have not yet remade the temperate gene pool.
periods.culturesNote: TRB, Michelsberg, Chasséen, megalithic Atlantic, GAC, Trypillia + HG holdouts (Pitted Ware, Narva/Comb Ware).

iberia.culture:
Collective burial and tomb re-entry invent a politics of ancestry: who belongs is argued in chambers and offerings. Labour for quarrying and levering stones implies seasonal aggregation beyond the single household. Prestige goods mark differentiation short of named kings.

Villages and herding intensified on Atlantic and southern soils; monument clusters suggest regional pilgrimage and alliance without a single Iberian capital.

Tomb re-entry across generations turns kinship into a public archive: bones are rearranged, offerings refreshed, and claims on pasture rehearsed in front of the dead.

Key sites: Antequera dolmens (Menga, Viera, El Romeral); Atlantic Portuguese and Galician passage graves; Alentejo / southwestern engraved schist plaque zones; Los Millares precursor landscapes (toward Copper Age).

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous tomb builders and plaque carvers; no attested rulers or sages.
iberia.description:
By the later fourth millennium BCE, Iberia’s Neolithic had thickened from coastal pioneer villages into inland farming and a monumental Atlantic–southern façade. Passage graves, tholoi, and engraved schist plaques made ancestry visible for kilometres. Collective tomb reuse staged politics of belonging in stone chambers; amber, variscite, and exotic axes circulated as prestige beside the dead.

Genomically the population remained EEF-dominated, yet WHG ancestry rose again—especially on Atlantic megalithic façades versus some southern inland cores. This was a within-culture farmer cline, not a return to Mesolithic life, and steppe-related ancestry was still essentially absent. Identity was practice (tomb, plough, plaque), not genomic purity.

Exchange networks for jadeitite, Iberian greenstone, and marine shell stitched coasts to hinterlands, foreshadowing Copper Age complexity without yet importing Yamnaya genetics. Languages stayed unwritten and pre-IE in any recoverable sense; historical Iberian scripts lie millennia ahead.
iberia.linguisticNote: Unknown pre-IE. Historical Iberian script languages are Copper/Iron Age attestations, not proven megalithic speech.
iberia.ancestryNote: EEF majority; WHG higher on Atlantic megalithic façades than in southern inland cores.

ancestryCline.label: Atlantic façade → inland south
ancestryCline.note: WHG% rises toward Atlantic megalithic zones; EEF higher inland/south.

iberia.art:
Monumental gallery architecture—corbelled chambers, corridors, engraved kerbs—replaces the quiet Cardial household aesthetic with public stone theatre. Geometric plaque ‘idols’ and eye motifs hint at personified powers. Amber, variscite, and greenstone axes become luminous prestige media inside and beside tombs.

Schist plaques vary enough to hint at workshop habits and local ‘faces,’ yet standardised enough to travel as a recognisable sacred medium.
iberia.ideas:
Ancestry made landscape-scale: tombs as claims, horizons as ritual frames. Long-distance stone sourcing implies remembered exchange routes and surveying of outcrops. WHG gene flow into farmer bodies shows that ‘Neolithic’ culture could absorb forager ancestry while keeping farmer practice.

Horizon alignments and corridor plans imply shared surveying lore among communities that never formed a single Iberian state.
iberia.philosophy:
Megaliths stage a cosmology of the dead as landscape anchors: chambers aligned to horizons, offerings, and successive depositions keep ancestors present. Engraved plaques suggest powers without readable pantheons. Ritual time is generational—re-entering the tomb—rather than priestly scripture. No invented named philosophers.

Eye motifs and geometric bodies on plaques invite personhood without yielding a pantheon list—powers felt, not catalogued.
iberia.science:
Builders mastered quarrying, levering, and sighting large stones into stable chambers. Agricultural intensification paired with herding; archaeobotany and isotopes show mixed farming tuned to regional rainfall. Long-distance lithic sourcing is applied geology and logistics.

Corbelling and capstone balance are empirical structural engineering taught by failure and success across tomb generations.
iberia.summary: Passage graves, tholoi, and engraved plaques turn Atlantic and southern Iberia into ancestor theatres while EEF farmers absorb renewed WHG ancestry—still pre-steppe.

britain.culture:
Monument clusters imply regional gathering, labour mobilisation, and competitive prestige among farming communities. Kinship and land claims were argued in stone: who builds, who buries, who feasts. Specialised flint mines and axe factories (Grimes Graves, Langdale) show craft economies feeding ritual and clearance alike.

Quarry crews, tomb teams, and feast hosts form overlapping labour publics; prestige accrues to those who can move stone and meat at landscape scale.

Key sites: Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange, Knowth, Dowth); Maeshowe and Orkney World Heritage monuments; Skara Brae; Stonehenge landscape (pre-/early stone phases in this era’s long tail); Langdale axe quarries; Grimes Graves flint mines.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous astronomer-builders and quarry specialists; no attested personal names.
britain.description:
The Middle–Late Neolithic islands raised some of Atlantic Europe’s densest ritual landscapes: Newgrange and the Boyne tombs, Orkney’s Maeshowe-type chambers and villages such as Skara Brae, and the long Wessex sequence toward Stonehenge’s stone phases. Grooved Ware pottery and carved stone balls added portable grammar to outdoor galleries of kerbs, spirals, and aligned passages.

Genomically these were still Anatolian farmer–related populations with WHG admixture—often higher in north/west monument zones than in denser southern farming—and still without steppe ancestry. This is precisely the gene pool later replaced in the Beaker age; culturally they look triumphant, demographically they were doomed relative to the third millennium.

Irish Sea and northern networks shared tomb forms and ceramics—an Atlantic ceremonial commons of pilgrimage, alliance, and competitive display.
britain.ancestryNote: Neolithic Britain without steppe; WHG higher in north/west monument zones than in denser southern farming.
britain.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE; later Celtic is not continuous by default.

ancestryCline.label: North/west → southern farming
ancestryCline.note: WHG% higher in northern/western Neolithic landscapes; EEF higher in denser southern farming.

britain.art: Passage tombs of the Boyne Valley, Orkney’s Maeshowe-type chambers, and stone circles culminating toward Stonehenge turn islands into ritual landscapes of carved kerbs, spiral art, and aligned passages. Grooved Ware pottery and carved stone balls add portable grammar to the monumental outdoor gallery. Skara Brae’s stone furniture shows domestic design as carefully composed as tombs.
britain.ideas:
Pilgrimage and alliance across the Irish Sea; monuments as political arguments. Cattle feasting fuels labour. A north/west versus south cline in WHG share shows that even ‘British Neolithic’ was not one uniform percentage.

Monument clusters compete and collaborate—pilgrimage can knit rivals as easily as it can stage them.
britain.philosophy:
Solar and lunar alignments (Newgrange’s midwinter light; circle horizons) embed sky cosmology in architecture. Collective and successive burials keep the dead as active community members. Philosophy here is practised astronomy-and-ancestry, not named schools.

Midwinter light and circle horizons turn astronomy into ethics: keeping time with the dead is a communal duty.
britain.science:
Surveying, megalith transport, horizon astronomy, manuring and mixed farming, flint mining, and axe distribution form an integrated technical world. Precision of alignment is remarkable for pre-literate societies.

Axe factories and flint mines imply apprenticeship and quality control; not every block becomes a travelling axe.
britain.summary: Boyne Valley, Orkney, and Wessex monument societies—EEF+WHG farmers whose stone cosmologies precede Beaker demographic collapse.

france.culture:
Chasséen networks standardised pottery and flint across wide tracts—a soft political grammar. Monument labour on Armorica implies seasonal aggregation and prestige competition. Enclosures gathered people for feasts and boundary-making inland.

Alignment and tumulus projects imply sponsors able to call labour across multiple settlements—soft hierarchies visible in stone even without named lords.

Key sites: Carnac alignments (Ménec, Kermario); Tumulus Saint-Michel / Morbihan monumental tombs; Cairn of Barnenez; Chasséen enclosure and settlement sites of interior France.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous alignment builders and jade-axe patrons; no attested names.
france.description:
Middle Neolithic France became a cultural mosaic: Chasséen and related facies organising much of the interior with pottery and enclosures, while northwest Armorica raised Europe’s densest stone theatre—Carnac’s alignments, Morbihan tumuli, Barnenez-type cairns. Jadeitite ceremonial axes from Alpine sources appear broken or deposited as luminous green prestige art.

Farmer–forager admixture was ongoing; WHG ran higher on the Atlantic megalithic west than in some eastern Chasséen cores. Steppe ancestry was still absent. Northern France’s mixed Cardial–Danubian heritage helped launch megalithic ideas toward Britain and the North Sea.

Competitive ritual economies—who raises the longest alignment, who buries with Alpine jade—structured Atlantic elites without kings we can name.
france.linguisticNote: Unknown pre-Celtic farmer languages of Chasséen/megalithic France; Gaulish appears only in the Iron Age record.
france.ancestryNote: EEF majority + WHG; WHG higher on Atlantic megalithic west than in eastern Chasséen cores.

ancestryCline.label: Atlantic west → eastern Chasséen
ancestryCline.note: WHG% higher on the megalithic Atlantic façade; EEF higher in eastern Chasséen farming.

france.art: Carnac’s alignments, Morbihan tumuli, and Barnenez-type cairns make northwest France Europe’s densest stone theatre; Chasséen pottery and enclosures organise the interior. Jadeitite ceremonial axes from Alpine sources appear broken or deposited as luminous green prestige art. Engraved stones and monumental façades turn geology into sculpture at landscape scale.
france.ideas:
Ritual competition and soft standardisation replace Early Neolithic pioneer dualism with denser regional systems. Atlantic megalithic ideas radiate toward the islands. Ancestry clines show culture shared across genetically slightly different farmer bodies.

Chasséen standardisation inland and Armorican spectacle on the coast are complementary politics—one of networks, one of skylines.
france.philosophy:
Menhirs and passage graves stage skyline, ancestor, and processional path. Broken axe deposits suggest sacrifice of wealth to powers of place or death. Sacred time is seasonal and funerary—solstice light, tomb re-entry—not treatise.

Processional avenues between menhirs script bodies into ritual movement; belief is walked, not written.
france.science:
Moving multi-tonne menhirs demands levers, ropes, ramps, and labour accounting. Horizon astronomy and careful siting bind monuments to landmarks. Intensive farming on Armorican and Paris-Basin soils underwrites calorie surplus behind stone spectacle.

Erecting menhirs teaches soil, fulcrum, and rope as civic sciences; failures leave toppled lessons at field edges.
france.summary: Carnac alignments, Morbihan tumuli, and Chasséen networks—Atlantic ritual economies and interior enclosures in a still pre-steppe EEF+WHG France.

central.culture:
Enclosures gather people for feasts, rites, and boundary-making—temporary earthworks as political technology. Flint daggers and specialist mining (Rijckholt tradition) mark status and industry. Northern TRB contact transfers farming know-how toward Scandinavia.

Enclosure feasts redistribute meat and obligations; Middle Neolithic politics is calendrical as much as territorial.

Key sites: Michelsberg enclosure sites of the Rhineland; Northern TRB megalithic tombs (North European Plain); Rijckholt and related flint-mine systems; Early Globular Amphora burial contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous enclosure builders and flint miners.
central.description:
After LBK’s crisis, Central Europe multiplied regional cultures: Michelsberg tulip beakers and enclosures, Funnelbeaker (TRB) links on the northern plain with megalithic tombs, and toward the late fourth millennium early Globular Amphora (GAC) hints of cattle-centred wealth and new burial politics. WHG ancestry resurges inside farmer populations; forager blood returns without restoring forager life.

TRB is not genetically uniform—WHG higher in northern TRB, EEF higher in southern/central cores. Steppe-related ancestry is still essentially absent; Corded Ware transformations lie ahead. GAC forms part of the farmer world that will later mix into Corded Ware.

Languages remain unknown; CW-linked Indo-European models concern the next age.
central.linguisticNote: Unknown. CW-linked IE comes next, not yet.
central.ancestryNote: TRB/Michelsberg farmers: WHG higher in northern TRB; EEF higher in southern/central agricultural cores. GAC forms as the farmer side later mixed into Corded Ware.

ancestryCline.label: Northern TRB → central/south core
ancestryCline.note: WHG% rises north (and toward forager contact); EEF highest in Michelsberg / southern TRB cores.

central.art:
Michelsberg tulip beakers, Funnelbeaker pottery, northern megaliths, flint daggers, later Globular Amphora jars—diversified post-LBK visual field. Monumentality patchier than Atlantic but still marks ancestors.

Tulip beakers and flint daggers stage status at the mouth and the belt—portable rank markers for a post-longhouse age.
central.ideas: After LBK’s crisis, regional cultures multiply—enclosures, new flint economies, and northern TRB links. WHG ancestry resurges inside farmer populations; forager blood returns without restoring forager life. Early Globular Amphora hints at cattle-centred wealth and new burial politics toward the late 4th millennium.
central.philosophy:
Causewayed and ditched enclosures as temporary sacred cities of earth. Megalithic and flat graves encode competing claims about who the dead remain. Belief practice-rich and name-poor.

Earthwork sanctuaries are temporary cities of meaning; when the feast ends, the sacred ditch remains as a scar of assembly.
central.science:
Deep flint mining and specialist axe production approach industrial extraction before metal. Crop–livestock intensification; enclosures imply surplus and organised labour. TRB northern transfer of agronomy.

Mine shafts and debitage piles are textbooks in chalk geology written by specialised labour.
central.summary: Post-LBK regionalisation: Michelsberg enclosures, Funnelbeaker north, rising WHG in farmers, early GAC—still pre-steppe.

scandinavia.culture:
Tomb building and forest clearance mobilise communal labour. Dual TRB/Pitted Ware lifeways mean parallel prestige systems—cattle and flint inland, seals and marine hunting on coasts. Amber and flint daggers circulate as bright prestige.

TRB tomb builders and Pitted Ware seal hunters may share beaches and still refuse each other’s full moral economy—parallel Scandinavias in one era. Cattle feasts and seal oil lamps light different nights of the same archipelago.

Key sites: Danish TRB dolmens and passage graves; Early Scandinavian flint mines; Pitted Ware coastal sites (e.g. Ajvide-type contexts in wider tradition); Southern Swedish TRB farming settlements.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous dolmen builders and Pitted Ware seal hunters.
scandinavia.description:
Funnelbeaker farming and megaliths arrive as a northern package, absorbing and displacing Ertebølle unevenly. Funnel-necked beakers, polished flint axes, and dolmens/passage graves rewrite land tenure with clearing and cattle. Beside TRB, Pitted Ware groups keep a contrasting seal-hunter ceramic style on coasts with high HG ancestry—dual societies in places, not a single Scandinavian Neolithic mix.

Schematic ancestry splits with geography: EEF-led TRB inland/south versus SHG/WHG-rich Pitted Ware holdouts. Pre-Germanic linguistic models attach to later Battle Axe stages, not automatically to TRB.

Wetland axe and pottery depositions continue older water rites inside a new farming religion of fertility and lineage.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Unknown TRB-related speech; pre-Germanic tied to later Battle Axe models.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: TRB farmers inland/south vs Pitted Ware forager holdouts on coasts — two genetic regimes under one map period.

ancestryCline.label: Pitted Ware coasts → TRB farms
ancestryCline.note: Coastal Pitted Ware keeps high SHG/WHG; southern/inland TRB is EEF-led with residual HG.

scandinavia.art:
Funnelbeakers, dolmens, polished axes, amber; Pitted Ware’s contrasting coastal ceramic style. Monumentality is architectural more than figurative.

Funnelbeakers and dolmens announce farmer spectacle; Pitted Ware keeps a rougher coastal ceramic voice beside them. Amber and flint daggers glitter as prestige in both conversations.
scandinavia.ideas:
Agriculture as northern package; dual societies as lived politics. Cattle, clearing, and tombs rewrite tenure while coasts refuse full conversion.

Dual societies prove that maps labelled ‘Neolithic Scandinavia’ flatten a lived argument. Land tenure by tomb and clearing coexists with coastal hunting rights that never fully convert.
scandinavia.philosophy:
Dolmens gather bones of many under caps open to sky. Wetland depositions fuse older water sacredness with megalithic ancestor/sky themes.

Bog offerings of axes show water keeping its old rights inside farming religion. Dolmen collectives open bones to the sky while wetlands still take polished gifts.
scandinavia.science:
Adapting cereals and livestock to short northern seasons—agricultural R&D at climatic margin. Megalith transport and Danish flint-mine intensification. Pitted Ware preserves parallel marine science beside the plough.

Short-season cereals and frost-kill risk make northern TRB an applied climate laboratory. Flint mines and megalith logistics organise labour at scales Ertebølle never needed.
scandinavia.summary: TRB farmers bring cereals, cattle, and dolmens north while Pitted Ware coastal foragers keep SHG-rich seal hunting—two genetic regimes under one map period.

italy.culture:
Regional pottery fashions mark identities across a still-EEF genetic world with rising local HG admixture. Craft specialisation and exotic stone mark status gradients without palaces.

Grave goods begin to sort persons more loudly; Italy’s Middle Neolithic learns ranking without yet inventing palace redistributive states. Obsidian and greenstone specialists stitch coasts to Alpine paths.

Key sites: Serra d’Alto and Diana culture type sites; Obsidian-rich Middle Neolithic settlements; Alpine foreland early copper contexts (toward Remedello); Statue-menhir and megalithic zones of Alpine/Italian regions.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous potters, sailors, and early metal experimenters.
italy.description:
Middle–Late Neolithic Italy consolidated regional ceramic ‘dialects’ (Diana, Serra d’Alto, and kin) while genetics remained EEF+WHG without meaningful steppe yet. Some regions raised megaliths and statue-menhir traditions; obsidian and greenstone axes stayed prestige media. Toward the period’s end, copper experiments in the Alpine foreland added metallurgical trial-and-error beside stone.

Social differentiation shows in grave goods before true metal-age chiefdoms. Alpine jadeitite and island stone kept Italy wired into wider western exchange.

Deep linguistic layers remain unrecoverable beneath later Italic and Etruscan.

Regional fine wares such as Diana and Serra d’Alto did not merely decorate kitchens; they advertised affiliations across Tyrrhenian and southern networks while Alpine jade and island glass kept northern and maritime paths open. Copper’s first experiments in the foreland did not abolish stone—they added a new specialist craft beside increasingly skilled ceramic chemistry.
italy.linguisticNote: Unknown; pre-Italic / pre-Etruscan deep layers unrecoverable.
italy.ancestryNote: EEF-led; steppe arrives mainly in the Bronze Age.
italy.art:
Fine painted and polished wares push pottery toward display; figurines, early megaliths, and statue-menhirs in some zones; copper ornaments begin to glint in the north.

Painted and polished display wares push pottery toward gallery status; statue-menhirs, where present, drag the human outline into public stone. Copper ornaments begin to glint beside stone axes in northern graves.
italy.ideas:
Ceramic dialects as identity. Western exchange in jade and obsidian. Gradual ranking before Remedello/Gaudo metal-age politics.

Ceramic ‘dialects’ are political speech in clay—readable affiliation when spoken languages are lost to us. Western exchange keeps Italy inside a broader farmer conversation still free of steppe genetics.
italy.philosophy:
Figurines, structured deposits, caves, trenches, early megaliths—plural local rites. Ancestor and fertility themes dominate inference; named pantheons wait for later ages.

Plural burial modes (cave, trench, early megalith) imply plural local answers to ancestry, not a peninsula-wide church. Figurines and structured deposits remain the readable theology.
italy.science:
Specialised pottery firing and surface chemistry. Mixed farming intensifies. Early copper experiments in Alpine foreland. Obsidian sourcing confirms sailors’ mental maps of volcanoes.

Kiln temperature control and pigment recipes become craft secrets worth marrying for; metallurgy joins that apprenticeship world at the edges. Sailors’ volcanic maps remain measurable in obsidian chemistry.
italy.summary: Diana, Serra d’Alto, and related farmer cultures—fine wares, rising HG admixture, Alpine jade and island stone—copper glinting at the northern edge.

balkans.culture:
Tell mega-villages support craft specialists. House-based ritual and possible intentional house burning encode renewal cycles. Ranking visible in goods before palace economies.

Craft specialists on copper and fine ware imply patronage and surplus; ranking rises without dissolving household ritual centres into temple bureaucracy. Tell mega-villages concentrate people who still bury and burn close to home.

Key sites: Vinča-Belo Brdo and major Vinča tells; Pločnik and related early copper contexts; Late Neolithic tell belts of the middle Danube; Sites with Vinča symbols / notations.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous metallurgists and figurine makers; Vinča symbols have no deciphered authors.
balkans.description:
Vinča and successor Late Neolithic / Copper Age facies concentrate population and craft on river plains. Dark-burnished ware, elaborate figurines, house models, and early copper ornaments (later tools) create a proto-metal aesthetic. Some signs point toward proto-writing or symbolic inventories (Vinča symbols)—still debated, never deciphered literature.

Farmer ancestry dominates; early steppe signals appear regionally toward the Copper Age on the northeast Black Sea–Danube edge as Eneolithic steppe societies form. Social ranking edges upward without full urban states. Mycenaean Greek remains a millennium+ away.

Exchange in Balkan copper and Aegean links foreshadows Eneolithic complexity.
balkans.linguisticNote: Unknown. Mycenaean Greek is still a millennium+ away.
balkans.ancestryNote: EEF+local HG; early steppe signals appear regionally toward the Copper Age.
balkans.art:
Dark-burnished Vinča ware, dense figurine cosmologies, house models, shrine-like rooms, copper gleam—household-centred visual theology.

Dark burnish and figurine intensity make Vinča visual culture feel ‘busy’—a clay cosmos of repeated gestures and faces. Copper’s first gleam joins that cosmos as precious redness.
balkans.ideas:
Craft specialisation and symbolic inventories (undeciphered). Copper as new prestige and technical frontier. Steppe contact intensifying on the northeast edge.

Vinča symbols tempt script fantasies; responsible reading keeps them as open notation, not decoded chronicles. Northeast steppe contact foreshadows Copper Age weather without yet remaking the tells.
balkans.philosophy:
Figurine multiplicity suggests many small powers or roles rather than one dogma. House renewal rites bind buildings to persons. Cosmology intimate—courtyard and oven—not Near Eastern temple-state.

Many figurine types suggest role diversity in the sacred—ages, genders, animals—rather than monotheism avant la lettre. Courtyard and oven remain the cathedral.
balkans.science:
Vinča-region copper mining and smelting among Europe’s earliest metallurgical sciences. Agricultural surplus on river plains. Symbolic notations on pots remain an open research question, not decoded script.

Smelting experiments are iterative and local; slag and malachite stains are lab notebooks in dirt. Agricultural surplus on river plains is what frees hands for metal and marks.
balkans.summary: Dense tells, Vinča dark-burnished ware, elaborate figurines, early copper—proto-metal complexity with debated Vinča symbols, still mostly pre-steppe.

eastern.culture:
Low-hierarchy mega-population experiments—thousands in planned circuits facing the steppe. Cattle and manure management sustain aggregation. Neighboring steppe burial politics offer a contrasting social grammar just beyond the painted-pottery world.

Megasite circuits imply assembly rules—where houses face, how cattle are fenced, when houses burn—soft urbanism without kings. Neighboring steppe Eneolithic burial politics offer a contrasting grammar just beyond the painted rings.

Key sites: Nebelivka, Maidanetske, Talianki megasites; Cucuteni painted-pottery heartlands; Usatove and Serednii Stih Eneolithic steppe contexts; Burned-house horizons of Trypillia settlements.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous megasite planners and potters; steppe Eneolithic burial elites remain nameless.
eastern.description:
Cucuteni–Trypillia painted pottery—spirals, meanders, swirling polychrome—is among prehistoric Europe’s great ceramic arts; clay figurines and house models fill settlements. Megasites such as Nebelivka, Maidanetske, and Talianki arrange houses in vast concentric circuits—urban-scale design without palaces. Burned-house horizons create dramatic archaeological colour.

Isotope food-webs show dung-manured pulse–cereal systems and fenced cattle pastures feeding mega-populations. Decline looks social as much as climatic. Neighboring Pontic Eneolithic groups keep different burial politics; aDNA tracks Caucasus–Lower Volga–related waves into Usatove and Serednii Stih—precursors of Yamnaya—while incorporating farmer and forager outsiders.

Schematic ancestry keeps EHG + CHG-related as separate ingredients beside Trypillia EEF—forming the steppe package, not yet scored as full WSH. Language: contact zone; early IE on the steppe side only as hypothesis.
eastern.ancestryNote: Pre-Yamnaya Pontic: EHG + CHG-related as separate ingredients beside Trypillia EEF — forming steppe package, not scored as WSH yet.
eastern.linguisticNote: Unknown. Possible early IE on the steppe side only as hypothesis.

ancestryCline.label: Trypillia farms → Pontic steppe edge
ancestryCline.note: EEF higher in Trypillia; EHG/CHG-related rise toward Usatove / Serednii Stih (pre-WSH fusion).

eastern.art:
Polychrome painted pottery at artistic peak; figurines; house models; burned daub and ash horizons as inadvertent palette. Megasite planning as design at 100–300+ ha scale.

Polychrome pottery at this peak is not folk decoration; it is competitive virtuosity across settlements that could see each other’s smoke. House models and figurines fill domestic space with portable architecture and bodies.
eastern.ideas: Megasites (Nebelivka, Maidanetske, Talianki) experiment with low-hierarchy mega-population living—thousands in planned circuits facing the steppe. Cattle, pulses, and manure management sustain the idea of aggregation; decline looks social as much as climatic. Neighboring steppe Eneolithic groups keep different burial politics just beyond the painted-pottery world.
eastern.philosophy:
Figurines, house models, and possible deliberate house burning suggest renewal rites binding household, woman/ancestor imagery, and settlement cycle. Painted pottery may encode mythic pattern language—beautiful, undeciphered. Village-wide and ceramic, not temple-priestly in a Near Eastern sense.

House models and figurines keep cosmology domestic even when settlement size looks urban to our eyes. Painted meanders may be mythic pattern language—beautiful, undeciphered.
eastern.science:
Integrated agro-science: manured pulses/cereals, fenced cattle, surplus for craft. Settlement surveying at mega-hectare scale. Pottery pigment and firing chemistry at peak before Corded Ware–steppe transformations remake the east.

Manure isotopes and settlement surveying show agro-engineering capable of feeding thousands before the steppe remakes the board. Pigment chemistry and firing control reach artistic-technical peaks on the forest-steppe edge.
eastern.summary: Trypillia megasites and swirling painted pottery meet Eneolithic steppe groups—pre-Yamnaya crucible of EEF, EHG, and CHG-related ancestries.

mapLayers.art: Material signature of Narva / Comb Ware foragers: the objects, monuments, and dress styles that archaeologists use to draw this substrate layer on the Middle–Late Neolithic map.
mapLayers.ideas: Narva / Comb Ware foragers ideas of belonging are read from graves, enclosures, and exchange—who is buried with what, who shares ceramic recipes, who is kept outside the ditch.
mapLayers.philosophy: Named philosophers are anachronistic for Narva / Comb Ware foragers. Treat cosmology as ritual geometry, ancestor practice, and craft taboo—reconstructed, not quoted.

GBR.name: British megalith builders
GBR.summary: Boyne Valley, Orkney, and Wessex monument societies—EEF+WHG farmers whose stone cosmologies precede Beaker demographic collapse.
GBR.conflicts: Regional monument competition; gene pool later collapses in Beaker age.
GBR.literature: Megalithic Europe speaks in stone alignments and passage-grave orientations — a literature of astronomy and ancestry without alphabet. Later folklore about giants and stone tables is a distant echo, not a primary source. Insular voices and North Sea contact give this place a distinctive accent in the wider European chorus.
GBR.art: Passage tombs of the Boyne Valley, Orkney’s Maeshowe-type chambers, and stone circles culminating toward Stonehenge turn islands into ritual landscapes of carved kerbs, spiral art, and aligned passages. Grooved Ware pottery and carved stone balls add portable grammar to the monumental outdoor gallery. Skara Brae’s stone furniture shows domestic design as carefully composed as tombs.
GBR.religion: Atlantic megalithic religion: collective tombs, ancestor bone circulation, and solar-aligned monuments (e.g. Stonehenge landscape). Ritual feasting at causewayed enclosures.
GBR.ideas:
Pilgrimage and alliance across the Irish Sea; monuments as political arguments. Cattle feasting fuels labour. A north/west versus south cline in WHG share shows that even ‘British Neolithic’ was not one uniform percentage.

Monument clusters compete and collaborate—pilgrimage can knit rivals as easily as it can stage them.
GBR.philosophy:
Solar and lunar alignments (Newgrange’s midwinter light; circle horizons) embed sky cosmology in architecture. Collective and successive burials keep the dead as active community members. Philosophy here is practised astronomy-and-ancestry, not named schools.

Midwinter light and circle horizons turn astronomy into ethics: keeping time with the dead is a communal duty.
GBR.science:
Surveying, megalith transport, horizon astronomy, manuring and mixed farming, flint mining, and axe distribution form an integrated technical world. Precision of alignment is remarkable for pre-literate societies.

Axe factories and flint mines imply apprenticeship and quality control; not every block becomes a travelling axe.
GBR.culture:
Monument clusters imply regional gathering, labour mobilisation, and competitive prestige among farming communities. Kinship and land claims were argued in stone: who builds, who buries, who feasts. Specialised flint mines and axe factories (Grimes Graves, Langdale) show craft economies feeding ritual and clearance alike.

Quarry crews, tomb teams, and feast hosts form overlapping labour publics; prestige accrues to those who can move stone and meat at landscape scale.

Key sites: Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange, Knowth, Dowth); Maeshowe and Orkney World Heritage monuments; Skara Brae; Stonehenge landscape (pre-/early stone phases in this era’s long tail); Langdale axe quarries; Grimes Graves flint mines.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous astronomer-builders and quarry specialists; no attested personal names.
GBR.description:
The Middle–Late Neolithic islands raised some of Atlantic Europe’s densest ritual landscapes: Newgrange and the Boyne tombs, Orkney’s Maeshowe-type chambers and villages such as Skara Brae, and the long Wessex sequence toward Stonehenge’s stone phases. Grooved Ware pottery and carved stone balls added portable grammar to outdoor galleries of kerbs, spirals, and aligned passages.

Genomically these were still Anatolian farmer–related populations with WHG admixture—often higher in north/west monument zones than in denser southern farming—and still without steppe ancestry. This is precisely the gene pool later replaced in the Beaker age; culturally they look triumphant, demographically they were doomed relative to the third millennium.

Irish Sea and northern networks shared tomb forms and ceramics—an Atlantic ceremonial commons of pilgrimage, alliance, and competitive display.

FRA.name: Chasséen / megalithic France
FRA.summary: Carnac alignments, Morbihan tumuli, and Chasséen networks—Atlantic ritual economies and interior enclosures in a still pre-steppe EEF+WHG France.
FRA.conflicts: Regional farmer identities; steppe still absent.
FRA.literature: Megalithic Europe speaks in stone alignments and passage-grave orientations — a literature of astronomy and ancestry without alphabet. Later folklore about giants and stone tables is a distant echo, not a primary source. French courts and vernaculars repeatedly set continental fashions of word and dress.
FRA.art: Carnac’s alignments, Morbihan tumuli, and Barnenez-type cairns make northwest France Europe’s densest stone theatre; Chasséen pottery and enclosures organise the interior. Jadeitite ceremonial axes from Alpine sources appear broken or deposited as luminous green prestige art. Engraved stones and monumental façades turn geology into sculpture at landscape scale.
FRA.religion: Chasséen / Breton–Atlantic megaliths: passage graves, menhirs, and enclosure ceremonies. Ancestor veneration and landscape sacralization dominate the evidence.
FRA.ideas:
Ritual competition and soft standardisation replace Early Neolithic pioneer dualism with denser regional systems. Atlantic megalithic ideas radiate toward the islands. Ancestry clines show culture shared across genetically slightly different farmer bodies.

Chasséen standardisation inland and Armorican spectacle on the coast are complementary politics—one of networks, one of skylines.
FRA.philosophy:
Menhirs and passage graves stage skyline, ancestor, and processional path. Broken axe deposits suggest sacrifice of wealth to powers of place or death. Sacred time is seasonal and funerary—solstice light, tomb re-entry—not treatise.

Processional avenues between menhirs script bodies into ritual movement; belief is walked, not written.
FRA.science:
Moving multi-tonne menhirs demands levers, ropes, ramps, and labour accounting. Horizon astronomy and careful siting bind monuments to landmarks. Intensive farming on Armorican and Paris-Basin soils underwrites calorie surplus behind stone spectacle.

Erecting menhirs teaches soil, fulcrum, and rope as civic sciences; failures leave toppled lessons at field edges.
FRA.culture:
Chasséen networks standardised pottery and flint across wide tracts—a soft political grammar. Monument labour on Armorica implies seasonal aggregation and prestige competition. Enclosures gathered people for feasts and boundary-making inland.

Alignment and tumulus projects imply sponsors able to call labour across multiple settlements—soft hierarchies visible in stone even without named lords.

Key sites: Carnac alignments (Ménec, Kermario); Tumulus Saint-Michel / Morbihan monumental tombs; Cairn of Barnenez; Chasséen enclosure and settlement sites of interior France.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous alignment builders and jade-axe patrons; no attested names.
FRA.description:
Middle Neolithic France became a cultural mosaic: Chasséen and related facies organising much of the interior with pottery and enclosures, while northwest Armorica raised Europe’s densest stone theatre—Carnac’s alignments, Morbihan tumuli, Barnenez-type cairns. Jadeitite ceremonial axes from Alpine sources appear broken or deposited as luminous green prestige art.

Farmer–forager admixture was ongoing; WHG ran higher on the Atlantic megalithic west than in some eastern Chasséen cores. Steppe ancestry was still absent. Northern France’s mixed Cardial–Danubian heritage helped launch megalithic ideas toward Britain and the North Sea.

Competitive ritual economies—who raises the longest alignment, who buries with Alpine jade—structured Atlantic elites without kings we can name.

DEU.name: TRB / Michelsberg
DEU.summary: Post-LBK regionalisation: Michelsberg enclosures, Funnelbeaker north, rising WHG in farmers, early GAC—still pre-steppe.
DEU.conflicts: GAC forms toward Late Neolithic; pressure from east later.
DEU.literature: Megalithic Europe speaks in stone alignments and passage-grave orientations — a literature of astronomy and ancestry without alphabet. Later folklore about giants and stone tables is a distant echo, not a primary source. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.
DEU.art:
Michelsberg tulip beakers, Funnelbeaker pottery, northern megaliths, flint daggers, later Globular Amphora jars—diversified post-LBK visual field. Monumentality patchier than Atlantic but still marks ancestors.

Tulip beakers and flint daggers stage status at the mouth and the belt—portable rank markers for a post-longhouse age.
DEU.religion: TRB / Michelsberg: enclosure rituals, cattle offerings, and early megalithic tombs. Community ancestor cult more visible than individual named deities.
DEU.ideas: After LBK’s crisis, regional cultures multiply—enclosures, new flint economies, and northern TRB links. WHG ancestry resurges inside farmer populations; forager blood returns without restoring forager life. Early Globular Amphora hints at cattle-centred wealth and new burial politics toward the late 4th millennium.
DEU.philosophy:
Causewayed and ditched enclosures as temporary sacred cities of earth. Megalithic and flat graves encode competing claims about who the dead remain. Belief practice-rich and name-poor.

Earthwork sanctuaries are temporary cities of meaning; when the feast ends, the sacred ditch remains as a scar of assembly.
DEU.science:
Deep flint mining and specialist axe production approach industrial extraction before metal. Crop–livestock intensification; enclosures imply surplus and organised labour. TRB northern transfer of agronomy.

Mine shafts and debitage piles are textbooks in chalk geology written by specialised labour.
DEU.culture:
Enclosures gather people for feasts, rites, and boundary-making—temporary earthworks as political technology. Flint daggers and specialist mining (Rijckholt tradition) mark status and industry. Northern TRB contact transfers farming know-how toward Scandinavia.

Enclosure feasts redistribute meat and obligations; Middle Neolithic politics is calendrical as much as territorial.

Key sites: Michelsberg enclosure sites of the Rhineland; Northern TRB megalithic tombs (North European Plain); Rijckholt and related flint-mine systems; Early Globular Amphora burial contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous enclosure builders and flint miners.
DEU.description:
After LBK’s crisis, Central Europe multiplied regional cultures: Michelsberg tulip beakers and enclosures, Funnelbeaker (TRB) links on the northern plain with megalithic tombs, and toward the late fourth millennium early Globular Amphora (GAC) hints of cattle-centred wealth and new burial politics. WHG ancestry resurges inside farmer populations; forager blood returns without restoring forager life.

TRB is not genetically uniform—WHG higher in northern TRB, EEF higher in southern/central cores. Steppe-related ancestry is still essentially absent; Corded Ware transformations lie ahead. GAC forms part of the farmer world that will later mix into Corded Ware.

Languages remain unknown; CW-linked Indo-European models concern the next age.

UKR.name: Cucuteni–Trypillia
UKR.summary: Trypillia megasites and swirling painted pottery meet Eneolithic steppe groups—pre-Yamnaya crucible of EEF, EHG, and CHG-related ancestries.
UKR.conflicts: Contact and conflict/exchange with Pontic Eneolithic steppe groups (Usatove, Serednii Stih).
UKR.literature: Megalithic Europe speaks in stone alignments and passage-grave orientations — a literature of astronomy and ancestry without alphabet. Later folklore about giants and stone tables is a distant echo, not a primary source. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art:
Polychrome painted pottery at artistic peak; figurines; house models; burned daub and ash horizons as inadvertent palette. Megasite planning as design at 100–300+ ha scale.

Polychrome pottery at this peak is not folk decoration; it is competitive virtuosity across settlements that could see each other’s smoke. House models and figurines fill domestic space with portable architecture and bodies.
UKR.religion: Cucuteni–Trypillia: house figurines, intentional house burning, and cemetery rites — domestic and settlement-scale cult practice at huge agrarian sites.
UKR.ideas: Megasites (Nebelivka, Maidanetske, Talianki) experiment with low-hierarchy mega-population living—thousands in planned circuits facing the steppe. Cattle, pulses, and manure management sustain the idea of aggregation; decline looks social as much as climatic. Neighboring steppe Eneolithic groups keep different burial politics just beyond the painted-pottery world.
UKR.philosophy:
Figurines, house models, and possible deliberate house burning suggest renewal rites binding household, woman/ancestor imagery, and settlement cycle. Painted pottery may encode mythic pattern language—beautiful, undeciphered. Village-wide and ceramic, not temple-priestly in a Near Eastern sense.

House models and figurines keep cosmology domestic even when settlement size looks urban to our eyes. Painted meanders may be mythic pattern language—beautiful, undeciphered.
UKR.science:
Integrated agro-science: manured pulses/cereals, fenced cattle, surplus for craft. Settlement surveying at mega-hectare scale. Pottery pigment and firing chemistry at peak before Corded Ware–steppe transformations remake the east.

Manure isotopes and settlement surveying show agro-engineering capable of feeding thousands before the steppe remakes the board. Pigment chemistry and firing control reach artistic-technical peaks on the forest-steppe edge.
UKR.culture:
Low-hierarchy mega-population experiments—thousands in planned circuits facing the steppe. Cattle and manure management sustain aggregation. Neighboring steppe burial politics offer a contrasting social grammar just beyond the painted-pottery world.

Megasite circuits imply assembly rules—where houses face, how cattle are fenced, when houses burn—soft urbanism without kings. Neighboring steppe Eneolithic burial politics offer a contrasting grammar just beyond the painted rings.

Key sites: Nebelivka, Maidanetske, Talianki megasites; Cucuteni painted-pottery heartlands; Usatove and Serednii Stih Eneolithic steppe contexts; Burned-house horizons of Trypillia settlements.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous megasite planners and potters; steppe Eneolithic burial elites remain nameless.
UKR.description:
Cucuteni–Trypillia painted pottery—spirals, meanders, swirling polychrome—is among prehistoric Europe’s great ceramic arts; clay figurines and house models fill settlements. Megasites such as Nebelivka, Maidanetske, and Talianki arrange houses in vast concentric circuits—urban-scale design without palaces. Burned-house horizons create dramatic archaeological colour.

Isotope food-webs show dung-manured pulse–cereal systems and fenced cattle pastures feeding mega-populations. Decline looks social as much as climatic. Neighboring Pontic Eneolithic groups keep different burial politics; aDNA tracks Caucasus–Lower Volga–related waves into Usatove and Serednii Stih—precursors of Yamnaya—while incorporating farmer and forager outsiders.

Schematic ancestry keeps EHG + CHG-related as separate ingredients beside Trypillia EEF—forming the steppe package, not yet scored as full WSH. Language: contact zone; early IE on the steppe side only as hypothesis.

DNK.name: TRB Scandinavia
DNK.summary: TRB farmers bring cereals, cattle, and dolmens north while Pitted Ware coastal foragers keep SHG-rich seal hunting—two genetic regimes under one map period.
DNK.conflicts: Residual forager (Pitted Ware) coexistence on coasts.
DNK.literature: Megalithic Europe speaks in stone alignments and passage-grave orientations — a literature of astronomy and ancestry without alphabet. Later folklore about giants and stone tables is a distant echo, not a primary source. Danish gatekeeping of the Baltic Sound makes culture a toll-booth as well as a stage.
DNK.art:
Funnelbeakers, dolmens, polished axes, amber; Pitted Ware’s contrasting coastal ceramic style. Monumentality is architectural more than figurative.

Funnelbeakers and dolmens announce farmer spectacle; Pitted Ware keeps a rougher coastal ceramic voice beside them. Amber and flint daggers glitter as prestige in both conversations.
DNK.religion: TRB Scandinavia: megalithic tombs, amber offerings, and wetland deposits. Ancestor burial architecture is the clearest ritual signature.
DNK.ideas:
Agriculture as northern package; dual societies as lived politics. Cattle, clearing, and tombs rewrite tenure while coasts refuse full conversion.

Dual societies prove that maps labelled ‘Neolithic Scandinavia’ flatten a lived argument. Land tenure by tomb and clearing coexists with coastal hunting rights that never fully convert.
DNK.philosophy:
Dolmens gather bones of many under caps open to sky. Wetland depositions fuse older water sacredness with megalithic ancestor/sky themes.

Bog offerings of axes show water keeping its old rights inside farming religion. Dolmen collectives open bones to the sky while wetlands still take polished gifts.
DNK.science:
Adapting cereals and livestock to short northern seasons—agricultural R&D at climatic margin. Megalith transport and Danish flint-mine intensification. Pitted Ware preserves parallel marine science beside the plough.

Short-season cereals and frost-kill risk make northern TRB an applied climate laboratory. Flint mines and megalith logistics organise labour at scales Ertebølle never needed.
DNK.culture:
Tomb building and forest clearance mobilise communal labour. Dual TRB/Pitted Ware lifeways mean parallel prestige systems—cattle and flint inland, seals and marine hunting on coasts. Amber and flint daggers circulate as bright prestige.

TRB tomb builders and Pitted Ware seal hunters may share beaches and still refuse each other’s full moral economy—parallel Scandinavias in one era. Cattle feasts and seal oil lamps light different nights of the same archipelago.

Key sites: Danish TRB dolmens and passage graves; Early Scandinavian flint mines; Pitted Ware coastal sites (e.g. Ajvide-type contexts in wider tradition); Southern Swedish TRB farming settlements.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous dolmen builders and Pitted Ware seal hunters.
DNK.description:
Funnelbeaker farming and megaliths arrive as a northern package, absorbing and displacing Ertebølle unevenly. Funnel-necked beakers, polished flint axes, and dolmens/passage graves rewrite land tenure with clearing and cattle. Beside TRB, Pitted Ware groups keep a contrasting seal-hunter ceramic style on coasts with high HG ancestry—dual societies in places, not a single Scandinavian Neolithic mix.

Schematic ancestry splits with geography: EEF-led TRB inland/south versus SHG/WHG-rich Pitted Ware holdouts. Pre-Germanic linguistic models attach to later Battle Axe stages, not automatically to TRB.

Wetland axe and pottery depositions continue older water rites inside a new farming religion of fertility and lineage.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous dolmen builders and Pitted Ware seal hunters.
SWE.description:
Funnelbeaker farming and megaliths arrive as a northern package, absorbing and displacing Ertebølle unevenly. Funnel-necked beakers, polished flint axes, and dolmens/passage graves rewrite land tenure with clearing and cattle. Beside TRB, Pitted Ware groups keep a contrasting seal-hunter ceramic style on coasts with high HG ancestry—dual societies in places, not a single Scandinavian Neolithic mix.

Schematic ancestry splits with geography: EEF-led TRB inland/south versus SHG/WHG-rich Pitted Ware holdouts. Pre-Germanic linguistic models attach to later Battle Axe stages, not automatically to TRB.

Wetland axe and pottery depositions continue older water rites inside a new farming religion of fertility and lineage.
