POL.name: TRB / early GAC Poland
POL.summary: Post-LBK regionalisation: Michelsberg enclosures, Funnelbeaker north, rising WHG in farmers, early GAC—still pre-steppe.
POL.literature: Megalithic Europe speaks in stone alignments and passage-grave orientations — a literature of astronomy and ancestry without alphabet. Later folklore about giants and stone tables is a distant echo, not a primary source. Polish–Lithuanian and later Polish culture specializes in noble liberty myths and romantic survival art.
POL.art:
Michelsberg tulip beakers, Funnelbeaker pottery, northern megaliths, flint daggers, later Globular Amphora jars—diversified post-LBK visual field. Monumentality patchier than Atlantic but still marks ancestors.

Tulip beakers and flint daggers stage status at the mouth and the belt—portable rank markers for a post-longhouse age.
POL.religion: TRB / early GAC: megalithic and flat cemeteries, animal offerings, and enclosure rites. GAC cattle-and-amber ritual intensifies toward the steppe contact zone.
POL.ideas: After LBK’s crisis, regional cultures multiply—enclosures, new flint economies, and northern TRB links. WHG ancestry resurges inside farmer populations; forager blood returns without restoring forager life. Early Globular Amphora hints at cattle-centred wealth and new burial politics toward the late 4th millennium.
POL.philosophy:
Causewayed and ditched enclosures as temporary sacred cities of earth. Megalithic and flat graves encode competing claims about who the dead remain. Belief practice-rich and name-poor.

Earthwork sanctuaries are temporary cities of meaning; when the feast ends, the sacred ditch remains as a scar of assembly.
POL.science:
Deep flint mining and specialist axe production approach industrial extraction before metal. Crop–livestock intensification; enclosures imply surplus and organised labour. TRB northern transfer of agronomy.

Mine shafts and debitage piles are textbooks in chalk geology written by specialised labour.
POL.culture:
Enclosures gather people for feasts, rites, and boundary-making—temporary earthworks as political technology. Flint daggers and specialist mining (Rijckholt tradition) mark status and industry. Northern TRB contact transfers farming know-how toward Scandinavia.

Enclosure feasts redistribute meat and obligations; Middle Neolithic politics is calendrical as much as territorial.

Key sites: Michelsberg enclosure sites of the Rhineland; Northern TRB megalithic tombs (North European Plain); Rijckholt and related flint-mine systems; Early Globular Amphora burial contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous enclosure builders and flint miners.
POL.description:
After LBK’s crisis, Central Europe multiplied regional cultures: Michelsberg tulip beakers and enclosures, Funnelbeaker (TRB) links on the northern plain with megalithic tombs, and toward the late fourth millennium early Globular Amphora (GAC) hints of cattle-centred wealth and new burial politics. WHG ancestry resurges inside farmer populations; forager blood returns without restoring forager life.

TRB is not genetically uniform—WHG higher in northern TRB, EEF higher in southern/central cores. Steppe-related ancestry is still essentially absent; Corded Ware transformations lie ahead. GAC forms part of the farmer world that will later mix into Corded Ware.

Languages remain unknown; CW-linked Indo-European models concern the next age.

ESP.description:
By the later fourth millennium BCE, Iberia’s Neolithic had thickened from coastal pioneer villages into inland farming and a monumental Atlantic–southern façade. Passage graves, tholoi, and engraved schist plaques made ancestry visible for kilometres. Collective tomb reuse staged politics of belonging in stone chambers; amber, variscite, and exotic axes circulated as prestige beside the dead.

Genomically the population remained EEF-dominated, yet WHG ancestry rose again—especially on Atlantic megalithic façades versus some southern inland cores. This was a within-culture farmer cline, not a return to Mesolithic life, and steppe-related ancestry was still essentially absent. Identity was practice (tomb, plough, plaque), not genomic purity.

Exchange networks for jadeitite, Iberian greenstone, and marine shell stitched coasts to hinterlands, foreshadowing Copper Age complexity without yet importing Yamnaya genetics. Languages stayed unwritten and pre-IE in any recoverable sense; historical Iberian scripts lie millennia ahead.
ESP.summary: Passage graves, tholoi, and engraved plaques turn Atlantic and southern Iberia into ancestor theatres while EEF farmers absorb renewed WHG ancestry—still pre-steppe.
ESP.culture:
Collective burial and tomb re-entry invent a politics of ancestry: who belongs is argued in chambers and offerings. Labour for quarrying and levering stones implies seasonal aggregation beyond the single household. Prestige goods mark differentiation short of named kings.

Villages and herding intensified on Atlantic and southern soils; monument clusters suggest regional pilgrimage and alliance without a single Iberian capital.

Tomb re-entry across generations turns kinship into a public archive: bones are rearranged, offerings refreshed, and claims on pasture rehearsed in front of the dead.

Key sites: Antequera dolmens (Menga, Viera, El Romeral); Atlantic Portuguese and Galician passage graves; Alentejo / southwestern engraved schist plaque zones; Los Millares precursor landscapes (toward Copper Age).

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous tomb builders and plaque carvers; no attested rulers or sages.
ESP.art:
Monumental gallery architecture—corbelled chambers, corridors, engraved kerbs—replaces the quiet Cardial household aesthetic with public stone theatre. Geometric plaque ‘idols’ and eye motifs hint at personified powers. Amber, variscite, and greenstone axes become luminous prestige media inside and beside tombs.

Schist plaques vary enough to hint at workshop habits and local ‘faces,’ yet standardised enough to travel as a recognisable sacred medium.
ESP.ideas:
Ancestry made landscape-scale: tombs as claims, horizons as ritual frames. Long-distance stone sourcing implies remembered exchange routes and surveying of outcrops. WHG gene flow into farmer bodies shows that ‘Neolithic’ culture could absorb forager ancestry while keeping farmer practice.

Horizon alignments and corridor plans imply shared surveying lore among communities that never formed a single Iberian state.
ESP.philosophy:
Megaliths stage a cosmology of the dead as landscape anchors: chambers aligned to horizons, offerings, and successive depositions keep ancestors present. Engraved plaques suggest powers without readable pantheons. Ritual time is generational—re-entering the tomb—rather than priestly scripture. No invented named philosophers.

Eye motifs and geometric bodies on plaques invite personhood without yielding a pantheon list—powers felt, not catalogued.
ESP.science:
Builders mastered quarrying, levering, and sighting large stones into stable chambers. Agricultural intensification paired with herding; archaeobotany and isotopes show mixed farming tuned to regional rainfall. Long-distance lithic sourcing is applied geology and logistics.

Corbelling and capstone balance are empirical structural engineering taught by failure and success across tomb generations.

IRL.description:
The Middle–Late Neolithic islands raised some of Atlantic Europe’s densest ritual landscapes: Newgrange and the Boyne tombs, Orkney’s Maeshowe-type chambers and villages such as Skara Brae, and the long Wessex sequence toward Stonehenge’s stone phases. Grooved Ware pottery and carved stone balls added portable grammar to outdoor galleries of kerbs, spirals, and aligned passages.

Genomically these were still Anatolian farmer–related populations with WHG admixture—often higher in north/west monument zones than in denser southern farming—and still without steppe ancestry. This is precisely the gene pool later replaced in the Beaker age; culturally they look triumphant, demographically they were doomed relative to the third millennium.

Irish Sea and northern networks shared tomb forms and ceramics—an Atlantic ceremonial commons of pilgrimage, alliance, and competitive display.
IRL.summary: Boyne Valley, Orkney, and Wessex monument societies—EEF+WHG farmers whose stone cosmologies precede Beaker demographic collapse.
IRL.culture:
Monument clusters imply regional gathering, labour mobilisation, and competitive prestige among farming communities. Kinship and land claims were argued in stone: who builds, who buries, who feasts. Specialised flint mines and axe factories (Grimes Graves, Langdale) show craft economies feeding ritual and clearance alike.

Quarry crews, tomb teams, and feast hosts form overlapping labour publics; prestige accrues to those who can move stone and meat at landscape scale.

Key sites: Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange, Knowth, Dowth); Maeshowe and Orkney World Heritage monuments; Skara Brae; Stonehenge landscape (pre-/early stone phases in this era’s long tail); Langdale axe quarries; Grimes Graves flint mines.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous astronomer-builders and quarry specialists; no attested personal names.
IRL.art:
Passage-tomb art, stone circles, Grooved Ware, carved stone balls, and Skara Brae’s stone furniture compose domestic and funerary design at equal intensity. Spirals and lozenges on kerbs turn geology into a shared Atlantic iconography.

Passage-tomb art and Grooved Ware circulate as a shared Atlantic grammar, readable from Orkney to the Boyne even when dialects of motif diverge.
IRL.ideas:
Pilgrimage and alliance across the Irish Sea; monuments as political arguments. Cattle feasting fuels labour. A north/west versus south cline in WHG share shows that even ‘British Neolithic’ was not one uniform percentage.

Monument clusters compete and collaborate—pilgrimage can knit rivals as easily as it can stage them.
IRL.philosophy:
Solar and lunar alignments (Newgrange’s midwinter light; circle horizons) embed sky cosmology in architecture. Collective and successive burials keep the dead as active community members. Philosophy here is practised astronomy-and-ancestry, not named schools.

Midwinter light and circle horizons turn astronomy into ethics: keeping time with the dead is a communal duty.
IRL.science:
Surveying, megalith transport, horizon astronomy, manuring and mixed farming, flint mining, and axe distribution form an integrated technical world. Precision of alignment is remarkable for pre-literate societies.

Axe factories and flint mines imply apprenticeship and quality control; not every block becomes a travelling axe.

Monument clusters imply regional gathering, labour mobilisation, and competitive prestige among farming communities. Kinship and land claims were argued in stone: who builds, who buries, who feasts. Specialised flint mines and axe factories (Grimes Graves, Langdale) show craft economies feeding ritual and clearance alike.

Quarry crews, tomb teams, and feast hosts form overlapping labour publics; prestige accrues to those who can move stone and meat at landscape scale.

Key sites: Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange, Knowth, Dowth); Maeshowe and Orkney World Heritage monuments; Skara Brae; Stonehenge landscape (pre-/early stone phases in this era’s long tail); Langdale axe quarries; Grimes Graves flint mines.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous astronomer-builders and quarry specialists; no attested personal names.
IMN.art:
Passage-tomb art, stone circles, Grooved Ware, carved stone balls, and Skara Brae’s stone furniture compose domestic and funerary design at equal intensity. Spirals and lozenges on kerbs turn geology into a shared Atlantic iconography.

Passage-tomb art and Grooved Ware circulate as a shared Atlantic grammar, readable from Orkney to the Boyne even when dialects of motif diverge.
IMN.ideas:
Pilgrimage and alliance across the Irish Sea; monuments as political arguments. Cattle feasting fuels labour. A north/west versus south cline in WHG share shows that even ‘British Neolithic’ was not one uniform percentage.

Monument clusters compete and collaborate—pilgrimage can knit rivals as easily as it can stage them.
IMN.philosophy:
Solar and lunar alignments (Newgrange’s midwinter light; circle horizons) embed sky cosmology in architecture. Collective and successive burials keep the dead as active community members. Philosophy here is practised astronomy-and-ancestry, not named schools.

Midwinter light and circle horizons turn astronomy into ethics: keeping time with the dead is a communal duty.
IMN.science:
Surveying, megalith transport, horizon astronomy, manuring and mixed farming, flint mining, and axe distribution form an integrated technical world. Precision of alignment is remarkable for pre-literate societies.

Axe factories and flint mines imply apprenticeship and quality control; not every block becomes a travelling axe.

MCO.description:
Middle Neolithic France became a cultural mosaic: Chasséen and related facies organising much of the interior with pottery and enclosures, while northwest Armorica raised Europe’s densest stone theatre—Carnac’s alignments, Morbihan tumuli, Barnenez-type cairns. Jadeitite ceremonial axes from Alpine sources appear broken or deposited as luminous green prestige art.

Farmer–forager admixture was ongoing; WHG ran higher on the Atlantic megalithic west than in some eastern Chasséen cores. Steppe ancestry was still absent. Northern France’s mixed Cardial–Danubian heritage helped launch megalithic ideas toward Britain and the North Sea.

Competitive ritual economies—who raises the longest alignment, who buries with Alpine jade—structured Atlantic elites without kings we can name.
MCO.summary: Carnac alignments, Morbihan tumuli, and Chasséen networks—Atlantic ritual economies and interior enclosures in a still pre-steppe EEF+WHG France.
MCO.culture:
Chasséen networks standardised pottery and flint across wide tracts—a soft political grammar. Monument labour on Armorica implies seasonal aggregation and prestige competition. Enclosures gathered people for feasts and boundary-making inland.

Alignment and tumulus projects imply sponsors able to call labour across multiple settlements—soft hierarchies visible in stone even without named lords.

Key sites: Carnac alignments (Ménec, Kermario); Tumulus Saint-Michel / Morbihan monumental tombs; Cairn of Barnenez; Chasséen enclosure and settlement sites of interior France.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous alignment builders and jade-axe patrons; no attested names.
MCO.art:
Menhir alignments, passage graves, engraved stones, monumental façades, Chasséen ceramics, and broken jadeitite axes compose landscape-scale sculpture plus portable prestige.

Broken jadeitite is anti-display as display: the most beautiful axe is the one removed from circulation into sacred ground.
MCO.ideas:
Ritual competition and soft standardisation replace Early Neolithic pioneer dualism with denser regional systems. Atlantic megalithic ideas radiate toward the islands. Ancestry clines show culture shared across genetically slightly different farmer bodies.

Chasséen standardisation inland and Armorican spectacle on the coast are complementary politics—one of networks, one of skylines.
MCO.philosophy:
Menhirs and passage graves stage skyline, ancestor, and processional path. Broken axe deposits suggest sacrifice of wealth to powers of place or death. Sacred time is seasonal and funerary—solstice light, tomb re-entry—not treatise.

Processional avenues between menhirs script bodies into ritual movement; belief is walked, not written.
MCO.science:
Moving multi-tonne menhirs demands levers, ropes, ramps, and labour accounting. Horizon astronomy and careful siting bind monuments to landmarks. Intensive farming on Armorican and Paris-Basin soils underwrites calorie surplus behind stone spectacle.

Erecting menhirs teaches soil, fulcrum, and rope as civic sciences; failures leave toppled lessons at field edges.

CZE.description:
After LBK’s crisis, Central Europe multiplied regional cultures: Michelsberg tulip beakers and enclosures, Funnelbeaker (TRB) links on the northern plain with megalithic tombs, and toward the late fourth millennium early Globular Amphora (GAC) hints of cattle-centred wealth and new burial politics. WHG ancestry resurges inside farmer populations; forager blood returns without restoring forager life.

TRB is not genetically uniform—WHG higher in northern TRB, EEF higher in southern/central cores. Steppe-related ancestry is still essentially absent; Corded Ware transformations lie ahead. GAC forms part of the farmer world that will later mix into Corded Ware.

Languages remain unknown; CW-linked Indo-European models concern the next age.
CZE.summary: Post-LBK regionalisation: Michelsberg enclosures, Funnelbeaker north, rising WHG in farmers, early GAC—still pre-steppe.
CZE.culture:
Enclosures gather people for feasts, rites, and boundary-making—temporary earthworks as political technology. Flint daggers and specialist mining (Rijckholt tradition) mark status and industry. Northern TRB contact transfers farming know-how toward Scandinavia.

Enclosure feasts redistribute meat and obligations; Middle Neolithic politics is calendrical as much as territorial.

Key sites: Michelsberg enclosure sites of the Rhineland; Northern TRB megalithic tombs (North European Plain); Rijckholt and related flint-mine systems; Early Globular Amphora burial contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous enclosure builders and flint miners.
CZE.art:
Michelsberg tulip beakers, Funnelbeaker pottery, northern megaliths, flint daggers, later Globular Amphora jars—diversified post-LBK visual field. Monumentality patchier than Atlantic but still marks ancestors.

Tulip beakers and flint daggers stage status at the mouth and the belt—portable rank markers for a post-longhouse age.
CZE.ideas:
Regionalisation after pioneer uniformity. WHG resurgence inside farmer practice. Early GAC cattle politics foreshadow Late Neolithic wealth idioms.

WHG resurgence inside farmers shows genes can return along paths culture does not—hunters’ ancestry, ploughmen’s lives.
CZE.philosophy:
Causewayed and ditched enclosures as temporary sacred cities of earth. Megalithic and flat graves encode competing claims about who the dead remain. Belief practice-rich and name-poor.

Earthwork sanctuaries are temporary cities of meaning; when the feast ends, the sacred ditch remains as a scar of assembly.
CZE.science:
Deep flint mining and specialist axe production approach industrial extraction before metal. Crop–livestock intensification; enclosures imply surplus and organised labour. TRB northern transfer of agronomy.

Mine shafts and debitage piles are textbooks in chalk geology written by specialised labour.

NOR.description:
Funnelbeaker farming and megaliths arrive as a northern package, absorbing and displacing Ertebølle unevenly. Funnel-necked beakers, polished flint axes, and dolmens/passage graves rewrite land tenure with clearing and cattle. Beside TRB, Pitted Ware groups keep a contrasting seal-hunter ceramic style on coasts with high HG ancestry—dual societies in places, not a single Scandinavian Neolithic mix.

Schematic ancestry splits with geography: EEF-led TRB inland/south versus SHG/WHG-rich Pitted Ware holdouts. Pre-Germanic linguistic models attach to later Battle Axe stages, not automatically to TRB.

Wetland axe and pottery depositions continue older water rites inside a new farming religion of fertility and lineage.
NOR.summary: TRB farmers bring cereals, cattle, and dolmens north while Pitted Ware coastal foragers keep SHG-rich seal hunting—two genetic regimes under one map period.
NOR.culture:
Tomb building and forest clearance mobilise communal labour. Dual TRB/Pitted Ware lifeways mean parallel prestige systems—cattle and flint inland, seals and marine hunting on coasts. Amber and flint daggers circulate as bright prestige.

TRB tomb builders and Pitted Ware seal hunters may share beaches and still refuse each other’s full moral economy—parallel Scandinavias in one era. Cattle feasts and seal oil lamps light different nights of the same archipelago.

Key sites: Danish TRB dolmens and passage graves; Early Scandinavian flint mines; Pitted Ware coastal sites (e.g. Ajvide-type contexts in wider tradition); Southern Swedish TRB farming settlements.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous dolmen builders and Pitted Ware seal hunters.
NOR.art:
Funnelbeakers, dolmens, polished axes, amber; Pitted Ware’s contrasting coastal ceramic style. Monumentality is architectural more than figurative.

Funnelbeakers and dolmens announce farmer spectacle; Pitted Ware keeps a rougher coastal ceramic voice beside them. Amber and flint daggers glitter as prestige in both conversations.
NOR.ideas:
Agriculture as northern package; dual societies as lived politics. Cattle, clearing, and tombs rewrite tenure while coasts refuse full conversion.

Dual societies prove that maps labelled ‘Neolithic Scandinavia’ flatten a lived argument. Land tenure by tomb and clearing coexists with coastal hunting rights that never fully convert.
NOR.philosophy:
Dolmens gather bones of many under caps open to sky. Wetland depositions fuse older water sacredness with megalithic ancestor/sky themes.

Bog offerings of axes show water keeping its old rights inside farming religion. Dolmen collectives open bones to the sky while wetlands still take polished gifts.
NOR.science:
Adapting cereals and livestock to short northern seasons—agricultural R&D at climatic margin. Megalith transport and Danish flint-mine intensification. Pitted Ware preserves parallel marine science beside the plough.

Short-season cereals and frost-kill risk make northern TRB an applied climate laboratory. Flint mines and megalith logistics organise labour at scales Ertebølle never needed.

ITA.description:
Middle–Late Neolithic Italy consolidated regional ceramic ‘dialects’ (Diana, Serra d’Alto, and kin) while genetics remained EEF+WHG without meaningful steppe yet. Some regions raised megaliths and statue-menhir traditions; obsidian and greenstone axes stayed prestige media. Toward the period’s end, copper experiments in the Alpine foreland added metallurgical trial-and-error beside stone.

Social differentiation shows in grave goods before true metal-age chiefdoms. Alpine jadeitite and island stone kept Italy wired into wider western exchange.

Deep linguistic layers remain unrecoverable beneath later Italic and Etruscan.

Regional fine wares such as Diana and Serra d’Alto did not merely decorate kitchens; they advertised affiliations across Tyrrhenian and southern networks while Alpine jade and island glass kept northern and maritime paths open. Copper’s first experiments in the foreland did not abolish stone—they added a new specialist craft beside increasingly skilled ceramic chemistry.
ITA.summary: Diana, Serra d’Alto, and related farmer cultures—fine wares, rising HG admixture, Alpine jade and island stone—copper glinting at the northern edge.
ITA.culture:
Regional pottery fashions mark identities across a still-EEF genetic world with rising local HG admixture. Craft specialisation and exotic stone mark status gradients without palaces.

Grave goods begin to sort persons more loudly; Italy’s Middle Neolithic learns ranking without yet inventing palace redistributive states. Obsidian and greenstone specialists stitch coasts to Alpine paths.

Key sites: Serra d’Alto and Diana culture type sites; Obsidian-rich Middle Neolithic settlements; Alpine foreland early copper contexts (toward Remedello); Statue-menhir and megalithic zones of Alpine/Italian regions.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous potters, sailors, and early metal experimenters.
ITA.art:
Fine painted and polished wares push pottery toward display; figurines, early megaliths, and statue-menhirs in some zones; copper ornaments begin to glint in the north.

Painted and polished display wares push pottery toward gallery status; statue-menhirs, where present, drag the human outline into public stone. Copper ornaments begin to glint beside stone axes in northern graves.
ITA.ideas:
Ceramic dialects as identity. Western exchange in jade and obsidian. Gradual ranking before Remedello/Gaudo metal-age politics.

Ceramic ‘dialects’ are political speech in clay—readable affiliation when spoken languages are lost to us. Western exchange keeps Italy inside a broader farmer conversation still free of steppe genetics.
ITA.philosophy:
Figurines, structured deposits, caves, trenches, early megaliths—plural local rites. Ancestor and fertility themes dominate inference; named pantheons wait for later ages.

Plural burial modes (cave, trench, early megalith) imply plural local answers to ancestry, not a peninsula-wide church. Figurines and structured deposits remain the readable theology.
ITA.science:
Specialised pottery firing and surface chemistry. Mixed farming intensifies. Early copper experiments in Alpine foreland. Obsidian sourcing confirms sailors’ mental maps of volcanoes.

Kiln temperature control and pigment recipes become craft secrets worth marrying for; metallurgy joins that apprenticeship world at the edges. Sailors’ volcanic maps remain measurable in obsidian chemistry.

GRC.description:
Vinča and successor Late Neolithic / Copper Age facies concentrate population and craft on river plains. Dark-burnished ware, elaborate figurines, house models, and early copper ornaments (later tools) create a proto-metal aesthetic. Some signs point toward proto-writing or symbolic inventories (Vinča symbols)—still debated, never deciphered literature.

Farmer ancestry dominates; early steppe signals appear regionally toward the Copper Age on the northeast Black Sea–Danube edge as Eneolithic steppe societies form. Social ranking edges upward without full urban states. Mycenaean Greek remains a millennium+ away.

Exchange in Balkan copper and Aegean links foreshadows Eneolithic complexity.
GRC.summary: Dense tells, Vinča dark-burnished ware, elaborate figurines, early copper—proto-metal complexity with debated Vinča symbols, still mostly pre-steppe.
GRC.culture:
Tell mega-villages support craft specialists. House-based ritual and possible intentional house burning encode renewal cycles. Ranking visible in goods before palace economies.

Craft specialists on copper and fine ware imply patronage and surplus; ranking rises without dissolving household ritual centres into temple bureaucracy. Tell mega-villages concentrate people who still bury and burn close to home.

Key sites: Vinča-Belo Brdo and major Vinča tells; Pločnik and related early copper contexts; Late Neolithic tell belts of the middle Danube; Sites with Vinča symbols / notations.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous metallurgists and figurine makers; Vinča symbols have no deciphered authors.
GRC.art:
Dark-burnished Vinča ware, dense figurine cosmologies, house models, shrine-like rooms, copper gleam—household-centred visual theology.

Dark burnish and figurine intensity make Vinča visual culture feel ‘busy’—a clay cosmos of repeated gestures and faces. Copper’s first gleam joins that cosmos as precious redness.
GRC.ideas:
Craft specialisation and symbolic inventories (undeciphered). Copper as new prestige and technical frontier. Steppe contact intensifying on the northeast edge.

Vinča symbols tempt script fantasies; responsible reading keeps them as open notation, not decoded chronicles. Northeast steppe contact foreshadows Copper Age weather without yet remaking the tells.
GRC.philosophy:
Figurine multiplicity suggests many small powers or roles rather than one dogma. House renewal rites bind buildings to persons. Cosmology intimate—courtyard and oven—not Near Eastern temple-state.

Many figurine types suggest role diversity in the sacred—ages, genders, animals—rather than monotheism avant la lettre. Courtyard and oven remain the cathedral.
GRC.science:
Vinča-region copper mining and smelting among Europe’s earliest metallurgical sciences. Agricultural surplus on river plains. Symbolic notations on pots remain an open research question, not decoded script.

Smelting experiments are iterative and local; slag and malachite stains are lab notebooks in dirt. Agricultural surplus on river plains is what frees hands for metal and marks.

stories.text: Signs incised on a pot may inventory, bless, or merely decorate. Millennia later we still cannot read them as literature—and should not pretend to.

BGR.description:
Vinča and successor Late Neolithic / Copper Age facies concentrate population and craft on river plains. Dark-burnished ware, elaborate figurines, house models, and early copper ornaments (later tools) create a proto-metal aesthetic. Some signs point toward proto-writing or symbolic inventories (Vinča symbols)—still debated, never deciphered literature.

Farmer ancestry dominates; early steppe signals appear regionally toward the Copper Age on the northeast Black Sea–Danube edge as Eneolithic steppe societies form. Social ranking edges upward without full urban states. Mycenaean Greek remains a millennium+ away.

Exchange in Balkan copper and Aegean links foreshadows Eneolithic complexity.
BGR.summary: Dense tells, Vinča dark-burnished ware, elaborate figurines, early copper—proto-metal complexity with debated Vinča symbols, still mostly pre-steppe.
BGR.culture:
Tell mega-villages support craft specialists. House-based ritual and possible intentional house burning encode renewal cycles. Ranking visible in goods before palace economies.

Craft specialists on copper and fine ware imply patronage and surplus; ranking rises without dissolving household ritual centres into temple bureaucracy. Tell mega-villages concentrate people who still bury and burn close to home.

Key sites: Vinča-Belo Brdo and major Vinča tells; Pločnik and related early copper contexts; Late Neolithic tell belts of the middle Danube; Sites with Vinča symbols / notations.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous metallurgists and figurine makers; Vinča symbols have no deciphered authors.
BGR.art:
Dark-burnished Vinča ware, dense figurine cosmologies, house models, shrine-like rooms, copper gleam—household-centred visual theology.

Dark burnish and figurine intensity make Vinča visual culture feel ‘busy’—a clay cosmos of repeated gestures and faces. Copper’s first gleam joins that cosmos as precious redness.
BGR.ideas:
Craft specialisation and symbolic inventories (undeciphered). Copper as new prestige and technical frontier. Steppe contact intensifying on the northeast edge.

Vinča symbols tempt script fantasies; responsible reading keeps them as open notation, not decoded chronicles. Northeast steppe contact foreshadows Copper Age weather without yet remaking the tells.
BGR.philosophy:
Figurine multiplicity suggests many small powers or roles rather than one dogma. House renewal rites bind buildings to persons. Cosmology intimate—courtyard and oven—not Near Eastern temple-state.

Many figurine types suggest role diversity in the sacred—ages, genders, animals—rather than monotheism avant la lettre. Courtyard and oven remain the cathedral.
BGR.science:
Vinča-region copper mining and smelting among Europe’s earliest metallurgical sciences. Agricultural surplus on river plains. Symbolic notations on pots remain an open research question, not decoded script.

Smelting experiments are iterative and local; slag and malachite stains are lab notebooks in dirt. Agricultural surplus on river plains is what frees hands for metal and marks.

BLR.description:
Cucuteni–Trypillia painted pottery—spirals, meanders, swirling polychrome—is among prehistoric Europe’s great ceramic arts; clay figurines and house models fill settlements. Megasites such as Nebelivka, Maidanetske, and Talianki arrange houses in vast concentric circuits—urban-scale design without palaces. Burned-house horizons create dramatic archaeological colour.

Isotope food-webs show dung-manured pulse–cereal systems and fenced cattle pastures feeding mega-populations. Decline looks social as much as climatic. Neighboring Pontic Eneolithic groups keep different burial politics; aDNA tracks Caucasus–Lower Volga–related waves into Usatove and Serednii Stih—precursors of Yamnaya—while incorporating farmer and forager outsiders.

Schematic ancestry keeps EHG + CHG-related as separate ingredients beside Trypillia EEF—forming the steppe package, not yet scored as full WSH. Language: contact zone; early IE on the steppe side only as hypothesis.
BLR.summary: Trypillia megasites and swirling painted pottery meet Eneolithic steppe groups—pre-Yamnaya crucible of EEF, EHG, and CHG-related ancestries.
BLR.culture:
Low-hierarchy mega-population experiments—thousands in planned circuits facing the steppe. Cattle and manure management sustain aggregation. Neighboring steppe burial politics offer a contrasting social grammar just beyond the painted-pottery world.

Megasite circuits imply assembly rules—where houses face, how cattle are fenced, when houses burn—soft urbanism without kings. Neighboring steppe Eneolithic burial politics offer a contrasting grammar just beyond the painted rings.

Key sites: Nebelivka, Maidanetske, Talianki megasites; Cucuteni painted-pottery heartlands; Usatove and Serednii Stih Eneolithic steppe contexts; Burned-house horizons of Trypillia settlements.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous megasite planners and potters; steppe Eneolithic burial elites remain nameless.
BLR.art:
Polychrome painted pottery at artistic peak; figurines; house models; burned daub and ash horizons as inadvertent palette. Megasite planning as design at 100–300+ ha scale.

Polychrome pottery at this peak is not folk decoration; it is competitive virtuosity across settlements that could see each other’s smoke. House models and figurines fill domestic space with portable architecture and bodies.
BLR.ideas:
Aggregation without palaces. Social decline hypotheses. Steppe Eneolithic neighbors as parallel politics. Pre-Yamnaya ingredient mixing.

Low-hierarchy mega-population is a political hypothesis lived at hectare scale—and abandoned when social costs rose. Pre-Yamnaya steppe packages assemble next door while Trypillia paints its last great centuries.
BLR.philosophy:
Figurines, house models, and possible deliberate house burning suggest renewal rites binding household, woman/ancestor imagery, and settlement cycle. Painted pottery may encode mythic pattern language—beautiful, undeciphered. Village-wide and ceramic, not temple-priestly in a Near Eastern sense.

House models and figurines keep cosmology domestic even when settlement size looks urban to our eyes. Painted meanders may be mythic pattern language—beautiful, undeciphered.
BLR.science:
Integrated agro-science: manured pulses/cereals, fenced cattle, surplus for craft. Settlement surveying at mega-hectare scale. Pottery pigment and firing chemistry at peak before Corded Ware–steppe transformations remake the east.

Manure isotopes and settlement surveying show agro-engineering capable of feeding thousands before the steppe remakes the board. Pigment chemistry and firing control reach artistic-technical peaks on the forest-steppe edge.

periods.label: Yamnaya on the steppe edge
periods.narrative: At 3000 BC Yamnaya wagon-and-herd societies dominate the Pontic–Caspian steppe while Late Neolithic farmer Europe — TRB, Globular Amphora, Iberian Copper Age, British monument builders — continues west. Steppe-related ancestry is high on the core steppe and falls off as a gradient, not an instant coat. Comparative linguistics places early Indo-European speech in this horizon; western Europe is not yet Corded or Beaker.
periods.culturesNote: Yamnaya/Yamna, Afanasievo (eastward), late Trypillia, Usatove contacts, Remedello/Gaudo in Italy, late TRB/Pitted Ware in the north.

iberia.culture: Copper Age Iberian society organises around fortified hilltop centres, craft specialisation, and collective tombs that imply corporate kinship rather than steppe pastoral kings. Households farm Mediterranean crops under increasing aridity while workshops cast copper blades and shape schematic idols. Atlantic façades and the southeast speak related but not identical dialects of prestige—walls and tholoi in one zone, megalithic afterlives and coastal exchange in another. Belonging is local, ancestral, and increasingly unequal.
iberia.description:
Around 3000 BC the Iberian peninsula is a Copper Age farmer world, not a Yamnaya province. On arid southeastern hills, fortified centres in the Los Millares tradition raise stone walls, tholos tombs, and craft quarters around copper working, while Atlantic and interior communities keep their own chambered tombs, idols, and exchange routes. Hierarchy intensifies through metal, exotic ivory, and defended villages; steppe pastoral packages remain a distant eastern story.

Collective burial chambers and engraved plaque-idols bind the living to ancestral corporations that control access to copper and long-distance goods. Beaker pottery is still only a whisper on the horizon. Dress stays wool and linen with personal ornaments; status is written in fortification and tomb architecture more than in kurgan mounds.

Genetically the peninsula remains almost entirely Early European Farmer with Western Hunter-Gatherer admixture. The drama of this tick is metallurgical and social reorganisation inside a Neolithic substrate—preparing the ground for later Beaker fashion without yet remaking Iberian ancestry.
iberia.linguisticNote: Unknown pre-IE. Do not equate Copper Age cultures with Celtic.
iberia.ancestryNote: Still largely EEF+WHG; steppe ≈ 0–few percent at Copper Age start.
iberia.art: Fortified circuits, tholos chambers, copper tools, and schematic ‘eye’ idols form a visual language of walls and collective death. Ivory and ostrich-egg shell imported through Mediterranean–Atlantic chains glitter beside local stone architecture. Dress and ornament remain Neolithic in cut—wool, linen, personal beads—while metal blades begin to mark elite bodies. Art is settlement geometry and tomb furniture, not figurative rock fleets or kurgan stelae.
iberia.ideas: Hierarchy is argued through metallurgy, fortification, and control of exotic exchange rather than through Yamnaya-style mobile kingship. Ancestral corporations in collective tombs claim copper and land. The idea of Iberia at 3000 BC is a farmer world organising itself for metal—prestige as architecture and craft—while steppe ancestry and Indo-European speech models remain almost irrelevant to the peninsula’s gene pool and material brand.
iberia.philosophy: No named schools survive. Cosmology is tomb and idol: tholoi and engraved plaques keep the dead as corporate ancestors, while schematic idols hint at personified powers without a readable pantheon. Sacred order is architectural—who may enter the chamber, who owns the copper—rather than doctrinal text. Ethics are inferred from walls, offerings, and the staging of collective memory.
iberia.science: Copper smelting, casting, and arsenical alloys are the period’s hard science, paired with surveying and labour organisation for hilltop fortifications. Farmers manage dryland Mediterranean agrosystems while sourcing ivory and ostrich-egg shell through long maritime chains. Ceramic and lithic chaînes opératoires standardise household production beside new metal workshops—an applied industrial shift inside a still-Neolithic demography.

stories.text: On a southeastern ridge, builders raise dry-stone circuits around houses and workshops while tholos chambers receive the corporate dead. Copper slag stains the soil; ivory beads travel farther than any steppe wagon. Iberia’s Copper Age writes power as fortification long before Beaker pots redefine the grave.
stories.title: Walls Before Beakers

stories.text: An engraved plaque-idol with staring eyes is placed among collective bones. No pantheon is named, yet the gaze implies a power that watches ancestral corporations. Sacred knowledge here is who may reopen the chamber—and who controls the copper outside.
stories.title: The Eye in the Chamber

stories.text: Ostrich-egg shell and African ivory reach an arid hillfort through Mediterranean–Atlantic chains. Beside local wool and copper blades, the exotics advertise a world already networked by sea, not by Pontic kurgans.
stories.title: Ivory on a Dry Hill

britain.culture: Society gathers around henges, avenues, and seasonal monuments that structure time and labour. Households farm chalk and clay while investing surplus in timber and stone spectacles. Jet, amber, and stone ornaments mark persons inside a still-collective ceremonial order. Belonging is pilgrimage and monument rebuild, not single-grave martial kits.
britain.description:
At 3000 BC Britain is still a Late Neolithic farmer island. Stonehenge’s later Neolithic phases, timber circles, Grooved Ware, and carved chalk objects keep a monumental aesthetic untouched by steppe kurgan art. Collective and cremation rites, carved stone, and ceremonial landscapes dominate; metal remains scarce.

Island ceremonial commons and ancestral monuments organise politics without Yamnaya pastoral kings. Gene pools stay Early European Farmer with Western Hunter-Gatherer admixture; the ‘steppe story’ is still a continental rumour. Labour and pilgrimage around henges imply large-scale cooperation among farming communities who do not yet know they are about to be replaced.

This tick’s drama is sky theatre and stone logistics—the last centuries of Neolithic Britain before the Beaker demographic break of the mid-third millennium.
britain.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE Neolithic speech about to be marginalized/replaced in IE-shift models.
britain.ancestryNote: Still Neolithic Britain — steppe negligible until Beaker.

ancestryCline.label: North/west → south
ancestryCline.note: Residual WHG cline within Late Neolithic Britain; steppe still ~0–few %.

britain.art: Stonehenge’s later Neolithic phases, timber circles, Grooved Ware, and carved chalk objects keep a monumental island aesthetic untouched by steppe kurgan art. Collective and cremation rites, carved stone, and ceremonial landscapes dominate; metal is still scarce. Dress and ornament remain Neolithic—jet, amber, and stone—before Beaker gold arrives.
britain.ideas: Island ceremonial commons and ancestral monuments organise politics without Yamnaya pastoral kings. Gene pools stay EEF+WHG; the ‘steppe story’ is still a continental rumour. Labour and pilgrimage around henges imply large-scale cooperation among farming communities who do not yet know they are about to be replaced.
britain.philosophy: Solar alignments, processional avenues, and successive monument rebuilds encode a sky-and-ancestor cosmology in stone and timber. The dead and the solstice structure time; no pantheon is named. Sacred knowledge is architectural and calendrical—how to stand stones to catch the sun—not philosophical prose.
britain.science: Megalithic and timber engineering, horizon astronomy, and quarry logistics (bluestones, sarsens) are peak Neolithic applied science. Mixed farming on chalk and clay fuels seasonal gatherings. Trackways and boat craft stitch coasts and rivers into a pre-metal transport web.

stories.text: Builders sight the midwinter sun down an avenue of timber and stone. No named god is carved, yet the horizon becomes doctrine. Late Neolithic Britain keeps time in architecture.
stories.title: Standing for the Solstice

stories.text: Stone from distant quarries travels by land and water toward a ceremonial heartland. Logistics and belief are the same labour—moving mountains before metal remakes the island.
stories.title: Bluestones on the Move

stories.text: Grooved Ware feasts and chalk carvings fill gatherings that still look genetically Neolithic. Within centuries those same skylines will host a people whose ancestry tells another story.
stories.title: The Quiet Before Beakers

france.culture: Collective tombs and regional ceramic traditions organise farmer communities even as new bloodlines enter northern families. Households keep Atlantic and loess agrosystems; prestige still speaks in polished axes and chamber access. Society is Neolithic in structure—ancestral corporations, megalithic rites—with pastoral signals rising in isotopes and ancestry before full steppe material packages dominate.
france.description:
Around 3000 BC France sits on a genetic and cultural hinge. Late Neolithic collective tombs, Chasséen and Artenacoid ceramics, and Armorican megalithic afterlives still look farmer-European, while early steppe-related ancestry trickles into some northern burials—admixture in real time, not a finished Corded Ware map.

Paris Basin and Atlantic façades keep distinct visual dialects of chamber, plaque, and polished axe. Kinship stretches to include eastern-connected men without instantly rewriting pottery brands. Pulses near 3000–2900 BC foreshadow later Beaker and Corded standardisation without yet imposing Britain’s cliff-edge replacement.

Copper knowledge spreads unevenly from south and east while flint networks and tomb carpentry remain the technical backbone. France at this tick is a corridor of first contacts.
france.ancestryNote: Site-variable early steppe (order ~10–20% in some modeled groups); not Britain-level replacement.
france.linguisticNote: Possible early IE speech with steppe gene flow — contested; no texts.
france.art: Late Neolithic collective tombs, Chasséen and Artenacoid ceramics, and Armorican megalithic afterlives still look farmer-European while early steppe ancestry trickles in. Art is chamber, plaque, and polished axe—not yet Corded battle-axe fashion everywhere. Paris Basin and Atlantic façades keep distinct visual dialects.
france.ideas: Bréviandes-type burials capture steppe ancestry arriving inside Neolithic families—admixture in real time, not a finished Corded Ware map. Ideas of kinship stretch to include eastern-connected men without instantly rewriting pottery brands. France is a hinge of pulses (~3000/2900 BC) before Beaker standardisation.
france.philosophy: Collective tombs continue ancestor corporations even as new lineages enter; cosmology remains megalithic and household. Ritual deposits and chamber reuse matter more than any steppe stela cult. Philosophy is practice at the tomb door—who may lie inside—during demographic opening.
france.science: Farmers keep Atlantic and loess agrosystems while copper knowledge spreads unevenly from south and east. Tomb carpentry, stone transport, and flint networks remain the technical backbone. Early pastoral signals appear in isotopes and ancestry before full steppe material packages dominate.

central.culture: Cattle-rich Globular Amphora households and late Funnelbeaker neighbours organise wealth around herds, amphorae, and flint. Eastern contact brings pastoral mobility and new burial politics without instantly erasing farmer settlements. Society stands between collective Neolithic claims and the single-grave order about to standardise gendered weapon kits across the plain.
central.description:
Around 3000 BC Central Europe is the hinge on which temperate Indo-Europeanization will turn. Globular Amphora jars, cattle burials, and flint axes still define late farmer display across the North European Plain, while Yamnaya-related incomers and ideas press from the east. Within a few centuries this collision midwifes Corded Ware—admixture as ethnogenesis rather than a finished map.

Art is ceramic body and animal deposit more than figurative stone; the visual hinge is amphora to cord-impressed beaker. Social ideas pivot from collective Neolithic claims toward single-grave politics. Wheel and wagon knowledge filters west with steppe contact as pastoral mobility rises inside mixed farming landscapes.

Late TRB and GAC communities remain farmer-led even as early steppe signals appear unevenly, higher toward the east. Central Europe at this tick is the factory floor being tooled for the Corded age.
central.linguisticNote: Leading archaeological correlate of early IE expansion into the European plain.
central.ancestryNote: Late TRB/GAC still farmer-led; early steppe signals uneven — higher toward the east.

central.ideas: GAC cattle wealth and Yamnaya-related incomers collide to midwife Corded Ware—admixture as ethnogenesis. Social ideas pivot from collective Neolithic claims toward single-grave politics. Central Europe becomes the factory floor of temperate Indo-Europeanization in standard models.
central.philosophy: Cattle offerings and amphora graves imply a pastoral sacred economy; Corded dawn adds gendered weapon burial. Cosmology is read from animals, pots, and posture—practice without named teachers. Ancestor and herd are the moral pair at the hinge.
central.science: Wheel and wagon knowledge filters west with steppe contact; GAC and early CW communities manage mixed farming with rising pastoral mobility. Flint and early metal chaînes opératoires intensify. Ceramic temper recipes and cord decoration are reproducible craft science across the plain.

scandinavia.culture: TRB farmsteads and megalithic chambers structure agrarian kinship; Pitted Ware camps organise sealing, fishing, and coastal exchange. Society is plural: pig and cattle ritual inland, marine mammal economies on the strand. Belonging is ecological as much as ethnic.
scandinavia.description:
At 3000 BC Scandinavia still hosts dual economies. Funnelbeaker megaliths and pottery organise farming inland and south, while Pitted Ware seal-hunter aesthetics—bone harpoons, marine mammal art, coastal camps—hold the shores. Visual Scandinavia is split: farmer stone tombs versus forager maritime kits.

Early steppe signals are slight; the coming Single Grave turnover is not yet destiny. Identity is diet and burial as much as pottery brand. Two ideas of the good life share one peninsula—fields and seals—before battle-axe fashion remakes the north.

Megalith engineering continues beside coastal navigation that is forager science. Steppe battle-axe packages are still approaching from the continent.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Pre-IE/transitional; pre-Germanic linked to ensuing Battle Axe/SGC.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Mostly pre–Single Grave; Pitted Ware coasts keep HG-rich profiles beside TRB farms.

scandinavia.art: Funnelbeaker megaliths and pottery coexist with Pitted Ware seal-hunter aesthetics—bone harpoons, marine mammal art, and coastal camps. Visual Scandinavia is split: farmer stone tombs inland/south versus forager maritime kits on the coasts. Steppe battle-axe fashion is still approaching.
scandinavia.ideas: Dual economies encode rival goods lives in one region. Early steppe ancestry remains limited; the idea of impending Single Grave replacement is archaeological hindsight, not contemporary fate. Identity tracks diet, burial, and shore versus field.
scandinavia.philosophy: Megalithic ancestor chambers versus coastal forager rites offer rival sacred geographies. Seals, pigs, and cattle likely carried different ritual charges. Cosmology is place-and-prey, not scripture.
scandinavia.science: TRB agronomy on northern soils meets Pitted Ware marine mammal hunting and sealing technology—two applied ecologies. Megalith engineering continues; coastal navigation is forager science. Pottery tempers diverge with lifestyle.

italy.culture: Weapon-grave and chamber-tomb communities organise honour around metal kits and subterranean ancestry. Households farm Mediterranean crops; specialists cast copper. Alpine and peninsular provinces keep distinct burial dialects while sharing the Copper Age turn toward inequality and craft.
italy.description:
Around 3000 BC Italy is a Mediterranean farmer–metal world, not a Yamnaya province. Remedello weapon graves in the north and Gaudo chamber tombs farther south define Copper Age rites with tanged daggers, halberds, and distinctive pottery—an aesthetic of metal and rock-cut tomb. Alpine fringe stelae hint at anthropomorphic display while steppe kurgan art remains foreign.

Peninsular and Po communities intensify metallurgy and hierarchy on largely Early European Farmer bases with Western Hunter-Gatherer admixture. Steppe ancestry is limited compared with the Corded north. Regional tomb rites encode local belonging more than any pastoral package from the Pontic grass sea.

Early copper daggers and arsenical alloys show specialised smithing beside Mediterranean crop systems. Italy’s Copper Age is hierarchy underground and metal in the hand.
italy.linguisticNote: Unknown. Historical Italic and Etruscan are still ahead.
italy.ancestryNote: Mostly EEF+WHG; limited early steppe vs CW heartland.
italy.art: Remedello weapon graves and Gaudo chamber tombs define Copper Age Italy with tanged daggers, halberds, and distinctive pottery—an aesthetic of metal and rock-cut tomb. Stele statues in the Alpine fringe hint at anthropomorphic display. Steppe kurgan art is still foreign.
italy.ideas: Peninsular and Po communities intensify metallurgy and hierarchy on largely EEF+WHG bases; steppe ancestry is limited versus the Corded north. Copper Age Italy is a Mediterranean farmer–metal world, not a Yamnaya province. Regional tomb rites encode local belonging.
italy.philosophy: Chamber tombs and weapon deposits locate honour and ancestry underground. Alpine stelae may personify ancestors or powers without yielding readable myths. Cosmology is funerary and martial-practical.
italy.science: Early copper daggers and arsenical alloys show specialised smithing. Rock-cut tomb engineering and Mediterranean crop systems continue Neolithic agronomy with metal tools. Alpine greenstone and metal routes sketch north–south technical exchange.

balkans.culture: Riverine farmers, tell communities, and incoming pastoral groups negotiate space along the Danube and Black Sea fringe. Metallurgy, figurines, and cemetery rites keep inland farmer identities while steppe kits appear at edges. Society is corridor diplomacy in material form.
balkans.description:
Around 3000 BC the Balkans are a corridor of packages, not a single people. Danube–Black Sea contact zones show kurgan-style burials beside older tell and cemetery traditions; ochre, weapons, and pastoral kits appear on farmer edges. Figurines and fine pottery of Balkan Eneolithic traditions persist inland.

Yamnaya horizons push into the Lower Danube while Aegean farmer substrates hold farther south. Patchy steppe ancestry means diplomacy, marriage, and raiding—not uniform replacement. Wheel, wagon, and pastoral mobility meet Balkan metallurgy that is already ancient in this arc.

Competing sacred geographies—kurgan theatre versus tell household cults—meet along the rivers. The Balkans teach contact as plural cosmology.
balkans.linguisticNote: Contact zone; Greek ancestor speech not yet Mycenaean-attested.
balkans.ancestryNote: Variable steppe on EEF-rich bases; not uniform Yamnaya replacement.
balkans.art: Danube–Black Sea contact zones show kurgan-style burials beside older tell and cemetery traditions; ochre, weapons, and pastoral kits appear on farmer edges. Figurines and fine pottery of Balkan Eneolithic traditions persist inland. Art is a contact collage—stela and tell.
balkans.ideas: Yamnaya horizons push into the Lower Danube while Aegean farmer substrates hold farther south. Patchy steppe ancestry means diplomacy, marriage, and raiding—not uniform replacement. The Balkans are a corridor of packages, not a single people.
balkans.philosophy: Kurgan rites import steppe afterlife theatre; tell communities keep household and cemetery cults. Competing sacred geographies meet along the rivers. Cosmology is plural and contact-shaped.
balkans.science: Wheel/wagon and pastoral mobility meet Balkan metallurgy already deep-rooted here. Riverine exchange and early horse presence are logistical sciences. Farmers and herders hybridise crop–livestock calendars on steppe edges.

eastern.culture: Mobile pastoral households organise around herds, dairy, and kurgan lineages. Seasonal mobility and wagon transport structure life across the Pontic–Caspian. Society amplifies certain male lineages in later expansions; wealth is animals, milk stores, and grave theatre rather than urban surplus.
eastern.description:
Around 3300–2600 BC Yamnaya (Yamna) Western Steppe Herders dominate the Pontic–Caspian grass sea. Kurgans with ochre-covered flexed burials, stone stelae, cord-decorated pots, and wagon fittings define the steppe look. Animal offerings and early metal daggers stage pastoral wealth in death; dress is wool, leather, and status pins—mobile prestige, not city walls.

CLV and Serednii Stih fusions (Lazaridis, Nikitin, and colleagues) create the Western Steppe Herder ancestry package that will remake temperate Europe; Afanasievo carries related ancestry to the Altai. Social ideas centre on herd, kurgan lineage, and mobility. Language candidates for late Proto-Indo-European are reconstructed from later tongues, not Yamnaya texts.

Wilkin and colleagues (2021) show ubiquitous ruminant dairying—and some horse milk—underwriting expansion. Wagon carpentry, pastoral scheduling, and early metallurgy are the measurable technologies of WSH success. This tick’s eastern region is the demographic and cultural engine, not a peripheral echo.
eastern.ancestryNote: Yamnaya = WSH package (EHG+CHG already fused). Shown as WSH, not re-split into EHG and CHG.
eastern.linguisticNote: Best archaeological match for late Proto-Indo-European (or a sister) in the steppe hypothesis — reconstructed lexicon, not Yamnaya inscriptions.

ancestryCline.label: Yamnaya core → farmer edge
ancestryCline.note: WSH% highest on Yamnaya core steppe; EEF rises toward late Trypillia / western contact.

eastern.art: Kurgans with ochre-covered flexed burials, stone stelae, cord-decorated pots, and wagon fittings define the steppe look. Animal offerings and early metal daggers stage pastoral wealth in death. Dress is wool, leather, and status pins—mobile prestige, not city walls.
eastern.ideas: CLV and Serednii Stih fusions (Lazaridis & Nikitin 2025) create WSH ancestry that will remake Europe; Afanasievo carries the package to the Altai. Social ideas centre on herd, kurgan lineage, and mobility. Language candidates (late PIE) are reconstructed from later tongues, not Yamnaya texts.
eastern.philosophy: Kurgan cosmology: ochre, wagon, animal, and sky over the mound—practice without scripture. Stelae may mark persons or powers; dairying and herd fertility likely charged the sacred. No named philosophers; the grave is the treatise.
eastern.science: Ruminant dairying (proteomic proof) underwrites expansion; horse-milk proteins appear in some individuals. Wagon/wheel carpentry, pastoral scheduling, and early metallurgy are core technologies. Secondary products, not just meat, power long-range mobility.

UKR.name: Yamnaya pastoralists
UKR.summary: Kurgan steppe societies of the Pontic–Caspian zone.
UKR.conflicts: Expansion into Danube/Carpathian Basin; pressure on Trypillia and GAC worlds.
UKR.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Comparative Indo-European poetics later reconstructs a world of sky gods, cattle wealth, and praise of patrons — a hypothetical echo chamber, not a recovered library. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: Kurgans with ochre-covered flexed burials, stone stelae, cord-decorated pots, and wagon fittings define the steppe look. Animal offerings and early metal daggers stage pastoral wealth in death. Dress is wool, leather, and status pins—mobile prestige, not city walls.
UKR.religion: Yamnaya steppe religion is read from kurgans: ochre-covered flexed burials, wagons/animal offerings, and stelae. Sky/ancestor pastoral cult inferred; no native texts.
UKR.ideas: CLV and Serednii Stih fusions (Lazaridis & Nikitin 2025) create WSH ancestry that will remake Europe; Afanasievo carries the package to the Altai. Social ideas centre on herd, kurgan lineage, and mobility. Language candidates (late PIE) are reconstructed from later tongues, not Yamnaya texts.
UKR.philosophy: Kurgan cosmology: ochre, wagon, animal, and sky over the mound—practice without scripture. Stelae may mark persons or powers; dairying and herd fertility likely charged the sacred. No named philosophers; the grave is the treatise.
UKR.science: Ruminant dairying (proteomic proof) underwrites expansion; horse-milk proteins appear in some individuals. Wagon/wheel carpentry, pastoral scheduling, and early metallurgy are core technologies. Secondary products, not just meat, power long-range mobility.
UKR.culture: Mobile pastoral households organise around herds, dairy, and kurgan lineages. Seasonal mobility and wagon transport structure life across the Pontic–Caspian. Society amplifies certain male lineages in later expansions; wealth is animals, milk stores, and grave theatre rather than urban surplus.
UKR.description:
Around 3300–2600 BC Yamnaya (Yamna) Western Steppe Herders dominate the Pontic–Caspian grass sea. Kurgans with ochre-covered flexed burials, stone stelae, cord-decorated pots, and wagon fittings define the steppe look. Animal offerings and early metal daggers stage pastoral wealth in death; dress is wool, leather, and status pins—mobile prestige, not city walls.

CLV and Serednii Stih fusions (Lazaridis, Nikitin, and colleagues) create the Western Steppe Herder ancestry package that will remake temperate Europe; Afanasievo carries related ancestry to the Altai. Social ideas centre on herd, kurgan lineage, and mobility. Language candidates for late Proto-Indo-European are reconstructed from later tongues, not Yamnaya texts.

Wilkin and colleagues (2021) show ubiquitous ruminant dairying—and some horse milk—underwriting expansion. Wagon carpentry, pastoral scheduling, and early metallurgy are the measurable technologies of WSH success. This tick’s eastern region is the demographic and cultural engine, not a peripheral echo.

HUN.name: Yamnaya in the Carpathian Basin
HUN.conflicts: Contact/conflict with local Late Neolithic/Copper communities.
HUN.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Comparative Indo-European poetics later reconstructs a world of sky gods, cattle wealth, and praise of patrons — a hypothetical echo chamber, not a recovered library. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. Hungarian culture keeps a steppe-origin memory inside a Latin-Christian and later Habsburg frame.
HUN.art: Globular Amphora jars, cattle burials, and flint axes define late farmer display before Corded Ware’s cord-impressed amphorae and battle-axes take over. Art is ceramic body and animal deposit more than figurative stone. The visual hinge is amphora → cord beaker within a few centuries.
HUN.religion: Yamnaya-related Carpathian Basin graves import kurgan burial grammar (ochre, mounds, pastoral goods) into farmer Europe’s ritual map.
HUN.ideas: GAC cattle wealth and Yamnaya-related incomers collide to midwife Corded Ware—admixture as ethnogenesis. Social ideas pivot from collective Neolithic claims toward single-grave politics. Central Europe becomes the factory floor of temperate Indo-Europeanization in standard models.
HUN.philosophy: Cattle offerings and amphora graves imply a pastoral sacred economy; Corded dawn adds gendered weapon burial. Cosmology is read from animals, pots, and posture—practice without named teachers. Ancestor and herd are the moral pair at the hinge.
HUN.science: Wheel and wagon knowledge filters west with steppe contact; GAC and early CW communities manage mixed farming with rising pastoral mobility. Flint and early metal chaînes opératoires intensify. Ceramic temper recipes and cord decoration are reproducible craft science across the plain.
HUN.culture: Cattle-rich Globular Amphora households and late Funnelbeaker neighbours organise wealth around herds, amphorae, and flint. Eastern contact brings pastoral mobility and new burial politics without instantly erasing farmer settlements. Society stands between collective Neolithic claims and the single-grave order about to standardise gendered weapon kits across the plain.
HUN.description:
Around 3000 BC Central Europe is the hinge on which temperate Indo-Europeanization will turn. Globular Amphora jars, cattle burials, and flint axes still define late farmer display across the North European Plain, while Yamnaya-related incomers and ideas press from the east. Within a few centuries this collision midwifes Corded Ware—admixture as ethnogenesis rather than a finished map.

Art is ceramic body and animal deposit more than figurative stone; the visual hinge is amphora to cord-impressed beaker. Social ideas pivot from collective Neolithic claims toward single-grave politics. Wheel and wagon knowledge filters west with steppe contact as pastoral mobility rises inside mixed farming landscapes.

Late TRB and GAC communities remain farmer-led even as early steppe signals appear unevenly, higher toward the east. Central Europe at this tick is the factory floor being tooled for the Corded age.

ESP.name: Los Millares & Copper Age Iberia
ESP.conflicts: Internal hierarchy; Beaker package arrives before major steppe ancestry.
ESP.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Comparative Indo-European poetics later reconstructs a world of sky gods, cattle wealth, and praise of patrons — a hypothetical echo chamber, not a recovered library. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: Fortified circuits, tholos chambers, copper tools, and schematic ‘eye’ idols form a visual language of walls and collective death. Ivory and ostrich-egg shell imported through Mediterranean–Atlantic chains glitter beside local stone architecture. Dress and ornament remain Neolithic in cut—wool, linen, personal beads—while metal blades begin to mark elite bodies. Art is settlement geometry and tomb furniture, not figurative rock fleets or kurgan stelae.
ESP.religion: Los Millares / Copper Age Iberia: fortified ritual centers, collective and emerging individual tombs, idol plaques — not Yamnaya kurgans, but parallel sacral intensification.
ESP.ideas: Hierarchy is argued through metallurgy, fortification, and control of exotic exchange rather than through Yamnaya-style mobile kingship. Ancestral corporations in collective tombs claim copper and land. The idea of Iberia at 3000 BC is a farmer world organising itself for metal—prestige as architecture and craft—while steppe ancestry and Indo-European speech models remain almost irrelevant to the peninsula’s gene pool and material brand.
ESP.philosophy: No named schools survive. Cosmology is tomb and idol: tholoi and engraved plaques keep the dead as corporate ancestors, while schematic idols hint at personified powers without a readable pantheon. Sacred order is architectural—who may enter the chamber, who owns the copper—rather than doctrinal text. Ethics are inferred from walls, offerings, and the staging of collective memory.
ESP.science: Copper smelting, casting, and arsenical alloys are the period’s hard science, paired with surveying and labour organisation for hilltop fortifications. Farmers manage dryland Mediterranean agrosystems while sourcing ivory and ostrich-egg shell through long maritime chains. Ceramic and lithic chaînes opératoires standardise household production beside new metal workshops—an applied industrial shift inside a still-Neolithic demography.
ESP.culture: Copper Age Iberian society organises around fortified hilltop centres, craft specialisation, and collective tombs that imply corporate kinship rather than steppe pastoral kings. Households farm Mediterranean crops under increasing aridity while workshops cast copper blades and shape schematic idols. Atlantic façades and the southeast speak related but not identical dialects of prestige—walls and tholoi in one zone, megalithic afterlives and coastal exchange in another. Belonging is local, ancestral, and increasingly unequal.
ESP.description:
Around 3000 BC the Iberian peninsula is a Copper Age farmer world, not a Yamnaya province. On arid southeastern hills, fortified centres in the Los Millares tradition raise stone walls, tholos tombs, and craft quarters around copper working, while Atlantic and interior communities keep their own chambered tombs, idols, and exchange routes. Hierarchy intensifies through metal, exotic ivory, and defended villages; steppe pastoral packages remain a distant eastern story.

Collective burial chambers and engraved plaque-idols bind the living to ancestral corporations that control access to copper and long-distance goods. Beaker pottery is still only a whisper on the horizon. Dress stays wool and linen with personal ornaments; status is written in fortification and tomb architecture more than in kurgan mounds.

Genetically the peninsula remains almost entirely Early European Farmer with Western Hunter-Gatherer admixture. The drama of this tick is metallurgical and social reorganisation inside a Neolithic substrate—preparing the ground for later Beaker fashion without yet remaking Iberian ancestry.

stories.text: On a southeastern ridge, builders raise dry-stone circuits around houses and workshops while tholos chambers receive the corporate dead. Copper slag stains the soil; ivory beads travel farther than any steppe wagon. Iberia’s Copper Age writes power as fortification long before Beaker pots redefine the grave.

GBR.name: Late Neolithic Britain
GBR.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Comparative Indo-European poetics later reconstructs a world of sky gods, cattle wealth, and praise of patrons — a hypothetical echo chamber, not a recovered library. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. Insular voices and North Sea contact give this place a distinctive accent in the wider European chorus.
GBR.art: Stonehenge’s later Neolithic phases, timber circles, Grooved Ware, and carved chalk objects keep a monumental island aesthetic untouched by steppe kurgan art. Collective and cremation rites, carved stone, and ceremonial landscapes dominate; metal is still scarce. Dress and ornament remain Neolithic—jet, amber, and stone—before Beaker gold arrives.
GBR.religion: Late Neolithic Britain: continuing megalithic and henge rites (Stonehenge landscape) before Beaker individual graves rewrite burial fashion.
GBR.ideas: Island ceremonial commons and ancestral monuments organise politics without Yamnaya pastoral kings. Gene pools stay EEF+WHG; the ‘steppe story’ is still a continental rumour. Labour and pilgrimage around henges imply large-scale cooperation among farming communities who do not yet know they are about to be replaced.
GBR.philosophy: Solar alignments, processional avenues, and successive monument rebuilds encode a sky-and-ancestor cosmology in stone and timber. The dead and the solstice structure time; no pantheon is named. Sacred knowledge is architectural and calendrical—how to stand stones to catch the sun—not philosophical prose.
GBR.science: Megalithic and timber engineering, horizon astronomy, and quarry logistics (bluestones, sarsens) are peak Neolithic applied science. Mixed farming on chalk and clay fuels seasonal gatherings. Trackways and boat craft stitch coasts and rivers into a pre-metal transport web.
GBR.culture: Society gathers around henges, avenues, and seasonal monuments that structure time and labour. Households farm chalk and clay while investing surplus in timber and stone spectacles. Jet, amber, and stone ornaments mark persons inside a still-collective ceremonial order. Belonging is pilgrimage and monument rebuild, not single-grave martial kits.
GBR.description:
At 3000 BC Britain is still a Late Neolithic farmer island. Stonehenge’s later Neolithic phases, timber circles, Grooved Ware, and carved chalk objects keep a monumental aesthetic untouched by steppe kurgan art. Collective and cremation rites, carved stone, and ceremonial landscapes dominate; metal remains scarce.

Island ceremonial commons and ancestral monuments organise politics without Yamnaya pastoral kings. Gene pools stay Early European Farmer with Western Hunter-Gatherer admixture; the ‘steppe story’ is still a continental rumour. Labour and pilgrimage around henges imply large-scale cooperation among farming communities who do not yet know they are about to be replaced.

This tick’s drama is sky theatre and stone logistics—the last centuries of Neolithic Britain before the Beaker demographic break of the mid-third millennium.

ITA.name: Remedello / Gaudo
ITA.conflicts: Limited early steppe vs CW north.
ITA.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Comparative Indo-European poetics later reconstructs a world of sky gods, cattle wealth, and praise of patrons — a hypothetical echo chamber, not a recovered library. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. Italian cities teach prestige: from Roman monumentality to Renaissance brand management of beauty.
ITA.art: Remedello weapon graves and Gaudo chamber tombs define Copper Age Italy with tanged daggers, halberds, and distinctive pottery—an aesthetic of metal and rock-cut tomb. Stele statues in the Alpine fringe hint at anthropomorphic display. Steppe kurgan art is still foreign.
ITA.religion: Remedello / Gaudo: Copper Age cemeteries with weapon graves and formal rite — Italian paths to status burial without steppe kurgans.
ITA.ideas: Peninsular and Po communities intensify metallurgy and hierarchy on largely EEF+WHG bases; steppe ancestry is limited versus the Corded north. Copper Age Italy is a Mediterranean farmer–metal world, not a Yamnaya province. Regional tomb rites encode local belonging.
ITA.philosophy: Chamber tombs and weapon deposits locate honour and ancestry underground. Alpine stelae may personify ancestors or powers without yielding readable myths. Cosmology is funerary and martial-practical.
ITA.science: Early copper daggers and arsenical alloys show specialised smithing. Rock-cut tomb engineering and Mediterranean crop systems continue Neolithic agronomy with metal tools. Alpine greenstone and metal routes sketch north–south technical exchange.
ITA.culture: Weapon-grave and chamber-tomb communities organise honour around metal kits and subterranean ancestry. Households farm Mediterranean crops; specialists cast copper. Alpine and peninsular provinces keep distinct burial dialects while sharing the Copper Age turn toward inequality and craft.
ITA.description:
Around 3000 BC Italy is a Mediterranean farmer–metal world, not a Yamnaya province. Remedello weapon graves in the north and Gaudo chamber tombs farther south define Copper Age rites with tanged daggers, halberds, and distinctive pottery—an aesthetic of metal and rock-cut tomb. Alpine fringe stelae hint at anthropomorphic display while steppe kurgan art remains foreign.

Peninsular and Po communities intensify metallurgy and hierarchy on largely Early European Farmer bases with Western Hunter-Gatherer admixture. Steppe ancestry is limited compared with the Corded north. Regional tomb rites encode local belonging more than any pastoral package from the Pontic grass sea.

Early copper daggers and arsenical alloys show specialised smithing beside Mediterranean crop systems. Italy’s Copper Age is hierarchy underground and metal in the hand.

DEU.name: GAC → Corded Ware dawn
DEU.summary: Globular Amphora farmers at the hinge.
DEU.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Comparative Indo-European poetics later reconstructs a world of sky gods, cattle wealth, and praise of patrons — a hypothetical echo chamber, not a recovered library. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.
DEU.art: Globular Amphora jars, cattle burials, and flint axes define late farmer display before Corded Ware’s cord-impressed amphorae and battle-axes take over. Art is ceramic body and animal deposit more than figurative stone. The visual hinge is amphora → cord beaker within a few centuries.
DEU.religion: GAC → Corded Ware dawn: cattle-centered offerings and changing grave rites as steppe-related practices approach temperate Europe.
DEU.ideas: GAC cattle wealth and Yamnaya-related incomers collide to midwife Corded Ware—admixture as ethnogenesis. Social ideas pivot from collective Neolithic claims toward single-grave politics. Central Europe becomes the factory floor of temperate Indo-Europeanization in standard models.
DEU.philosophy: Cattle offerings and amphora graves imply a pastoral sacred economy; Corded dawn adds gendered weapon burial. Cosmology is read from animals, pots, and posture—practice without named teachers. Ancestor and herd are the moral pair at the hinge.
DEU.science: Wheel and wagon knowledge filters west with steppe contact; GAC and early CW communities manage mixed farming with rising pastoral mobility. Flint and early metal chaînes opératoires intensify. Ceramic temper recipes and cord decoration are reproducible craft science across the plain.
DEU.culture: Cattle-rich Globular Amphora households and late Funnelbeaker neighbours organise wealth around herds, amphorae, and flint. Eastern contact brings pastoral mobility and new burial politics without instantly erasing farmer settlements. Society stands between collective Neolithic claims and the single-grave order about to standardise gendered weapon kits across the plain.
DEU.description:
Around 3000 BC Central Europe is the hinge on which temperate Indo-Europeanization will turn. Globular Amphora jars, cattle burials, and flint axes still define late farmer display across the North European Plain, while Yamnaya-related incomers and ideas press from the east. Within a few centuries this collision midwifes Corded Ware—admixture as ethnogenesis rather than a finished map.

Art is ceramic body and animal deposit more than figurative stone; the visual hinge is amphora to cord-impressed beaker. Social ideas pivot from collective Neolithic claims toward single-grave politics. Wheel and wagon knowledge filters west with steppe contact as pastoral mobility rises inside mixed farming landscapes.

Late TRB and GAC communities remain farmer-led even as early steppe signals appear unevenly, higher toward the east. Central Europe at this tick is the factory floor being tooled for the Corded age.
