PRT.description:
Around 3000 BC the Iberian peninsula is a Copper Age farmer world, not a Yamnaya province. On arid southeastern hills, fortified centres in the Los Millares tradition raise stone walls, tholos tombs, and craft quarters around copper working, while Atlantic and interior communities keep their own chambered tombs, idols, and exchange routes. Hierarchy intensifies through metal, exotic ivory, and defended villages; steppe pastoral packages remain a distant eastern story.

Collective burial chambers and engraved plaque-idols bind the living to ancestral corporations that control access to copper and long-distance goods. Beaker pottery is still only a whisper on the horizon. Dress stays wool and linen with personal ornaments; status is written in fortification and tomb architecture more than in kurgan mounds.

Genetically the peninsula remains almost entirely Early European Farmer with Western Hunter-Gatherer admixture. The drama of this tick is metallurgical and social reorganisation inside a Neolithic substrate—preparing the ground for later Beaker fashion without yet remaking Iberian ancestry.
PRT.culture: Copper Age Iberian society organises around fortified hilltop centres, craft specialisation, and collective tombs that imply corporate kinship rather than steppe pastoral kings. Households farm Mediterranean crops under increasing aridity while workshops cast copper blades and shape schematic idols. Atlantic façades and the southeast speak related but not identical dialects of prestige—walls and tholoi in one zone, megalithic afterlives and coastal exchange in another. Belonging is local, ancestral, and increasingly unequal.
PRT.art: Fortified circuits, tholos chambers, copper tools, and schematic ‘eye’ idols form a visual language of walls and collective death. Ivory and ostrich-egg shell imported through Mediterranean–Atlantic chains glitter beside local stone architecture. Dress and ornament remain Neolithic in cut—wool, linen, personal beads—while metal blades begin to mark elite bodies. Art is settlement geometry and tomb furniture, not figurative rock fleets or kurgan stelae.
PRT.ideas: Hierarchy is argued through metallurgy, fortification, and control of exotic exchange rather than through Yamnaya-style mobile kingship. Ancestral corporations in collective tombs claim copper and land. The idea of Iberia at 3000 BC is a farmer world organising itself for metal—prestige as architecture and craft—while steppe ancestry and Indo-European speech models remain almost irrelevant to the peninsula’s gene pool and material brand.
PRT.philosophy: No named schools survive. Cosmology is tomb and idol: tholoi and engraved plaques keep the dead as corporate ancestors, while schematic idols hint at personified powers without a readable pantheon. Sacred order is architectural—who may enter the chamber, who owns the copper—rather than doctrinal text. Ethics are inferred from walls, offerings, and the staging of collective memory.
PRT.science: Copper smelting, casting, and arsenical alloys are the period’s hard science, paired with surveying and labour organisation for hilltop fortifications. Farmers manage dryland Mediterranean agrosystems while sourcing ivory and ostrich-egg shell through long maritime chains. Ceramic and lithic chaînes opératoires standardise household production beside new metal workshops—an applied industrial shift inside a still-Neolithic demography.

stories.text: On a southeastern ridge, builders raise dry-stone circuits around houses and workshops while tholos chambers receive the corporate dead. Copper slag stains the soil; ivory beads travel farther than any steppe wagon. Iberia’s Copper Age writes power as fortification long before Beaker pots redefine the grave.
stories.title: Walls Before Beakers

IRL.description:
At 3000 BC Britain is still a Late Neolithic farmer island. Stonehenge’s later Neolithic phases, timber circles, Grooved Ware, and carved chalk objects keep a monumental aesthetic untouched by steppe kurgan art. Collective and cremation rites, carved stone, and ceremonial landscapes dominate; metal remains scarce.

Island ceremonial commons and ancestral monuments organise politics without Yamnaya pastoral kings. Gene pools stay Early European Farmer with Western Hunter-Gatherer admixture; the ‘steppe story’ is still a continental rumour. Labour and pilgrimage around henges imply large-scale cooperation among farming communities who do not yet know they are about to be replaced.

This tick’s drama is sky theatre and stone logistics—the last centuries of Neolithic Britain before the Beaker demographic break of the mid-third millennium.
IRL.culture: Society gathers around henges, avenues, and seasonal monuments that structure time and labour. Households farm chalk and clay while investing surplus in timber and stone spectacles. Jet, amber, and stone ornaments mark persons inside a still-collective ceremonial order. Belonging is pilgrimage and monument rebuild, not single-grave martial kits.
IRL.art: Sarsen and bluestone settings, timber circles, Grooved Ware, and carved chalk objects define an island aesthetic of monumental geometry. Dress and ornament remain Neolithic—jet, amber, stone—before Beaker gold. Art is landscape theatre: processional avenues and successive rebuilds that make the skyline a calendar.
IRL.ideas: Politics is cooperative labour around shared sky theatres rather than pastoral kingship. Ancestral monuments claim place without steppe ancestry. The idea of Late Neolithic Britain is ceremonial commons on the eve of rupture—continuity of stone about to meet discontinuity of flesh.
IRL.philosophy: Solar alignments, processional avenues, and monument rebuilds encode a sky-and-ancestor cosmology in stone and timber. The dead and the solstice structure time; no pantheon is named. Sacred knowledge is architectural and calendrical—how to stand stones to catch the sun—not philosophical prose.
IRL.science: Megalithic and timber engineering, horizon astronomy, and quarry logistics for bluestones and sarsens are peak Neolithic applied science. Mixed farming fuels seasonal gatherings. Trackways and boat craft stitch coasts and rivers into a pre-metal transport web.

FRA.description:
Around 3000 BC France sits on a genetic and cultural hinge. Late Neolithic collective tombs, Chasséen and Artenacoid ceramics, and Armorican megalithic afterlives still look farmer-European, while early steppe-related ancestry trickles into some northern burials—admixture in real time, not a finished Corded Ware map.

Paris Basin and Atlantic façades keep distinct visual dialects of chamber, plaque, and polished axe. Kinship stretches to include eastern-connected men without instantly rewriting pottery brands. Pulses near 3000–2900 BC foreshadow later Beaker and Corded standardisation without yet imposing Britain’s cliff-edge replacement.

Copper knowledge spreads unevenly from south and east while flint networks and tomb carpentry remain the technical backbone. France at this tick is a corridor of first contacts.
FRA.culture: Collective tombs and regional ceramic traditions organise farmer communities even as new bloodlines enter northern families. Households keep Atlantic and loess agrosystems; prestige still speaks in polished axes and chamber access. Society is Neolithic in structure—ancestral corporations, megalithic rites—with pastoral signals rising in isotopes and ancestry before full steppe material packages dominate.
FRA.art: Chamber tombs, engraved plaques, and polished axes define a farmer-European gallery. Art is regional: Armorican megalithic afterlives versus Paris Basin dialects, not yet a uniform Corded battle-axe fashion. Visual culture records continuity of stone theatres during a genetic hinge.
FRA.ideas: Bréviandes-type and related burials capture steppe ancestry arriving inside Neolithic families. Ideas of kinship stretch without instant ceramic revolution. France thinks in pulses and corridors—Rhine, Atlantic, Mediterranean—before Beaker standardisation.
FRA.philosophy: Collective tombs continue ancestor corporations even as new lineages enter; cosmology remains megalithic and household. Ritual deposits and chamber reuse matter more than any steppe stela cult. Philosophy is practice at the tomb door—who may lie inside—during demographic opening.
FRA.science: Farmers maintain Atlantic and loess agrosystems while copper knowledge spreads unevenly. Tomb carpentry, stone transport, and flint networks remain the technical spine. Early pastoral mobility appears in isotopes before wagons and Corded kits dominate the material record.
FRA.cultureLabel: Late Neolithic France — first steppe pulses

MCO.description:
Around 3000 BC France sits on a genetic and cultural hinge. Late Neolithic collective tombs, Chasséen and Artenacoid ceramics, and Armorican megalithic afterlives still look farmer-European, while early steppe-related ancestry trickles into some northern burials—admixture in real time, not a finished Corded Ware map.

Paris Basin and Atlantic façades keep distinct visual dialects of chamber, plaque, and polished axe. Kinship stretches to include eastern-connected men without instantly rewriting pottery brands. Pulses near 3000–2900 BC foreshadow later Beaker and Corded standardisation without yet imposing Britain’s cliff-edge replacement.

Copper knowledge spreads unevenly from south and east while flint networks and tomb carpentry remain the technical backbone. France at this tick is a corridor of first contacts.
MCO.culture: Collective tombs and regional ceramic traditions organise farmer communities even as new bloodlines enter northern families. Households keep Atlantic and loess agrosystems; prestige still speaks in polished axes and chamber access. Society is Neolithic in structure—ancestral corporations, megalithic rites—with pastoral signals rising in isotopes and ancestry before full steppe material packages dominate.
MCO.art: Chamber tombs, engraved plaques, and polished axes define a farmer-European gallery. Art is regional: Armorican megalithic afterlives versus Paris Basin dialects, not yet a uniform Corded battle-axe fashion. Visual culture records continuity of stone theatres during a genetic hinge.
MCO.ideas: Bréviandes-type and related burials capture steppe ancestry arriving inside Neolithic families. Ideas of kinship stretch without instant ceramic revolution. France thinks in pulses and corridors—Rhine, Atlantic, Mediterranean—before Beaker standardisation.
MCO.philosophy: Collective tombs continue ancestor corporations even as new lineages enter; cosmology remains megalithic and household. Ritual deposits and chamber reuse matter more than any steppe stela cult. Philosophy is practice at the tomb door—who may lie inside—during demographic opening.
MCO.science: Farmers maintain Atlantic and loess agrosystems while copper knowledge spreads unevenly. Tomb carpentry, stone transport, and flint networks remain the technical spine. Early pastoral mobility appears in isotopes before wagons and Corded kits dominate the material record.
MCO.cultureLabel: Late Neolithic France — first steppe pulses

POL.description:
Around 3000 BC Central Europe is the hinge on which temperate Indo-Europeanization will turn. Globular Amphora jars, cattle burials, and flint axes still define late farmer display across the North European Plain, while Yamnaya-related incomers and ideas press from the east. Within a few centuries this collision midwifes Corded Ware—admixture as ethnogenesis rather than a finished map.

Art is ceramic body and animal deposit more than figurative stone; the visual hinge is amphora to cord-impressed beaker. Social ideas pivot from collective Neolithic claims toward single-grave politics. Wheel and wagon knowledge filters west with steppe contact as pastoral mobility rises inside mixed farming landscapes.

Late TRB and GAC communities remain farmer-led even as early steppe signals appear unevenly, higher toward the east. Central Europe at this tick is the factory floor being tooled for the Corded age.
POL.culture: Cattle-rich Globular Amphora households and late Funnelbeaker neighbours organise wealth around herds, amphorae, and flint. Eastern contact brings pastoral mobility and new burial politics without instantly erasing farmer settlements. Society stands between collective Neolithic claims and the single-grave order about to standardise gendered weapon kits across the plain.
POL.art: Globular Amphora jars, cattle deposits, and polished flint axes define late farmer prestige before Corded Ware’s cord-impressed amphorae and battle-axes take over. Visual culture is ceramic body and animal offering—the amphora-to-cord hinge within a few centuries.
POL.ideas: GAC cattle wealth and Yamnaya-related incomers collide to midwife Corded Ware. Ideas of belonging shift from ancestral commons toward single-grave lineage politics. Central Europe becomes, in standard models, the workshop of temperate steppe-admixed ethnogenesis.
POL.philosophy: Cattle offerings and amphora graves imply a pastoral sacred economy; Corded dawn adds gendered weapon burial. Cosmology is read from animals, pots, and posture—practice without named teachers. Ancestor and herd are the moral pair at the hinge.
POL.science: Wheel and wagon knowledge filters west with steppe contact; communities manage mixed farming with rising pastoral mobility. Flint and early metal chaînes opératoires intensify. Ceramic temper recipes and cord decoration become reproducible craft science across hundreds of kilometres.

NOR.description:
At 3000 BC Scandinavia still hosts dual economies. Funnelbeaker megaliths and pottery organise farming inland and south, while Pitted Ware seal-hunter aesthetics—bone harpoons, marine mammal art, coastal camps—hold the shores. Visual Scandinavia is split: farmer stone tombs versus forager maritime kits.

Early steppe signals are slight; the coming Single Grave turnover is not yet destiny. Identity is diet and burial as much as pottery brand. Two ideas of the good life share one peninsula—fields and seals—before battle-axe fashion remakes the north.

Megalith engineering continues beside coastal navigation that is forager science. Steppe battle-axe packages are still approaching from the continent.
NOR.culture: TRB farmsteads and megalithic chambers structure agrarian kinship; Pitted Ware camps organise sealing, fishing, and coastal exchange. Society is plural: pig and cattle ritual inland, marine mammal economies on the strand. Belonging is ecological as much as ethnic.
NOR.art: Funnelbeaker megaliths and pottery coexist with Pitted Ware harpoons and marine mammal imagery. Art splits by livelihood—stone tomb geometry versus coastal bone and ceramic hunter kits—without steppe kurgan stelae.
NOR.ideas: Dual economies encode rival goods lives in one region. Early steppe ancestry remains limited; the idea of impending Single Grave replacement is archaeological hindsight, not contemporary fate. Identity tracks diet, burial, and shore versus field.
NOR.philosophy: Megalithic ancestor chambers versus coastal forager rites offer rival sacred geographies. Seals, pigs, and cattle likely carried different ritual charges. Cosmology is place-and-prey, not scripture.
NOR.science: TRB agronomy on northern soils meets Pitted Ware marine mammal hunting and sealing technology—two applied ecologies. Megalith engineering continues; coastal navigation is forager science. Pottery tempers diverge with lifestyle.

ALA.description:
At 3000 BC Scandinavia still hosts dual economies. Funnelbeaker megaliths and pottery organise farming inland and south, while Pitted Ware seal-hunter aesthetics—bone harpoons, marine mammal art, coastal camps—hold the shores. Visual Scandinavia is split: farmer stone tombs versus forager maritime kits.

Early steppe signals are slight; the coming Single Grave turnover is not yet destiny. Identity is diet and burial as much as pottery brand. Two ideas of the good life share one peninsula—fields and seals—before battle-axe fashion remakes the north.

Megalith engineering continues beside coastal navigation that is forager science. Steppe battle-axe packages are still approaching from the continent.
ALA.culture: TRB farmsteads and megalithic chambers structure agrarian kinship; Pitted Ware camps organise sealing, fishing, and coastal exchange. Society is plural: pig and cattle ritual inland, marine mammal economies on the strand. Belonging is ecological as much as ethnic.
ALA.art: Funnelbeaker megaliths and pottery coexist with Pitted Ware harpoons and marine mammal imagery. Art splits by livelihood—stone tomb geometry versus coastal bone and ceramic hunter kits—without steppe kurgan stelae.
ALA.ideas: Dual economies encode rival goods lives in one region. Early steppe ancestry remains limited; the idea of impending Single Grave replacement is archaeological hindsight, not contemporary fate. Identity tracks diet, burial, and shore versus field.
ALA.philosophy: Megalithic ancestor chambers versus coastal forager rites offer rival sacred geographies. Seals, pigs, and cattle likely carried different ritual charges. Cosmology is place-and-prey, not scripture.
ALA.science: TRB agronomy on northern soils meets Pitted Ware marine mammal hunting and sealing technology—two applied ecologies. Megalith engineering continues; coastal navigation is forager science. Pottery tempers diverge with lifestyle.

SMR.description:
Around 3000 BC Italy is a Mediterranean farmer–metal world, not a Yamnaya province. Remedello weapon graves in the north and Gaudo chamber tombs farther south define Copper Age rites with tanged daggers, halberds, and distinctive pottery—an aesthetic of metal and rock-cut tomb. Alpine fringe stelae hint at anthropomorphic display while steppe kurgan art remains foreign.

Peninsular and Po communities intensify metallurgy and hierarchy on largely Early European Farmer bases with Western Hunter-Gatherer admixture. Steppe ancestry is limited compared with the Corded north. Regional tomb rites encode local belonging more than any pastoral package from the Pontic grass sea.

Early copper daggers and arsenical alloys show specialised smithing beside Mediterranean crop systems. Italy’s Copper Age is hierarchy underground and metal in the hand.
SMR.culture: Weapon-grave and chamber-tomb communities organise honour around metal kits and subterranean ancestry. Households farm Mediterranean crops; specialists cast copper. Alpine and peninsular provinces keep distinct burial dialects while sharing the Copper Age turn toward inequality and craft.
SMR.art: Remedello daggers and Gaudo chambers, with Alpine stelae on the fringe, define a visual order of metal and rock-cut space. Art is funerary weaponry and anthropomorphic stone hints—not Corded cord-beakers or steppe ochre theatre.
SMR.ideas: Hierarchy and metallurgy intensify without cloning Yamnaya demography. Ideas of honour attach to dagger and tomb access. Italy thinks regionally—Po, peninsula, Alps—inside a farmer–metal world.
SMR.philosophy: Chamber tombs and weapon deposits locate honour and ancestry underground. Alpine stelae may personify ancestors or powers without yielding readable myths. Cosmology is funerary and martial-practical.
SMR.science: Early copper daggers and arsenical alloys show specialised smithing. Rock-cut tomb engineering and Mediterranean crop systems continue Neolithic agronomy with metal tools. Alpine greenstone and metal routes sketch north–south technical exchange.

GRC.description:
Around 3000 BC the Balkans are a corridor of packages, not a single people. Danube–Black Sea contact zones show kurgan-style burials beside older tell and cemetery traditions; ochre, weapons, and pastoral kits appear on farmer edges. Figurines and fine pottery of Balkan Eneolithic traditions persist inland.

Yamnaya horizons push into the Lower Danube while Aegean farmer substrates hold farther south. Patchy steppe ancestry means diplomacy, marriage, and raiding—not uniform replacement. Wheel, wagon, and pastoral mobility meet Balkan metallurgy that is already ancient in this arc.

Competing sacred geographies—kurgan theatre versus tell household cults—meet along the rivers. The Balkans teach contact as plural cosmology.
GRC.culture: Riverine farmers, tell communities, and incoming pastoral groups negotiate space along the Danube and Black Sea fringe. Metallurgy, figurines, and cemetery rites keep inland farmer identities while steppe kits appear at edges. Society is corridor diplomacy in material form.
GRC.art: Kurgan-style ochre burials and weapons collage with tell figurines and fine pottery. Art is contact collage—stela and tell—rather than one brand covering the peninsula.
GRC.ideas: Packages move without erasing Aegean-facing farmer worlds. Ideas of belonging are local and negotiated. The Balkans think in gradients from steppe edge to southern tells.
GRC.philosophy: Kurgan rites import steppe afterlife theatre; tell communities keep household and cemetery cults. Competing sacred geographies meet along the rivers. Cosmology is plural and contact-shaped.
GRC.science: Wheel/wagon and pastoral mobility meet Balkan metallurgy already deep-rooted here. Riverine exchange and early horse presence are logistical sciences. Farmers and herders hybridise crop–livestock calendars on steppe edges.

BLR.description:
Around 3300–2600 BC Yamnaya (Yamna) Western Steppe Herders dominate the Pontic–Caspian grass sea. Kurgans with ochre-covered flexed burials, stone stelae, cord-decorated pots, and wagon fittings define the steppe look. Animal offerings and early metal daggers stage pastoral wealth in death; dress is wool, leather, and status pins—mobile prestige, not city walls.

CLV and Serednii Stih fusions (Lazaridis, Nikitin, and colleagues) create the Western Steppe Herder ancestry package that will remake temperate Europe; Afanasievo carries related ancestry to the Altai. Social ideas centre on herd, kurgan lineage, and mobility. Language candidates for late Proto-Indo-European are reconstructed from later tongues, not Yamnaya texts.

Wilkin and colleagues (2021) show ubiquitous ruminant dairying—and some horse milk—underwriting expansion. Wagon carpentry, pastoral scheduling, and early metallurgy are the measurable technologies of WSH success. This tick’s eastern region is the demographic and cultural engine, not a peripheral echo.
BLR.culture: Mobile pastoral households organise around herds, dairy, and kurgan lineages. Seasonal mobility and wagon transport structure life across the Pontic–Caspian. Society amplifies certain male lineages in later expansions; wealth is animals, milk stores, and grave theatre rather than urban surplus.
BLR.art: Kurgans, ochre, stelae, corded pots, wagon fittings, and animal offerings compose the steppe gallery. Art is mound geometry and pastoral inventory—mobile prestige without city walls or palace frescoes.
BLR.ideas: Herd, lineage, and mobility define the good life. WSH ancestry becomes the template for later Corded and Beaker transformations west. Linguistic PIE homeland models place speech candidates on this horizon without claiming Yamnaya inscriptions.
BLR.philosophy: Kurgan cosmology—ochre, wagon, animal, and sky over the mound—is practice without scripture. Stelae may mark persons or powers; dairying and herd fertility likely charged the sacred. The grave is the treatise.
BLR.science: Ruminant dairying (proteomic proof) underwrites expansion; horse-milk proteins appear in some individuals. Wagon/wheel carpentry, pastoral scheduling, and early metallurgy are core technologies. Secondary products, not just meat, power long-range mobility.

CLV and Serednii Stih fusions (Lazaridis, Nikitin, and colleagues) create the Western Steppe Herder ancestry package that will remake temperate Europe; Afanasievo carries related ancestry to the Altai. Social ideas centre on herd, kurgan lineage, and mobility. Language candidates for late Proto-Indo-European are reconstructed from later tongues, not Yamnaya texts.

Wilkin and colleagues (2021) show ubiquitous ruminant dairying—and some horse milk—underwriting expansion. Wagon carpentry, pastoral scheduling, and early metallurgy are the measurable technologies of WSH success. This tick’s eastern region is the demographic and cultural engine, not a peripheral echo.
CYP.culture: Mobile pastoral households organise around herds, dairy, and kurgan lineages. Seasonal mobility and wagon transport structure life across the Pontic–Caspian. Society amplifies certain male lineages in later expansions; wealth is animals, milk stores, and grave theatre rather than urban surplus.
CYP.art: Kurgans, ochre, stelae, corded pots, wagon fittings, and animal offerings compose the steppe gallery. Art is mound geometry and pastoral inventory—mobile prestige without city walls or palace frescoes.
CYP.ideas: Herd, lineage, and mobility define the good life. WSH ancestry becomes the template for later Corded and Beaker transformations west. Linguistic PIE homeland models place speech candidates on this horizon without claiming Yamnaya inscriptions.
CYP.philosophy: Kurgan cosmology—ochre, wagon, animal, and sky over the mound—is practice without scripture. Stelae may mark persons or powers; dairying and herd fertility likely charged the sacred. The grave is the treatise.
CYP.science: Ruminant dairying (proteomic proof) underwrites expansion; horse-milk proteins appear in some individuals. Wagon/wheel carpentry, pastoral scheduling, and early metallurgy are core technologies. Secondary products, not just meat, power long-range mobility.

periods.label: Corded Ware and Bell Beaker rupture
periods.narrative: Around 2500 BC Corded Ware, Single Grave, and Bell Beaker packages carry Yamnaya-related ancestry deep into temperate Europe — fiercely in Britain and northern Corded zones, more gradually in Iberian Beaker. Prior Neolithic farmer pools collapse or dilute region by region; residual WHG–EEF clines survive under new pottery names. This is the main hypothesized window for Indo-Europeanization of much of temperate Europe.
periods.culturesNote: Corded Ware, Single Grave, Battle Axe, Bell Beaker (Britain high-turnover; Iberia more gradual) — steppe gradients, not one %.

iberia.culture: Beaker Iberian society grafts an archery-and-hospitality package onto Copper Age hierarchies. Single graves and gendered kits personalise death beside older collective chambers still in memory. Coastal and inland groups plug into pan-European Beaker exchange for metal and ornaments while Mediterranean farming continues. Status is portable—pot, dagger, wristguard—more than new megamonuments.
iberia.description:
By about 2500 BC the Bell Beaker package—maritime pots, archery kits, palmela points, gold ornaments—reshapes Iberian display while the underlying Copper Age bodies and farmer substrate largely endure. Tomb reuse and Beaker deposits restyle older megalithic stages without erasing them. The peninsula becomes a textbook of cultural fashion travelling farther than genes.

Steppe-related ancestry enters more gradually than in Britain, and often with a male-biased signature in uniparental markers. Communities negotiate belonging through Beaker rites inside a still-strong Early European Farmer base. Atlantic and interior networks compete: the same pottery brand, different demographic bargains.

This is not Olalde’s island cliff-edge replacement. Iberia’s Beaker age is admixture and prestige ethics—archery, drink, and metal at the grave—overlaid on Los Millares–descended social landscapes.
iberia.ancestryNote: Beaker Iberia: more gradual, often male-biased steppe intake — lower steppe% than Britain/SGC.
iberia.languages: Pre-IE Iberian substrates; early IE uncertain
iberia.linguisticNote: Culture≠language. IE (later Celtic/Italic-related?) is not automatic with Beaker pots; non-IE Iberian is attested in the Iron Age.

ancestryCline.label: Beaker steppe intake → EEF base
ancestryCline.note: Steppe rises with Beaker-associated lineages but usually stays below British/Danish levels; EEF remains the base.

iberia.art: Maritime Bell Beakers, palmela points, stone wristguards, and sheet-gold ornaments redefine elite display. Art is a portable prestige kit that looks pan-European yet sits on local Copper Age skeletons and tomb stages. Older megalithic theatres receive Beaker inserts; visual politics shifts from wall-and-tholos toward the individualised grave inventory.
iberia.ideas: The Beaker idea travels farther than steppe genes: cultural brand and alliance ritual, not Britain’s near-total turnover. Belonging is negotiated through drinking sets and archery kits inside a durable farmer substrate. Atlantic and interior corridors offer rival paths into the same ceramic fashion—one peninsula, many demographic contracts.
iberia.philosophy: Ritual centres on individualising Beaker graves and drinking sets that stage personhood and alliance. Cosmology stays oral; archaeology recovers gendered kits and ancestral tomb re-entry, not theology. Worldview is a prestige ethic of archery, metal, and hospitality performed at the grave—practice without named sages.
iberia.science: Copper and early bronze recipes refine casting and sheet-gold work; archery gear implies measured craft of bow, point, and wristguard. Farmers and herders keep Mediterranean agrosystems while joining Beaker exchange for metal and exotics. Coastal navigation and river logistics underwrite the Atlantic Beaker face as applied geography.

britain.culture: Single-grave barrow society personalises death with gendered kits—weapons, beakers, archery gear—while farming continues under new lineages. Continental links bring metal recipes and marriage networks. Social ideals shift from Neolithic ceremonial commons toward armed, provisioned personhood at the grave. Stonehenge’s stones remain; the congregation’s ancestry does not.
britain.description:
Around 2500 BC Bell Beaker Britain becomes the textbook of demic transformation. Copper daggers, wristguards, Beaker pots, and gold lunulae arrive with single graves under round barrows; the Amesbury Archer’s kit is portraiture in metal and stone. Older stone theatres stay standing while the people who gather there genetically transform—continuity of place, rupture of flesh.

Ancient DNA (Olalde and colleagues) indicates on the order of ninety percent turnover of the prior Neolithic population, with steppe-rich continental ancestry and R1b lineages rising sharply. Round-barrow individualism and archery prestige rewrite social ideals. Monuments are reused by newcomers who inherit landscapes they did not build.

The resulting ternary—steppe, Early European Farmer, Western Hunter-Gatherer—varies site to site, but the demographic cliff is the period’s defining British fact.
britain.ancestryNote: ~90% turnover of prior Neolithic ancestry; resulting ternary still varies site-to-site.
britain.linguisticNote: Often paired with IE language shift models (early Celtic or pre-Celtic IE). Exact branch and timing remain debated; no contemporary texts.

ancestryCline.label: Early Beaker pulse → later mix

britain.art: Beaker pots, copper daggers, wristguards, and gold lunulae/discs arrive with a new funerary fashion of single graves under round barrows. The Amesbury Archer’s kit is portraiture in metal and stone. Older stone theatres stay standing while the people who gather there genetically transform—continuity of place, rupture of flesh.
britain.ideas: Olalde et al.’s ~90% turnover makes Britain the textbook of demic Beaker transformation: steppe-rich continental ancestry and R1b lineages replace Neolithic pools within centuries. Round-barrow individualism and archery prestige rewrite social ideals. Monuments are reused by newcomers who inherit landscapes they did not build.
britain.philosophy: Single-grave ideology personalises the afterlife—weapons, beakers, and gendered kits for a journey—contrasting collective Neolithic chambers. Cosmology remains wordless; practice says the person, armed and provisioned, matters at death. No named sages; ritual drinking and barrow skyline are the doctrine.
britain.science: Early metallurgy (copper then bronze), barrow surveying, and continental navigation are the enabling sciences of the takeover. Isotope studies show mobile individuals; craft recipes for Beaker ceramics and goldworking spread with people. Farming continues, but smithing and archery tech mark the new skill elite.

france.culture: Northeast communities adopt Corded male weapon packages; western and southern groups stage Beaker hospitality and archery. Farmers adapt herds and cereals to more pastoral-influenced economies in the north while Mediterranean façades keep older crop logics. Society is a mosaic of alliance rituals sharing metal and ceramic fashions across corridors.
france.description:
By 2500 BC France becomes a patchwork of packages. Corded Ware reaches the northeast with single graves and battle-axes; Bell Beaker colours the west and south with maritime pots, archery kits, and gold. Megalithic stages host Beaker inserts—old stone theatres restyled.

Two demographic pulses—Corded-linked then Beaker-linked—mix with lasting Neolithic substrates more gently than in Britain. Steppe fractions run higher toward the Rhine and lower toward the southwest. Regional identities form along river and Atlantic corridors through prestige goods and marriage networks, not a single empire.

Gendered single graves and drinking sets personalise death beside older collective rites still in memory—thick practice, thin doctrine.

france.art: Corded Ware reaches the northeast with single graves and battle-axes; Bell Beaker colours the west and south with maritime pots, archery kits, and gold. Megalithic stages host Beaker inserts—old stone theatres restyled. Visual France becomes a patchwork of CW male packages and Beaker drinking sets.
france.ideas: Two demographic pulses—CW-linked then Beaker-linked—mix with lasting Neolithic substrates more gently than in Britain. Regional identities form along Rhine, Atlantic, and Mediterranean corridors. Prestige goods and marriage networks, not a single empire, remake belonging.
france.philosophy: Gendered single graves and Beaker kits personalise death beside older collective rites still in memory. Cosmology is inferred from posture, ochre, weapons, and tomb reuse—thick practice, thin doctrine. No schools; an ethic of alliance through drink, gift, and armed burial.
france.science: Copper–bronze metallurgy, archery craft, and ceramic standardisation spread with mobility. Farmers adapt herds and cereals to a more pastoral-influenced economy in the north. River and Atlantic routes become measured exchange sciences linking Bohemia to Brittany.

central.culture: Single-grave communities stage gendered kits—male weapon packages, female ornament sets—under barrow lines that create ritual geographies of lineage. Pastoral–agrarian scheduling and marital mobility knit the plain. Society selects and standardises; cemeteries record both openness and later Y-chromosome narrowing.
central.description:
By about 2500 BC Corded Ware stretches across Germany, Bohemia, and Poland as the classic temperate package: cord-impressed pottery, faceted battle-axes, hammer-headed pins, and single graves under mounds. Bohemian cemeteries show early diversity then Y-lineage narrowing—art kits standardise as lineages bottleneck.

Papac and colleagues demonstrate Corded Ware as Yamnaya-related plus farmer mix, not pure steppe clones; social selection reshapes Y-diversity by roughly 2600 BC. The culture expands as a marriage-and-migration system across the North European Plain. Belonging is amphora, axe, and mound alignment.

Steppe percentages run higher early and east; more Globular Amphora–like farmer ancestry persists west and south. Central Europe’s Corded age is replacement-tinged admixture with fierce regional clines—the demographic engine behind much later Indo-European modeling for temperate Europe.

central.linguisticNote: Core correlate of temperate European Indo-Europeanization in steppe models.

central.art: Cord-impressed pottery, faceted battle-axes, hammer-headed pins, and single graves under mounds are the classic look. Bohemian cemeteries show early diversity then Y-lineage narrowing—art kits standardise as lineages bottleneck. Male weapon packages and female ornament sets stage a gendered gallery of the dead.
central.ideas: Papac et al. show CW as Yamnaya-related plus farmer mix, not pure steppe clones; social selection reshapes Y-diversity by ~2600 BC. Corded Ware expands as a marriage-and-migration system across the North European Plain. Belonging is amphora, axe, and mound alignment.
central.philosophy: Single-grave ideology personalises destiny—flexed bodies, ochre, gendered gifts for an afterlife journey. Ancestral mound lines create ritual geographies of lineage. Doctrine is funerary geometry; named philosophers do not exist.
central.science: Pastoral–agrarian scheduling, early bronze uptake, and ceramic standardisation scale across hundreds of kilometres. Mobility (isotopes, aDNA) is itself a researched ancient practice of seasonal and marital movement. Battle-axe stone grinding and cord-paddle pottery are precision crafts.

scandinavia.culture: Barrow lineages and gendered kits organise a new pastoral–agrarian north. Stone battle-axes and corded pottery standardise prestige. Society is Corded in structure—single grave, mound line, martial male package—with regional Swedish and Danish names for the same continental system.
scandinavia.description:
In the mid-third millennium Scandinavian Corded Ware arrives as Single Grave Culture in Jutland and Battle Axe Culture in Sweden. Danish aDNA (Allentoft and colleagues, 2024) shows a second near-total turnover—steppe-rich Single Grave replacing Funnelbeaker pools and aligning ancestry toward later Danes. Battle Axe Sweden joins the Corded horizon with local farmer admixture.

Polished stone battle-axes become sculptural status; corded beakers and mound skylines replace collective TRB chambers as the dominant aesthetic. Pitted Ware art fades. The idea of the person-under-the-barrow conquers the megalith commons.

Steppe-related fractions often fall in roughly the sixty-to-eighty-five percent range in southern Single Grave contexts—among Europe’s sharpest Corded-era transformations north of the Alps.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Single Grave / Battle Axe: often ~60–85% steppe-related; southern SGC higher steppe than some inland mixes.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Standard archaeological correlate of pre-Germanic on the northern arc.

scandinavia.art: Danish Single Grave barrows with corded beakers and Swedish boat-shaped battle-axes remake the north’s funerary gallery. Polished stone axes become sculptural status; Pitted Ware art fades. Gendered kits and mound skylines replace collective TRB chambers as the dominant aesthetic.
scandinavia.ideas: Allentoft et al. 2024: a second near-total Danish turnover—steppe-rich SGC replaces Funnelbeaker pools, aligning ancestry toward later Danes. Battle Axe Sweden joins the Corded Ware horizon with local farmer admixture (Malmström 2019). The idea of the person-under-the-barrow conquers the megalith commons.
scandinavia.philosophy: Weapon burial and single graves preach an ethic of individual martial destiny and patrilineal mound lines. Older megaliths become landscape memory, not the main afterlife technology. No runes yet; cosmology is axe, ochre, and barrow.
scandinavia.science: Incoming pastoral–agrarian mixes, early metal trickle, and barrow construction reorganise northern landscapes. Isotopes show diet shifts with the cultural break. Stone battle-axe manufacture is standardised prestige engineering.

italy.culture: Northern contact zones stage Beaker kits; lake-shore communities invest in timber platforms and wet architecture. Peninsular groups keep stronger Copper Age habits. Society is mosaic—fashion without forced genomic unity—linking Alps, Po, and coasts through trade.
italy.description:
By 2500 BC Bell Beaker pots and archery kits appear in the north and along contact zones, then Early Bronze facies diversify. Polada lake-dwellings and related settlements add timber architecture to the Beaker portable package. Art mixes Beaker prestige with local tomb traditions.

Beaker fashion and moderate steppe ancestry enter without cloning British replacement levels. Italy remains a mosaic—EEF-heavy, regionally stubborn. Ideas of warrior archery and drinking alliance graft onto Copper Age hierarchies.

Bronze recipes spread; pile-dwelling carpentry in wet northern basins is environmental engineering. Caprine–cereal economies adapt to Apennine and Po ecologies as metal and amber trickle through Alpine passes.
italy.linguisticNote: IE (toward Italic) and non-IE (toward Etruscan) lineages both still ahead historically.
italy.ancestryNote: Moderate steppe on EEF+WHG base; not Danish SGC extremes.

italy.ideas: Beaker fashion and moderate steppe ancestry enter without cloning British replacement levels. Italy remains a mosaic—EEF-heavy, regionally stubborn. Ideas of warrior archery and drinking alliance graft onto Copper Age hierarchies.
italy.philosophy: Beaker single-grave gestures coexist with older collective habits; cosmology stays archaeological. Lake and tomb rites structure community without texts. Worldview is craft, feast, and burial posture.
italy.science: Bronze recipes spread; pile-dwelling carpentry in wet northern basins is environmental engineering. Caprine–cereal economies adapt to Apennine and Po ecologies. Metal and amber trickle through Alpine passes as measured trade.

balkans.culture: Regional Early Bronze communities organise tumuli, cemeteries, and metal workshops without one pan-Balkan brand. Southern zones look toward Aegean prestige; northern zones toward Carpathian metal. Society is a patchwork of steppe-admixed and farmer-persistent neighbours.
balkans.description:
By 2500 BC Early Bronze facies diversify—Ezero-related, Cetina, and regional metal styles—with tumuli and weapon graves in places. Aegean links foreshadow later shaft-grave glitter. Art is regional metal and pottery, not a single Beaker carpet.

Steppe-related ancestry consolidates unevenly; southern Balkans keep stronger farmer bases. Exchange toward the Aegean and Carpathians structures prestige. Cultural labels multiply quickly on a still-forming ternary ancestry.

Bronze casting spreads through Danube–Aegean corridors. Mining in the Carpathian–Balkan arc feeds wider Europe. Agricultural terraces and herding adapt to broken terrain as worldview remains archaeological—no Linear B yet.
balkans.linguisticNote: Early IE dialects + substrates; Greek becomes visible with Linear B later.
balkans.ancestryNote: Steppe present but typically lower than CW Poland/Germany averages.
balkans.art: Early Bronze facies diversify—Ezero-related, Cetina, and regional metal styles—with tumuli and weapon graves in places. Aegean links foreshadow later shaft-grave glitter. Art is regional metal and pottery, not a single Beaker carpet.
balkans.ideas: Steppe-related ancestry consolidates unevenly; southern Balkans keep stronger farmer bases. Exchange toward the Aegean and Carpathians structures prestige. Cultural labels multiply quickly on a still-forming ternary ancestry.
balkans.philosophy: Tumulus and cemetery rites encode local ancestor politics. Aegean contact brings new prestige theologies of metal and import. Worldview remains archaeological—thick deposits, thin doctrine.
balkans.science: Bronze casting spreads through Danube–Aegean corridors. Mining and metallurgy in the Carpathian–Balkan arc feed wider Europe. Agricultural terraces and herding adapt to broken terrain.

eastern.culture: Catacomb and late Yamnaya pastoral groups maintain kurgan landscapes with redesigned burial chambers. Regional polities structure herd territories and exchange. Society stays mobile and funerary-prestigious—sibling to Corded Ware, not a copy of Beaker Britain.
eastern.description:
While Corded Ware and Bell Beaker carry steppe ancestry into temperate Europe around 2500 BC, the eastern steppe diversifies through late Yamnaya and Catacomb horizons. Catacomb graves under kurgans, distinctive pottery, and continued weapon–ornament kits evolve the Yamnaya visual order. Corded Ware to the west is the temperate sibling package; on the steppe, catacomb architecture restyles the mound world.

Steppe societies organise regional pastoral polities without cities. East–west clines of exchange keep metal, animals, and people moving. Stelae and ochre traditions persist as Catacomb rites redesign the journey of the dead with side chambers and new postures.

Pastoral mobility, bronze uptake, and kurgan engineering continue. Horse management intensifies toward later chariot horizons. The east remains WSH-rich while feeding western transformations.
eastern.linguisticNote: Continuing steppe IE continuum (details of dialect geography unknown).
eastern.ancestryNote: Catacomb / steppe-contact as WSH package + farmer remainder — no separate EHG/CHG slices.

eastern.ideas: Steppe societies diversify after Yamnaya’s peak while feeding CW and Beaker west with ancestry and ideas. Catacomb horizons organise regional pastoral polities without cities. East–west clines of exchange keep metal, animals, and people moving.
eastern.philosophy: Catacomb burial redesigns the journey of the dead—side chambers, new postures—within kurgan sacred geography. Herd and ancestor remain the moral poles. Cosmology stays funerary and pastoral.
eastern.science: Pastoral mobility, bronze uptake, and kurgan engineering continue. Horse management intensifies toward later chariot horizons. Ceramic and metal recipes mark regional technical schools across the Pontic–Caspian.

periods.linguistics: Primary window hypothesized for Indo-Europeanization of temperate Europe. Pre-Germanic and other early IE lineages are often tied to CW/Battle Axe; Celtic/Italic pathways more debated. Iberian Beaker material culture does not imply IE speech.

DEU.name: Corded Ware Germany
DEU.conflicts: Overlaps and succession with Bell Beaker in the west; GAC substrate absorbed.
DEU.literature: Corded Ware’s central European heartland speaks through single-grave choreography and cord decoration — a ceramic dialect. Later Germanic verse is a distant cousin at best; do not put Beowulf in a Corded Ware mouth. Praise of patrons and cattle may be older Indo-European habits, but here they are archaeological silence surrounding loud pots.
DEU.art: Cord-impressed pottery, faceted battle-axes, hammer-headed pins, and single graves under mounds are the classic look. Bohemian cemeteries show early diversity then Y-lineage narrowing—art kits standardise as lineages bottleneck. Male weapon packages and female ornament sets stage a gendered gallery of the dead.
DEU.religion: Corded Ware: gendered single graves (battle-axe male package), amphora/beaker offerings, and ancestral mound reuse. Steppe-linked burial ideology over older megalithic collectivity.
DEU.ideas: Papac et al. show CW as Yamnaya-related plus farmer mix, not pure steppe clones; social selection reshapes Y-diversity by ~2600 BC. Corded Ware expands as a marriage-and-migration system across the North European Plain. Belonging is amphora, axe, and mound alignment.
DEU.philosophy: Single-grave ideology personalises destiny—flexed bodies, ochre, gendered gifts for an afterlife journey. Ancestral mound lines create ritual geographies of lineage. Doctrine is funerary geometry; named philosophers do not exist.
DEU.science: Pastoral–agrarian scheduling, early bronze uptake, and ceramic standardisation scale across hundreds of kilometres. Mobility (isotopes, aDNA) is itself a researched ancient practice of seasonal and marital movement. Battle-axe stone grinding and cord-paddle pottery are precision crafts.
DEU.culture: Single-grave communities stage gendered kits—male weapon packages, female ornament sets—under barrow lines that create ritual geographies of lineage. Pastoral–agrarian scheduling and marital mobility knit the plain. Society selects and standardises; cemeteries record both openness and later Y-chromosome narrowing.
DEU.description:
By about 2500 BC Corded Ware stretches across Germany, Bohemia, and Poland as the classic temperate package: cord-impressed pottery, faceted battle-axes, hammer-headed pins, and single graves under mounds. Bohemian cemeteries show early diversity then Y-lineage narrowing—art kits standardise as lineages bottleneck.

Papac and colleagues demonstrate Corded Ware as Yamnaya-related plus farmer mix, not pure steppe clones; social selection reshapes Y-diversity by roughly 2600 BC. The culture expands as a marriage-and-migration system across the North European Plain. Belonging is amphora, axe, and mound alignment.

Steppe percentages run higher early and east; more Globular Amphora–like farmer ancestry persists west and south. Central Europe’s Corded age is replacement-tinged admixture with fierce regional clines—the demographic engine behind much later Indo-European modeling for temperate Europe.

DNK.name: Single Grave Culture
DNK.conflicts: Near-complete turnover vs TRB; ~60–85% steppe-related ancestry.
DNK.literature: Still pre-literate. Meaning travels in burial theatre: single graves, gendered grave goods, drinking vessels. Later IE epic genres are centuries downstream — useful analogies, not Corded Ware novels. Danish gatekeeping of the Baltic Sound makes culture a toll-booth as well as a stage.
DNK.art: Danish Single Grave barrows with corded beakers and Swedish boat-shaped battle-axes remake the north’s funerary gallery. Polished stone axes become sculptural status; Pitted Ware art fades. Gendered kits and mound skylines replace collective TRB chambers as the dominant aesthetic.
DNK.religion: Single Grave: barrow burials with corded beaker and battle-axe kits. New funerary grammar replacing TRB megalithic collective rites.

DNK.description:
In the mid-third millennium Scandinavian Corded Ware arrives as Single Grave Culture in Jutland and Battle Axe Culture in Sweden. Danish aDNA (Allentoft and colleagues, 2024) shows a second near-total turnover—steppe-rich Single Grave replacing Funnelbeaker pools and aligning ancestry toward later Danes. Battle Axe Sweden joins the Corded horizon with local farmer admixture.

Steppe-related fractions often fall in roughly the sixty-to-eighty-five percent range in southern Single Grave contexts—among Europe’s sharpest Corded-era transformations north of the Alps.

GBR.name: Bell Beaker Britain
GBR.literature: Britain’s Beaker age leaves no texts, but it leaves a funerary grammar: beakers by the face, archer wrist-guards, copper knives. Later British poetry of barrows and ‘ancient Britons’ is Victorian dreamwork laid over this genomic rupture — read it as reception, not reportage. The real ‘literature’ is the grave as staged sentence: who drinks, who owns metal, who lies crouched.
GBR.art: Beaker pots, copper daggers, wristguards, and gold lunulae/discs arrive with a new funerary fashion of single graves under round barrows. The Amesbury Archer’s kit is portraiture in metal and stone. Older stone theatres stay standing while the people who gather there genetically transform—continuity of place, rupture of flesh.
GBR.religion: Bell Beaker Britain: individual graves with beaker, copper/bronze, and archer kits; henge landscapes still used. Beaker rite overlays older monumental religion.
GBR.ideas: Olalde et al.’s ~90% turnover makes Britain the textbook of demic Beaker transformation: steppe-rich continental ancestry and R1b lineages replace Neolithic pools within centuries. Round-barrow individualism and archery prestige rewrite social ideals. Monuments are reused by newcomers who inherit landscapes they did not build.
GBR.philosophy: Single-grave ideology personalises the afterlife—weapons, beakers, and gendered kits for a journey—contrasting collective Neolithic chambers. Cosmology remains wordless; practice says the person, armed and provisioned, matters at death. No named sages; ritual drinking and barrow skyline are the doctrine.
GBR.science: Early metallurgy (copper then bronze), barrow surveying, and continental navigation are the enabling sciences of the takeover. Isotope studies show mobile individuals; craft recipes for Beaker ceramics and goldworking spread with people. Farming continues, but smithing and archery tech mark the new skill elite.
GBR.culture: Single-grave barrow society personalises death with gendered kits—weapons, beakers, archery gear—while farming continues under new lineages. Continental links bring metal recipes and marriage networks. Social ideals shift from Neolithic ceremonial commons toward armed, provisioned personhood at the grave. Stonehenge’s stones remain; the congregation’s ancestry does not.
GBR.description:
Around 2500 BC Bell Beaker Britain becomes the textbook of demic transformation. Copper daggers, wristguards, Beaker pots, and gold lunulae arrive with single graves under round barrows; the Amesbury Archer’s kit is portraiture in metal and stone. Older stone theatres stay standing while the people who gather there genetically transform—continuity of place, rupture of flesh.

Ancient DNA (Olalde and colleagues) indicates on the order of ninety percent turnover of the prior Neolithic population, with steppe-rich continental ancestry and R1b lineages rising sharply. Round-barrow individualism and archery prestige rewrite social ideals. Monuments are reused by newcomers who inherit landscapes they did not build.

The resulting ternary—steppe, Early European Farmer, Western Hunter-Gatherer—varies site to site, but the demographic cliff is the period’s defining British fact.

ESP.name: Bell Beaker Iberia
ESP.summary: Beaker package on Neolithic-like genomes early on.
ESP.conflicts: Gradual steppe influx (often male-biased) vs Britain’s cliff replacement.
ESP.literature: Still pre-literate. Meaning travels in burial theatre: single graves, gendered grave goods, drinking vessels. Later IE epic genres are centuries downstream — useful analogies, not Corded Ware novels. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: Maritime Bell Beakers, palmela points, stone wristguards, and sheet-gold ornaments redefine elite display. Art is a portable prestige kit that looks pan-European yet sits on local Copper Age skeletons and tomb stages. Older megalithic theatres receive Beaker inserts; visual politics shifts from wall-and-tholos toward the individualised grave inventory.
ESP.religion: Bell Beaker Iberia: beaker graves and prestige metal beside older Copper Age idol/tomb traditions — mixed ritual landscape, not pure steppe copy.
ESP.ideas: The Beaker idea travels farther than steppe genes: cultural brand and alliance ritual, not Britain’s near-total turnover. Belonging is negotiated through drinking sets and archery kits inside a durable farmer substrate. Atlantic and interior corridors offer rival paths into the same ceramic fashion—one peninsula, many demographic contracts.
ESP.philosophy: Ritual centres on individualising Beaker graves and drinking sets that stage personhood and alliance. Cosmology stays oral; archaeology recovers gendered kits and ancestral tomb re-entry, not theology. Worldview is a prestige ethic of archery, metal, and hospitality performed at the grave—practice without named sages.
ESP.science: Copper and early bronze recipes refine casting and sheet-gold work; archery gear implies measured craft of bow, point, and wristguard. Farmers and herders keep Mediterranean agrosystems while joining Beaker exchange for metal and exotics. Coastal navigation and river logistics underwrite the Atlantic Beaker face as applied geography.
ESP.culture: Beaker Iberian society grafts an archery-and-hospitality package onto Copper Age hierarchies. Single graves and gendered kits personalise death beside older collective chambers still in memory. Coastal and inland groups plug into pan-European Beaker exchange for metal and ornaments while Mediterranean farming continues. Status is portable—pot, dagger, wristguard—more than new megamonuments.
ESP.description:
By about 2500 BC the Bell Beaker package—maritime pots, archery kits, palmela points, gold ornaments—reshapes Iberian display while the underlying Copper Age bodies and farmer substrate largely endure. Tomb reuse and Beaker deposits restyle older megalithic stages without erasing them. The peninsula becomes a textbook of cultural fashion travelling farther than genes.

Steppe-related ancestry enters more gradually than in Britain, and often with a male-biased signature in uniparental markers. Communities negotiate belonging through Beaker rites inside a still-strong Early European Farmer base. Atlantic and interior networks compete: the same pottery brand, different demographic bargains.

This is not Olalde’s island cliff-edge replacement. Iberia’s Beaker age is admixture and prestige ethics—archery, drink, and metal at the grave—overlaid on Los Millares–descended social landscapes.

FRA.name: Beaker / late CW France
FRA.literature: Still pre-literate. Meaning travels in burial theatre: single graves, gendered grave goods, drinking vessels. Later IE epic genres are centuries downstream — useful analogies, not Corded Ware novels. French courts and vernaculars repeatedly set continental fashions of word and dress.
FRA.art: Corded Ware reaches the northeast with single graves and battle-axes; Bell Beaker colours the west and south with maritime pots, archery kits, and gold. Megalithic stages host Beaker inserts—old stone theatres restyled. Visual France becomes a patchwork of CW male packages and Beaker drinking sets.
FRA.religion: Beaker / late CW France: beaker inhumations and residual megalithic reuse. Atlantic and continental ritual packages meet in cemeteries.
FRA.ideas: Two demographic pulses—CW-linked then Beaker-linked—mix with lasting Neolithic substrates more gently than in Britain. Regional identities form along Rhine, Atlantic, and Mediterranean corridors. Prestige goods and marriage networks, not a single empire, remake belonging.
FRA.philosophy: Gendered single graves and Beaker kits personalise death beside older collective rites still in memory. Cosmology is inferred from posture, ochre, weapons, and tomb reuse—thick practice, thin doctrine. No schools; an ethic of alliance through drink, gift, and armed burial.
FRA.science: Copper–bronze metallurgy, archery craft, and ceramic standardisation spread with mobility. Farmers adapt herds and cereals to a more pastoral-influenced economy in the north. River and Atlantic routes become measured exchange sciences linking Bohemia to Brittany.
FRA.culture: Northeast communities adopt Corded male weapon packages; western and southern groups stage Beaker hospitality and archery. Farmers adapt herds and cereals to more pastoral-influenced economies in the north while Mediterranean façades keep older crop logics. Society is a mosaic of alliance rituals sharing metal and ceramic fashions across corridors.
FRA.description:
By 2500 BC France becomes a patchwork of packages. Corded Ware reaches the northeast with single graves and battle-axes; Bell Beaker colours the west and south with maritime pots, archery kits, and gold. Megalithic stages host Beaker inserts—old stone theatres restyled.

Two demographic pulses—Corded-linked then Beaker-linked—mix with lasting Neolithic substrates more gently than in Britain. Steppe fractions run higher toward the Rhine and lower toward the southwest. Regional identities form along river and Atlantic corridors through prestige goods and marriage networks, not a single empire.

Gendered single graves and drinking sets personalise death beside older collective rites still in memory—thick practice, thin doctrine.

NLD.name: Dutch / Rhine Beakers
NLD.summary: Key Beaker node for northwest Europe.
NLD.conflicts: Link between CW world and British Beaker stream.
NLD.literature: Still pre-literate. Meaning travels in burial theatre: single graves, gendered grave goods, drinking vessels. Later IE epic genres are centuries downstream — useful analogies, not Corded Ware novels. Low Countries urbanism turns painting, print, and cloth into a civic theology of detail.
NLD.art: Cord-impressed pottery, faceted battle-axes, hammer-headed pins, and single graves under mounds are the classic look. Bohemian cemeteries show early diversity then Y-lineage narrowing—art kits standardise as lineages bottleneck. Male weapon packages and female ornament sets stage a gendered gallery of the dead.
NLD.religion: Dutch/Rhine Beakers: single graves with beaker sets along river corridors — classic western Beaker funerary package.
NLD.ideas: Papac et al. show CW as Yamnaya-related plus farmer mix, not pure steppe clones; social selection reshapes Y-diversity by ~2600 BC. Corded Ware expands as a marriage-and-migration system across the North European Plain. Belonging is amphora, axe, and mound alignment.
NLD.philosophy: Single-grave ideology personalises destiny—flexed bodies, ochre, gendered gifts for an afterlife journey. Ancestral mound lines create ritual geographies of lineage. Doctrine is funerary geometry; named philosophers do not exist.
NLD.science: Pastoral–agrarian scheduling, early bronze uptake, and ceramic standardisation scale across hundreds of kilometres. Mobility (isotopes, aDNA) is itself a researched ancient practice of seasonal and marital movement. Battle-axe stone grinding and cord-paddle pottery are precision crafts.
NLD.culture: Single-grave communities stage gendered kits—male weapon packages, female ornament sets—under barrow lines that create ritual geographies of lineage. Pastoral–agrarian scheduling and marital mobility knit the plain. Society selects and standardises; cemeteries record both openness and later Y-chromosome narrowing.
NLD.description:
By about 2500 BC Corded Ware stretches across Germany, Bohemia, and Poland as the classic temperate package: cord-impressed pottery, faceted battle-axes, hammer-headed pins, and single graves under mounds. Bohemian cemeteries show early diversity then Y-lineage narrowing—art kits standardise as lineages bottleneck.

Papac and colleagues demonstrate Corded Ware as Yamnaya-related plus farmer mix, not pure steppe clones; social selection reshapes Y-diversity by roughly 2600 BC. The culture expands as a marriage-and-migration system across the North European Plain. Belonging is amphora, axe, and mound alignment.

Steppe percentages run higher early and east; more Globular Amphora–like farmer ancestry persists west and south. Central Europe’s Corded age is replacement-tinged admixture with fierce regional clines—the demographic engine behind much later Indo-European modeling for temperate Europe.

UKR.name: Catacomb steppe
UKR.conflicts: Continues pastoralist steppe while CW remakes temperate Europe.
UKR.literature: Still pre-literate. Meaning travels in burial theatre: single graves, gendered grave goods, drinking vessels. Later IE epic genres are centuries downstream — useful analogies, not Corded Ware novels. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: Catacomb graves under kurgans, distinctive pottery, and continued weapon–ornament kits evolve the Yamnaya visual order. Corded Ware to the west is the temperate sibling package; on the steppe, catacomb architecture restyles the mound world. Stelae and ochre traditions persist.
UKR.religion: Catacomb steppe: niche graves under kurgans, ochre, and weapon offerings — evolved Yamnaya-related funerary religion on the Pontic plain.
UKR.ideas: Steppe societies diversify after Yamnaya’s peak while feeding CW and Beaker west with ancestry and ideas. Catacomb horizons organise regional pastoral polities without cities. East–west clines of exchange keep metal, animals, and people moving.
UKR.philosophy: Catacomb burial redesigns the journey of the dead—side chambers, new postures—within kurgan sacred geography. Herd and ancestor remain the moral poles. Cosmology stays funerary and pastoral.
UKR.science: Pastoral mobility, bronze uptake, and kurgan engineering continue. Horse management intensifies toward later chariot horizons. Ceramic and metal recipes mark regional technical schools across the Pontic–Caspian.
UKR.culture: Catacomb and late Yamnaya pastoral groups maintain kurgan landscapes with redesigned burial chambers. Regional polities structure herd territories and exchange. Society stays mobile and funerary-prestigious—sibling to Corded Ware, not a copy of Beaker Britain.
UKR.description:
While Corded Ware and Bell Beaker carry steppe ancestry into temperate Europe around 2500 BC, the eastern steppe diversifies through late Yamnaya and Catacomb horizons. Catacomb graves under kurgans, distinctive pottery, and continued weapon–ornament kits evolve the Yamnaya visual order. Corded Ware to the west is the temperate sibling package; on the steppe, catacomb architecture restyles the mound world.

Steppe societies organise regional pastoral polities without cities. East–west clines of exchange keep metal, animals, and people moving. Stelae and ochre traditions persist as Catacomb rites redesign the journey of the dead with side chambers and new postures.

Pastoral mobility, bronze uptake, and kurgan engineering continue. Horse management intensifies toward later chariot horizons. The east remains WSH-rich while feeding western transformations.

ITA.name: Italian Beaker / EBA
ITA.literature: Still pre-literate. Meaning travels in burial theatre: single graves, gendered grave goods, drinking vessels. Later IE epic genres are centuries downstream — useful analogies, not Corded Ware novels. Italian cities teach prestige: from Roman monumentality to Renaissance brand management of beauty.
ITA.art: Bell Beaker pots and archery kits appear in the north and along contact zones, then Early Bronze facies diversify. Polada lake-dwellings and related settlements add timber architecture to the Beaker portable package. Art mixes Beaker prestige with local tomb traditions.
ITA.religion: Italian Beaker / EBA: beaker graves and local Copper Age cemetery continuity; Mediterranean ritual vocabularies absorb the beaker fashion selectively.
ITA.ideas: Beaker fashion and moderate steppe ancestry enter without cloning British replacement levels. Italy remains a mosaic—EEF-heavy, regionally stubborn. Ideas of warrior archery and drinking alliance graft onto Copper Age hierarchies.
ITA.philosophy: Beaker single-grave gestures coexist with older collective habits; cosmology stays archaeological. Lake and tomb rites structure community without texts. Worldview is craft, feast, and burial posture.
ITA.science: Bronze recipes spread; pile-dwelling carpentry in wet northern basins is environmental engineering. Caprine–cereal economies adapt to Apennine and Po ecologies. Metal and amber trickle through Alpine passes as measured trade.
ITA.culture: Northern contact zones stage Beaker kits; lake-shore communities invest in timber platforms and wet architecture. Peninsular groups keep stronger Copper Age habits. Society is mosaic—fashion without forced genomic unity—linking Alps, Po, and coasts through trade.

PRT.description:
By about 2500 BC the Bell Beaker package—maritime pots, archery kits, palmela points, gold ornaments—reshapes Iberian display while the underlying Copper Age bodies and farmer substrate largely endure. Tomb reuse and Beaker deposits restyle older megalithic stages without erasing them. The peninsula becomes a textbook of cultural fashion travelling farther than genes.

Steppe-related ancestry enters more gradually than in Britain, and often with a male-biased signature in uniparental markers. Communities negotiate belonging through Beaker rites inside a still-strong Early European Farmer base. Atlantic and interior networks compete: the same pottery brand, different demographic bargains.

This is not Olalde’s island cliff-edge replacement. Iberia’s Beaker age is admixture and prestige ethics—archery, drink, and metal at the grave—overlaid on Los Millares–descended social landscapes.
PRT.culture: Beaker Iberian society grafts an archery-and-hospitality package onto Copper Age hierarchies. Single graves and gendered kits personalise death beside older collective chambers still in memory. Coastal and inland groups plug into pan-European Beaker exchange for metal and ornaments while Mediterranean farming continues. Status is portable—pot, dagger, wristguard—more than new megamonuments.
PRT.art: Maritime Bell Beakers, palmela points, stone wristguards, and sheet-gold ornaments redefine elite display. Art is a portable prestige kit that looks pan-European yet sits on local Copper Age skeletons and tomb stages. Older megalithic theatres receive Beaker inserts; visual politics shifts from wall-and-tholos toward the individualised grave inventory.
PRT.ideas: The Beaker idea travels farther than steppe genes: cultural brand and alliance ritual, not Britain’s near-total turnover. Belonging is negotiated through drinking sets and archery kits inside a durable farmer substrate. Atlantic and interior corridors offer rival paths into the same ceramic fashion—one peninsula, many demographic contracts.
PRT.philosophy: Ritual centres on individualising Beaker graves and drinking sets that stage personhood and alliance. Cosmology stays oral; archaeology recovers gendered kits and ancestral tomb re-entry, not theology. Worldview is a prestige ethic of archery, metal, and hospitality performed at the grave—practice without named sages.
PRT.science: Copper and early bronze recipes refine casting and sheet-gold work; archery gear implies measured craft of bow, point, and wristguard. Farmers and herders keep Mediterranean agrosystems while joining Beaker exchange for metal and exotics. Coastal navigation and river logistics underwrite the Atlantic Beaker face as applied geography.

IRL.description:
Around 2500 BC Bell Beaker Britain becomes the textbook of demic transformation. Copper daggers, wristguards, Beaker pots, and gold lunulae arrive with single graves under round barrows; the Amesbury Archer’s kit is portraiture in metal and stone. Older stone theatres stay standing while the people who gather there genetically transform—continuity of place, rupture of flesh.

Ancient DNA (Olalde and colleagues) indicates on the order of ninety percent turnover of the prior Neolithic population, with steppe-rich continental ancestry and R1b lineages rising sharply. Round-barrow individualism and archery prestige rewrite social ideals. Monuments are reused by newcomers who inherit landscapes they did not build.

The resulting ternary—steppe, Early European Farmer, Western Hunter-Gatherer—varies site to site, but the demographic cliff is the period’s defining British fact.
IRL.culture: Single-grave barrow society personalises death with gendered kits—weapons, beakers, archery gear—while farming continues under new lineages. Continental links bring metal recipes and marriage networks. Social ideals shift from Neolithic ceremonial commons toward armed, provisioned personhood at the grave. Stonehenge’s stones remain; the congregation’s ancestry does not.
IRL.art: Beaker ceramics, copper then bronze daggers, wristguards, and gold lunulae or discs define a new funerary gallery under round barrows. The Amesbury Archer assemblage reads as a biography in objects. Art is portable prestige against a backdrop of older megalithic silhouettes still charged with power.
IRL.ideas: Demic Beaker transformation makes Britain the extreme western case of steppe-related expansion. Ideas of belonging attach to barrow, beaker, and archery kit. Monument reuse shows newcomers claiming inherited sacred geography—ideological continuity of place after biological rupture.
IRL.philosophy: Single-grave ideology personalises the afterlife—weapons, beakers, and gendered gifts for a journey—contrasting collective Neolithic chambers. Cosmology remains wordless; practice says the armed and provisioned person matters at death. Ritual drinking and the barrow skyline are the doctrine.
IRL.science: Early metallurgy, barrow surveying, and continental navigation enable the takeover’s material face. Isotope studies show mobile individuals; craft recipes for Beaker ceramics and goldworking spread with people. Farming persists, but smithing and archery tech mark the new skill elite.

MCO.description:
By 2500 BC France becomes a patchwork of packages. Corded Ware reaches the northeast with single graves and battle-axes; Bell Beaker colours the west and south with maritime pots, archery kits, and gold. Megalithic stages host Beaker inserts—old stone theatres restyled.

Two demographic pulses—Corded-linked then Beaker-linked—mix with lasting Neolithic substrates more gently than in Britain. Steppe fractions run higher toward the Rhine and lower toward the southwest. Regional identities form along river and Atlantic corridors through prestige goods and marriage networks, not a single empire.

Gendered single graves and drinking sets personalise death beside older collective rites still in memory—thick practice, thin doctrine.
MCO.culture: Northeast communities adopt Corded male weapon packages; western and southern groups stage Beaker hospitality and archery. Farmers adapt herds and cereals to more pastoral-influenced economies in the north while Mediterranean façades keep older crop logics. Society is a mosaic of alliance rituals sharing metal and ceramic fashions across corridors.
MCO.art: Cord-impressed pottery and faceted battle-axes mark the northeast; maritime Beakers, wristguards, and gold mark the Atlantic and south. Visual France is a collage of CW kits and Beaker drinking sets on reused megalithic stages—two prestige dialects in one landmass.
MCO.ideas: Belonging is negotiated through corridor politics—Rhine Corded, Atlantic Beaker, Mediterranean contacts—rather than island-style total replacement. Prestige goods and marriages remake identity while Neolithic memory persists in stone and ancestry.
MCO.philosophy: Gendered single graves and Beaker kits personalise destiny beside collective chambers still charged with power. Cosmology is inferred from posture, ochre, weapons, and tomb reuse. No schools; an ethic of alliance through drink, gift, and armed burial.
MCO.science: Copper–bronze metallurgy, archery craft, and ceramic standardisation spread with mobility. River and Atlantic routes become measured exchange sciences linking Bohemia to Brittany. Herd–cereal scheduling adapts to pastoral influence without abandoning farming.
MCO.cultureLabel: Bell Beaker & late Corded Ware France

CZE.description:
By about 2500 BC Corded Ware stretches across Germany, Bohemia, and Poland as the classic temperate package: cord-impressed pottery, faceted battle-axes, hammer-headed pins, and single graves under mounds. Bohemian cemeteries show early diversity then Y-lineage narrowing—art kits standardise as lineages bottleneck.

Papac and colleagues demonstrate Corded Ware as Yamnaya-related plus farmer mix, not pure steppe clones; social selection reshapes Y-diversity by roughly 2600 BC. The culture expands as a marriage-and-migration system across the North European Plain. Belonging is amphora, axe, and mound alignment.

Steppe percentages run higher early and east; more Globular Amphora–like farmer ancestry persists west and south. Central Europe’s Corded age is replacement-tinged admixture with fierce regional clines—the demographic engine behind much later Indo-European modeling for temperate Europe.
CZE.culture: Single-grave communities stage gendered kits—male weapon packages, female ornament sets—under barrow lines that create ritual geographies of lineage. Pastoral–agrarian scheduling and marital mobility knit the plain. Society selects and standardises; cemeteries record both openness and later Y-chromosome narrowing.
CZE.art: Cord-impressed pottery, faceted battle-axes, pins, and ochre-flecked flexed burials form the classic look. Male and female kits stage a gendered gallery of the dead. Visual culture is funerary geometry repeated across hundreds of kilometres.
CZE.ideas: Corded Ware is ethnogenesis through admixture and social selection, not a clone army from the steppe. Ideas of personhood under the mound and patrilineal barrow lines remake politics. Marriage networks carry the package farther than any single migration chronicle.
CZE.philosophy: Single-grave ideology personalises destiny—flexed bodies, ochre, gendered gifts for an afterlife journey. Ancestral mound lines create ritual geographies of lineage. Doctrine is funerary geometry; named philosophers do not exist.
CZE.science: Pastoral–agrarian scheduling, early bronze uptake, and ceramic standardisation scale across the plain. Mobility evidenced by isotopes and aDNA is itself ancient practice of seasonal and marital movement. Battle-axe grinding and cord-paddle pottery are precision crafts.

NOR.description:
In the mid-third millennium Scandinavian Corded Ware arrives as Single Grave Culture in Jutland and Battle Axe Culture in Sweden. Danish aDNA (Allentoft and colleagues, 2024) shows a second near-total turnover—steppe-rich Single Grave replacing Funnelbeaker pools and aligning ancestry toward later Danes. Battle Axe Sweden joins the Corded horizon with local farmer admixture.

Polished stone battle-axes become sculptural status; corded beakers and mound skylines replace collective TRB chambers as the dominant aesthetic. Pitted Ware art fades. The idea of the person-under-the-barrow conquers the megalith commons.

Steppe-related fractions often fall in roughly the sixty-to-eighty-five percent range in southern Single Grave contexts—among Europe’s sharpest Corded-era transformations north of the Alps.
NOR.culture: Barrow lineages and gendered kits organise a new pastoral–agrarian north. Stone battle-axes and corded pottery standardise prestige. Society is Corded in structure—single grave, mound line, martial male package—with regional Swedish and Danish names for the same continental system.
NOR.art: Danish Single Grave barrows with corded beakers and Swedish boat-shaped battle-axes remake the funerary gallery. Polished axes are sculptural status; Pitted Ware aesthetics recede. Gendered kits and mound skylines replace megalithic commons.
NOR.ideas: Near-total Danish turnover makes Scandinavia a northern twin to Britain’s Beaker cliff. Ideas of martial personhood and patrilineal mounds erase TRB ceremonial commons as the main afterlife technology. Continental Corded belonging arrives as demographic fact.
NOR.philosophy: Weapon burial and single graves preach individual martial destiny and mound lineage. Older megaliths become landscape memory. No runes yet; cosmology is axe, ochre, and barrow.
NOR.science: Incoming pastoral–agrarian mixes, early metal trickle, and barrow construction reorganise northern landscapes. Isotopes show diet shifts with the cultural break. Stone battle-axe manufacture is standardised prestige engineering.
