SMR.description:
By 2500 BC Bell Beaker pots and archery kits appear in the north and along contact zones, then Early Bronze facies diversify. Polada lake-dwellings and related settlements add timber architecture to the Beaker portable package. Art mixes Beaker prestige with local tomb traditions.

Beaker fashion and moderate steppe ancestry enter without cloning British replacement levels. Italy remains a mosaic—EEF-heavy, regionally stubborn. Ideas of warrior archery and drinking alliance graft onto Copper Age hierarchies.

Bronze recipes spread; pile-dwelling carpentry in wet northern basins is environmental engineering. Caprine–cereal economies adapt to Apennine and Po ecologies as metal and amber trickle through Alpine passes.
SMR.culture: Northern contact zones stage Beaker kits; lake-shore communities invest in timber platforms and wet architecture. Peninsular groups keep stronger Copper Age habits. Society is mosaic—fashion without forced genomic unity—linking Alps, Po, and coasts through trade.
SMR.art: Bell Beaker pots and archery kits meet local tomb traditions; Polada timber settlements add architectural art of piles and platforms. Visual culture is hybrid prestige rather than a single funerary brand.
SMR.ideas: Beaker alliance ethics graft onto Copper Age inequality without Danish extremes of replacement. Italy’s idea of the age is selective adoption—ports and passes as filters of fashion and ancestry.
SMR.philosophy: Beaker single-grave gestures coexist with older collective habits; cosmology stays archaeological. Lake and tomb rites structure community without texts. Worldview is craft, feast, and burial posture.
SMR.science: Bronze recipes spread; pile-dwelling carpentry in wet northern basins is environmental engineering. Caprine–cereal economies adapt to Apennine and Po ecologies. Metal and amber trickle through Alpine passes as measured trade.

GRC.description:
By 2500 BC Early Bronze facies diversify—Ezero-related, Cetina, and regional metal styles—with tumuli and weapon graves in places. Aegean links foreshadow later shaft-grave glitter. Art is regional metal and pottery, not a single Beaker carpet.

Steppe-related ancestry consolidates unevenly; southern Balkans keep stronger farmer bases. Exchange toward the Aegean and Carpathians structures prestige. Cultural labels multiply quickly on a still-forming ternary ancestry.

Bronze casting spreads through Danube–Aegean corridors. Mining in the Carpathian–Balkan arc feeds wider Europe. Agricultural terraces and herding adapt to broken terrain as worldview remains archaeological—no Linear B yet.
GRC.culture: Regional Early Bronze communities organise tumuli, cemeteries, and metal workshops without one pan-Balkan brand. Southern zones look toward Aegean prestige; northern zones toward Carpathian metal. Society is a patchwork of steppe-admixed and farmer-persistent neighbours.
GRC.art: Tumuli, weapon graves, and regional ceramics diversify display. Aegean-facing glitter begins to matter. Visual culture is provincial metal fashion, not Corded uniformity or later palace frescoes.

KOS.description:
By 2500 BC Early Bronze facies diversify—Ezero-related, Cetina, and regional metal styles—with tumuli and weapon graves in places. Aegean links foreshadow later shaft-grave glitter. Art is regional metal and pottery, not a single Beaker carpet.

Steppe-related ancestry consolidates unevenly; southern Balkans keep stronger farmer bases. Exchange toward the Aegean and Carpathians structures prestige. Cultural labels multiply quickly on a still-forming ternary ancestry.

Bronze casting spreads through Danube–Aegean corridors. Mining in the Carpathian–Balkan arc feeds wider Europe. Agricultural terraces and herding adapt to broken terrain as worldview remains archaeological—no Linear B yet.
KOS.culture: Regional Early Bronze communities organise tumuli, cemeteries, and metal workshops without one pan-Balkan brand. Southern zones look toward Aegean prestige; northern zones toward Carpathian metal. Society is a patchwork of steppe-admixed and farmer-persistent neighbours.
KOS.art: Tumuli, weapon graves, and regional ceramics diversify display. Aegean-facing glitter begins to matter. Visual culture is provincial metal fashion, not Corded uniformity or later palace frescoes.
KOS.ideas: Prestige follows corridors to Aegean and Carpathians. Ideas of belonging multiply with facies names on a forming WHG–EEF–steppe ternary. The age anticipates Mycenaean demand without yet writing Greek.
KOS.philosophy: Tumulus and cemetery rites encode local ancestor politics. Aegean contact brings new prestige theologies of metal and import. Worldview remains archaeological—thick deposits, thin doctrine.
KOS.science: Bronze casting spreads through Danube–Aegean corridors. Carpathian–Balkan mining feeds wider Europe. Terracing and herding adapt agronomy to broken terrain.

BLR.description:
While Corded Ware and Bell Beaker carry steppe ancestry into temperate Europe around 2500 BC, the eastern steppe diversifies through late Yamnaya and Catacomb horizons. Catacomb graves under kurgans, distinctive pottery, and continued weapon–ornament kits evolve the Yamnaya visual order. Corded Ware to the west is the temperate sibling package; on the steppe, catacomb architecture restyles the mound world.

Steppe societies organise regional pastoral polities without cities. East–west clines of exchange keep metal, animals, and people moving. Stelae and ochre traditions persist as Catacomb rites redesign the journey of the dead with side chambers and new postures.

Pastoral mobility, bronze uptake, and kurgan engineering continue. Horse management intensifies toward later chariot horizons. The east remains WSH-rich while feeding western transformations.
BLR.culture: Catacomb and late Yamnaya pastoral groups maintain kurgan landscapes with redesigned burial chambers. Regional polities structure herd territories and exchange. Society stays mobile and funerary-prestigious—sibling to Corded Ware, not a copy of Beaker Britain.
BLR.art: Catacomb architecture under mounds, regional pottery, weapons, and ornaments restyle Yamnaya aesthetics. Visual order remains kurgan-centred; temperate Corded Ware is the western sibling look.
BLR.ideas: Diversification after Yamnaya’s peak feeds CW and Beaker west with ancestry and ideas while the steppe keeps pastoral polity logic. Belonging is regional horizon and mound rite, not urban citizenship.
BLR.philosophy: Catacomb burial redesigns the journey of the dead—side chambers, new postures—within kurgan sacred geography. Herd and ancestor remain the moral poles. Cosmology stays funerary and pastoral.
BLR.science: Pastoral mobility, bronze uptake, and kurgan engineering continue. Horse management intensifies toward later chariot horizons. Ceramic and metal recipes mark regional technical schools across the Pontic–Caspian.

periods.label: Bronze Age prestige networks
periods.narrative: By 1400 BC the Nordic Bronze Age is a Scandinavian prestige world of rock art, amber, and imported bronze on a gene pool already reset by Single Grave. Farther south Tumulus then Urnfield rites, El Argar, Terramare, and Mycenaean palaces (Linear B = early Greek) mark regional Bronze Age states. Deep ancestry is the WHG–EEF–steppe ternary in local proportions; culture names now change faster than genetic turnovers.
periods.culturesNote: Nordic Bronze Age, Wessex, El Argar, Tumulus, Urnfield, Terramare/Apennine, Mycenaean, Srubnaya — BA facies on post-3000 BCE mixes.

iberia.culture: El Argar organises labour, metal, and burial under house floors inside defended centres; Atlantic façades participate in pan-European bronze exchange and hoarding. Inequality is visible in diadems, weapon sets, and settlement hierarchy. Society is provincial—southeast courts and western warrior circuits—yet both belong to a metal age in which recycling, fortification, and dryland storage structure daily life.
iberia.description:
By the mid–second millennium BC southeast Iberia’s El Argar tradition experiments with early complex society: fortified hill settlements, marked inequality, intramural urn burials, and stark silver diadems. Farther west, Atlantic Bronze networks join wider European sword and scrap-bronze circuits. Visual politics splits by province—argaric goblets and fortress graves versus Atlantic warrior hoards.

Steppe-related ancestry is established yet diluted beside a durable Neolithic substrate; rough schematics near half EEF with substantial WHG and moderate steppe capture continuity-with-admixture, not a second British-style replacement. Culture names and metal fashions change faster than genes.

These regional ‘kingdoms’ of craft and coercion precede Celtic ethnonyms by centuries. Iberia’s Bronze Age is hierarchical provisioning, watery hoards, and metallurgical specialisation on a ternary already set in the Beaker centuries.
iberia.linguisticNote: Likely mosaic of early IE and non-IE; Iberian (non-IE) and Celtic appear in later written record.
iberia.ancestryNote: Ternary mix with higher EEF retention than Britain; rough schematic ~50/20/30 EEF/WHG/steppe varies by site.
iberia.art: El Argar’s hillforts, intramural urn burials, and stark silver diadems create a severe court style in the southeast; Atlantic Bronze hoards and warrior gear shine farther west. Pottery and metal diverge by province—argaric goblets versus Atlantic carp’s-tongue swords. Visual politics is fortress, grave under the floor, and hoarded bronze.
iberia.ideas: Southeast Iberia experiments with early complex society—controlled metal, marked inequality, fortified centres—while Atlantic façades join wider European bronze circuits. Steppe ancestry is present but diluted beside a durable Neolithic substrate; culture change outruns genetic revolution. Regional kingdoms of craft and coercion precede Celtic names by centuries.
iberia.philosophy: Intramural burial under houses binds the dead to domestic space—an ancestor theology of the threshold. Atlantic hoards in rivers and bogs suggest offerings to water powers or sworn destruction of weapons and wealth. No philosophers; ethics of honour and metal debt are inferred from diadems, blades, and deposition rites.
iberia.science: Argolic metallurgy, silver working, and fortification engineering mark specialised technical classes. Atlantic smiths cast, alloy, and recycle within pan-European scrap-bronze economies—recycling as industrial practice. Dryland farming and storage inside defended sites are survival science under hierarchical provisioning.

britain.culture: Barrow cemeteries, roundhouses, and emerging field systems organise agrarian and lineage life. Elites display continental metal and amber while smiths alloy local tin into bronze. Society is chiefly and funerary—mound skylines as claims—rather than palace bureaucracy. Belonging is cemetery, exchange partner, and control of metal routes.
britain.description:
In the mid–second millennium BC post-Beaker Britain consolidates a barrow aristocracy under facies such as Wessex: gold lozenges, amber, bronze daggers, and later Deverel–Rimbury urnfields. Stonehenge’s Bronze Age reworkings keep the old sky theatre in elite service. Rock art is scarcer than in Scandinavia; prestige is portable gold and continental-style weaponry.

Ancestry remains the Beaker-set WHG–EEF–steppe ternary without another island-wide replacement. Chiefly exchange with Brittany, the Rhine, and Nordic zones advertises belonging to a European bronze club. Land, herds, and barrow cemeteries fix lineage claims in chalk country.

Southwest tin makes the islands a strategic node in bronze recipes across Europe—applied geography at continental scale on a gene pool already reset in the Beaker centuries.
britain.linguisticNote: On the path hypothesized toward Insular Celtic; absolute Celtic chronology debated.
britain.ancestryNote: Continuous with Beaker Britain; steppe typically near ~half in many models.
britain.art: Wessex rich graves—gold lozenges, amber, bronze daggers—and later Deverel–Rimbury urnfields stage a barrow aristocracy in metal and cloth. Stonehenge’s Bronze Age reworkings keep the old sky theatre in elite service. Rock art is scarcer than in Scandinavia; prestige is portable gold and continental-style weaponry.
britain.ideas: Post-Beaker Britain consolidates a WHG–EEF–steppe ternary under named archaeological facies (Wessex, etc.) without another island-wide replacement. Chiefly exchange with Brittany, the Rhine, and Nordic zones advertises belonging to a European bronze club. Land, herds, and barrow cemeteries fix lineage claims in chalk country.
britain.philosophy: Barrow cemeteries and hoards in watery places suggest ancestors and offerings structuring obligation. Solar and martial symbolism travels with continental metal styles more than with local scripture. Worldview is elite funerary theatre—gold, dagger, and mound—plus older henge memory still charged with power.
britain.science: Tin from southwest Britain makes the islands a strategic node in bronze recipes across Europe. Smiths alloy, cast, and recycle; field systems and roundhouses organise agrarian production. Seagoing exchange of metal and amber is applied geography at continental scale.

france.culture: Barrow aristocracies, hilltop occupations, and field systems organise production and defence. Atlantic hoards and Tumulus weapon graves stage warrior ethics; later urnfields gather cremation communities. Society is provincial yet networked—weights, alloys, and seasonal trade binding France into European bronze circuits.
france.description:
By 1400 BC Bronze Age provinces overlie the third-millennium genetic settlement. Tumulus barrows, Atlantic bronze hoards, and later Urnfield cremation urns diversify funerary art. Swords, spears, and ornamented bronze advertise warrior fashion shared with Central Europe.

Ancestry is a stable ternary relative to Corded/Beaker formation; culture names change faster than genes. Atlantic and Tumulus networks pull elites into pan-European exchange. Toward Urnfield, cremation communities reimagine the dead as ash collectives—an idea of belonging through fire.

Monumentality shifts from megalith to mound and hoard. Metal becomes the sculptural medium of obligation, vow, and display across a corridor land between Channel and Mediterranean.
france.linguisticNote: Toward early Celtic; Gaulish attested only in the Iron Age.
france.ancestryNote: Established ternary; no Denmark-scale new pulse.
france.art: Tumulus barrows, Atlantic bronze hoards, and later Urnfield cremation urns diversify funerary art. Swords, spears, and ornamented bronze advertise warrior fashion shared with Central Europe. Monumentality shifts from megalith to mound and hoard—metal as the sculptural medium.
france.ideas: Bronze Age provinces overlie the third-millennium genetic settlement; culture names change faster than ancestry. Atlantic and Tumulus networks pull elites into pan-European exchange. Toward Urnfield, cremation communities reimagine the dead as ash collectives—an idea of belonging through fire.
france.philosophy: Hoards in rivers and bogs look like gifts to watery powers or ritual destruction of weapons. Cremation reorients the body–soul problem without texts to explain it. Sacred life is depositional and funerary—sun, metal, and mound—not academy philosophy.
france.science: Bronze casting, sheet-working, and long-distance scrap economies are industrial knowledge. Field systems and hilltop occupations organise production and defence. Tin, copper, and amber routes make France a corridor science of weights, alloys, and seasonal trade.

central.culture: Tumulus elites display weapons under mounds; Urnfield communities gather cremation cemeteries as cities of ash. Hillforts organise surplus and defence; smiths and miners feed scrap circuits. Society is warrior-fashionable and metallurgically specialised on a genetically settled plain.
central.description:
By 1400 BC Central Europe moves through Middle Bronze Tumulus weapon graves toward Late Bronze Urnfield cremation cemeteries—urns, bronze swords, and situla art on the southern edge. Visual culture shifts from body-under-mound to ash-in-urn. Hillforts and hoards punctuate the landscape.

Genetic continuity with Corded-descended mixes underlies rapid cultural renaming. Urnfield networks may seed later Celtic linguistic zones—debated, yet the idea of wide cremation communities is clear. Warrior fashion and bronze scrap economies integrate the Carpathian–Alpine arc.

Advanced casting, eastern Alpine mining, and recycling economies make this an industrial Bronze Age. Culture change vastly outruns genetic replacement: the ternary set after Corded Ware mostly holds while rites of fire remake the dead.
central.linguisticNote: Pre-Celtic / early Celtic hypotheses for Urnfield–Hallstatt arc — debated.
central.ancestryNote: CW-descended ternary; cultural change ≫ genetic replacement.
central.art: Middle Bronze Tumulus weapon graves yield to Late Bronze Urnfield cremation cemeteries—urns, bronze swords, and situla art on the southern edge. Visual culture shifts from body-under-mound to ash-in-urn. Hillforts and hoards add landscape punctuation.
central.ideas: Genetic continuity with CW-descended mixes under rapid cultural renaming. Urnfield networks may seed later Celtic linguistic zones—debated, but the idea of wide cremation communities is clear. Warrior fashion and bronze scrap economies integrate the Carpathian–Alpine arc.
central.philosophy: Cremation reframes the person as fire-transformed; urnfields are cities of the dead without biographies. Hoards suggest vows, trophies, or offerings to powers of water and earth. Worldview is ritual technology of fire and metal, not written ethics.
central.science: Advanced bronze casting (including early lost-wax flourishes), mining in the eastern Alps, and recycling economies are industrial science. Urnfield agronomy and fortification engineering organise surplus and defence. Weight systems and ingot trade imply quantitative exchange literacy.

scandinavia.culture: Longhouse farms, barrow labour, and chiefly exchange organise surplus around amber and bronze. Communities gather at rock-art panels and wet offering places. Society is maritime-prestige and agrarian—ships carved on stone, cloth and bronze on the dead—without Mycenaean palaces.
scandinavia.description:
From roughly 1700 to 500 BC the Nordic Bronze Age makes Scandinavia Europe’s great image culture of the metal age. Figurative rock art at Tanum, Bohuslän, and Østfold; the Trundholm sun chariot; oak-coffin costumes; lurs; and Viksø helmets stage ships, sun discs, warriors, and ploughs on coastal bedrock and in bog finds. Denmark’s dressed dead are prehistoric couture.

Imported metal founds a prestige economy—amber out, bronze in—binding chiefs to Únětice, Carpathian, and later Italian copper routes. Genetically the region is continuous with Battle Axe / Single Grave; this is cultural climax, not a third replacement. Rock-art fleets advertise maritime ideology and meeting places for exchange.

Sun-cult imagery and watery hoards stage a cosmology of light, voyage, and offering. Scandinavia’s science is network metallurgy: sourcing, alloying, and recycling foreign copper with local strategies, plus ship carpentry inferred from rock art and later boat finds.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Post–Single Grave ternary; WHG residual higher than in some southern BA zones.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Mainstream view: pre-Germanic speakers in a Nordic BA cultural frame — reconstructed, not attested.
scandinavia.art: Figurative rock art (Tanum, Bohuslän, Østfold), the Trundholm sun chariot, oak-coffin costumes, lurs, and Viksø helmets make Scandinavia Bronze Age Europe’s great image culture. Ships, sun discs, warriors, and ploughs cover coastal bedrock. Denmark’s dressed dead are prehistoric couture.
scandinavia.ideas: Imported metal founds a prestige economy—amber out, bronze in—binding chiefs to Únětice, Carpathian, then Italian copper routes (Nørgaard et al. 2021). Genetically continuous with Battle Axe/SGC; this is cultural climax, not third replacement. Rock-art fleets advertise maritime ideology and meeting places for exchange.
scandinavia.philosophy: Sun-cult imagery (Trundholm; rock-art discs) and watery hoards stage a cosmology of light, voyage, and offering. Processions and twin myths are guessed from paired figures and horns—reconstructed ritual, not named theology. Sacred knowledge is metal, ship, and sun performed on rock and in bog.
scandinavia.science: Scandinavia’s science is network metallurgy: sourcing, alloying, and recycling foreign copper with local tin strategies, plus ship carpentry inferred from rock art and later boat finds. Longhouse farms and barrow labour organise surplus. Amber grading and route knowledge are commercial geography.

italy.culture: Terramare communities organise ditch, bank, and house grid as communal labour; Apennine groups move seasonally between upland and lowland. Society is settlement-disciplined on the plain and pastoral-mobile in the mountains—two Bronze Age Italies sharing metal age inequality.
italy.description:
By 1400 BC the Po plain’s Terramare embanked villages—planned ditches, banks, and dense housing—are civic art in earth and timber, while Apennine pottery and pastoral sites mark the mountains. Cremation and inhumation rites vary by facies. Visual identity is settlement geometry more than Nordic rock-art fleets.

Organised Po settlements imply collective labour and perhaps proto-urban control of floodplain wealth. Apennine mobility links coasts to uplands. Ancestry keeps Italian Early European Farmer weight with moderate Bronze Age steppe—foundation tones for later Italic and Etruscan genetic landscapes.

Hydraulic and embankment engineering, bronze workshops, and floodplain agronomy are Terramare sciences. Northern Italian copper later feeds Nordic networks—Italy as ore science for the amber north.
italy.linguisticNote: Toward Proto-Italic and non-IE (Etruscan) lines — historical split still ahead.
italy.ancestryNote: EEF-heavier than CW north; steppe present but moderate.
italy.art: Terramare embanked villages of the Po plain—planned ditches, banks, and dense housing—are civic art in earth and timber; Apennine pottery and pastoral sites mark the mountains. Cremation and inhumation rites vary by facies. Visual identity is settlement geometry more than rock-art fleets.
italy.ideas: Organised Po settlements imply collective labour and perhaps proto-urban control of floodplain wealth. Apennine mobility links coasts to uplands. Ancestry keeps Italian EEF weight with moderate BA steppe—foundation for later Italic/Etruscan genetic landscapes.
italy.philosophy: Settlement rituals, structured deposits, and cemeteries suggest civic-sacral order without Nordic sun chariots. Water, ditch, and bank may themselves be charged boundaries. Ethics of communal embankment and pastoral seasonality stand in for written philosophy.
italy.science: Hydraulic and embankment engineering, bronze workshops, and floodplain agronomy are Terramare sciences. Apennine herding calendars manage vertical mobility. Northern Italian copper later feeds Nordic networks—Italy as ore science for the north.

balkans.culture: Wanax-centred palaces organise workshops, warriors, and redistributive feasts; sanctuaries receive accounted offerings. Northern Balkan communities keep non-palace metal-age societies linked by trade. Belonging is palace catchment or regional metal network, not a single Balkan ethnos.
balkans.description:
By 1400 BC Mycenaean palace societies create Europe’s first palace visual regime in the Aegean: megarons, shaft and tholos tombs, gold masks, frescoes, and chamber tombs. Linear B tablets write early Greek as administrative marks—offerings, rations, inventories—not epic manuscripts. Northern Balkans join Carpathian metal fashions without sharing palaces.

Palace centres redistribute goods, sponsor warriors, and stage sanctuary reciprocity. Genomes show moderate steppe on Aegean farmer bases—language attested, demography not Corded-Denmark. Northern Balkan Bronze Age networks parallel Mycenaean demand through metal and amber routes.

Linear B records offerings to named gods (forms related to Zeus, Poseidon, and female deities)—a real pantheon in accounting. Thought is ritual and administrative; Homer lies ahead as epic memory of this world.
balkans.ancestryNote: Mycenaean steppe fraction model-dependent, generally moderate (<< CW Denmark).
balkans.linguisticNote: Mycenaean Greek is attested. Other Balkan IE (later Thracian/Illyrian) poorly documented.
balkans.art: Mycenaean palaces, shaft and tholos tombs, gold masks, frescoes, and chamber tombs create Europe’s first palace visual regime; northern Balkans join Carpathian metal fashions. Linear B tablets are administrative marks, not epic manuscripts. Art is gold, megarons, and painted plaster.
balkans.ideas: Palace centres redistribute goods, sponsor warriors, and write early Greek—political theology of wanax and sanctuary. Genomes show moderate steppe on Aegean farmer bases—language attested, demography not CW-Denmark. Northern Balkan BA networks parallel Mycenaean without sharing palaces.
balkans.philosophy: Linear B records offerings to named gods (e.g. di-we / Zeus forms, Poseidon, female deities)—a real pantheon in accounting, not philosophy seminars. Sanctuary deposits and funerary gold stage honour and divine reciprocity. Thought is ritual and administrative; Homer is still ahead as epic memory.
balkans.science: Palace metrology, seal administration, chariot workshops, and Mediterranean shipping are bureaucratic sciences. Bronze armour, fresco chemistry, and ashlar masonry are specialised crafts. Northern Balkan metallurgy and amber routes link Aegean demand to Carpathian supply.

eastern.culture: Timber-grave pastoral groups and forest-steppe neighbours organise around herds, kurgans, and metal workshops. Sintashta-related fortified settlements farther east intensify warrior and chariot specialisation. Society is confederative and mobile, with farming edges softening pure steppe lifeways.
eastern.description:
By the mid–second millennium BC Srubnaya (Timber-grave) and related forest-steppe cultures keep a pastoral-steppe aesthetic of timber-lined graves under kurgans, bone and bronze weapon sets, and settlement traces. Forest-steppe edges mix farmer motifs. Chariot-related imagery and horse gear echo Sintashta innovations farther east in the Urals.

Srubnaya and kin maintain steppe-rich ancestry on pathways often linked—cautiously—toward early Indo-Iranian, parallel to European Bronze Age diversification west. Fortified Sintashta-type experiments show war-tech and metallurgy intensifying. Identity is pastoral confederacy more than Mycenaean palace.

Spoked-wheel chariots, horse teams, and bronze arsenals are peak steppe engineering of the early second millennium. Timber-grave communities manage herds, metallurgy, and forest-steppe farming edges. Long-distance horse and metal knowledge feeds both European and Asian Bronze Ages.
eastern.linguisticNote: Often linked toward early Indo-Iranian; details contested.
eastern.art: Timber-grave (Srubnaya) kurgans, bone and bronze weapon sets, and settlement traces keep a pastoral-steppe aesthetic; forest-steppe edges mix farmer motifs. Chariot-related imagery and horse gear echo Sintashta innovations farther east. Art is grave timber, weapon, and herd wealth.
eastern.ideas: Srubnaya and kin maintain steppe-rich ancestry on pathways often linked toward early Indo-Iranian—parallel to European BA diversification west. Fortified Sintashta-type experiments (Urals) show war-tech and metallurgy intensifying. Identity is pastoral confederacy more than Mycenaean palace.
eastern.philosophy: Kurgan and timber-grave rites continue ancestor–herd cosmologies; chariot burials farther east sacralise speed and war. Fire, horse, and sky motifs are reconstructed from Indo-Iranian comparisons with caution—not quoted steppe scripture. Ethics of guest, raid, and offering are inferred, not authored.
eastern.science: Sintashta–Petrovka chariots (spoked wheels, horse teams) and bronze arsenals are peak steppe engineering of the early 2nd millennium BC. Timber-grave communities manage herds, metallurgy, and forest-steppe farming edges. Long-distance horse and metal knowledge feeds both European and Asian Bronze Ages.

DNK.name: Nordic Bronze Age Denmark
DNK.conflicts: Rival chiefly networks across south Scandinavia; links to Tumulus Europe.
DNK.literature: The Trundholm chariot is a one-object poem: a gilded sun pulled by a bronze horse on a ritual wagon. Oak-coffin burials with textiles preserve bodies as soft sculpture. No runes yet — meaning is metal and cloth.

GBR.name: Wessex / British BA
GBR.conflicts: Regional chiefdom competition; Irish BA exchange.
GBR.literature: No native scripts in the Nordic zone; meaning is cut into rock and cast in bronze. Later Eddic myth is a distant Iron/Viking-Age reframing — handle as comparative poetry, not Bronze Age reportage. Insular voices and North Sea contact give this place a distinctive accent in the wider European chorus.
GBR.art: Wessex rich graves—gold lozenges, amber, bronze daggers—and later Deverel–Rimbury urnfields stage a barrow aristocracy in metal and cloth. Stonehenge’s Bronze Age reworkings keep the old sky theatre in elite service. Rock art is scarcer than in Scandinavia; prestige is portable gold and continental-style weaponry.
GBR.religion: Wessex / British BA: rich barrow burials, ceremonial landscapes around older henges, and prestige metal deposition — ancestor and status cult in chalk country.
GBR.ideas: Post-Beaker Britain consolidates a WHG–EEF–steppe ternary under named archaeological facies (Wessex, etc.) without another island-wide replacement. Chiefly exchange with Brittany, the Rhine, and Nordic zones advertises belonging to a European bronze club. Land, herds, and barrow cemeteries fix lineage claims in chalk country.
GBR.philosophy: Barrow cemeteries and hoards in watery places suggest ancestors and offerings structuring obligation. Solar and martial symbolism travels with continental metal styles more than with local scripture. Worldview is elite funerary theatre—gold, dagger, and mound—plus older henge memory still charged with power.
GBR.science: Tin from southwest Britain makes the islands a strategic node in bronze recipes across Europe. Smiths alloy, cast, and recycle; field systems and roundhouses organise agrarian production. Seagoing exchange of metal and amber is applied geography at continental scale.
GBR.culture: Barrow cemeteries, roundhouses, and emerging field systems organise agrarian and lineage life. Elites display continental metal and amber while smiths alloy local tin into bronze. Society is chiefly and funerary—mound skylines as claims—rather than palace bureaucracy. Belonging is cemetery, exchange partner, and control of metal routes.
GBR.description:
In the mid–second millennium BC post-Beaker Britain consolidates a barrow aristocracy under facies such as Wessex: gold lozenges, amber, bronze daggers, and later Deverel–Rimbury urnfields. Stonehenge’s Bronze Age reworkings keep the old sky theatre in elite service. Rock art is scarcer than in Scandinavia; prestige is portable gold and continental-style weaponry.

Ancestry remains the Beaker-set WHG–EEF–steppe ternary without another island-wide replacement. Chiefly exchange with Brittany, the Rhine, and Nordic zones advertises belonging to a European bronze club. Land, herds, and barrow cemeteries fix lineage claims in chalk country.

Southwest tin makes the islands a strategic node in bronze recipes across Europe—applied geography at continental scale on a gene pool already reset in the Beaker centuries.

ESP.name: El Argar
ESP.conflicts: Fortified centers; rivalry with Atlantic Bronze networks.
ESP.literature: No native scripts in the Nordic zone; meaning is cut into rock and cast in bronze. Later Eddic myth is a distant Iron/Viking-Age reframing — handle as comparative poetry, not Bronze Age reportage. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: El Argar’s hillforts, intramural urn burials, and stark silver diadems create a severe court style in the southeast; Atlantic Bronze hoards and warrior gear shine farther west. Pottery and metal diverge by province—argaric goblets versus Atlantic carp’s-tongue swords. Visual politics is fortress, grave under the floor, and hoarded bronze.
ESP.religion: El Argar: intramural and cemetery burials with sharp status grading; Argaric ritual is household/tomb-focused rather than Nordic sun-chariot religion.
ESP.ideas: Southeast Iberia experiments with early complex society—controlled metal, marked inequality, fortified centres—while Atlantic façades join wider European bronze circuits. Steppe ancestry is present but diluted beside a durable Neolithic substrate; culture change outruns genetic revolution. Regional kingdoms of craft and coercion precede Celtic names by centuries.
ESP.philosophy: Intramural burial under houses binds the dead to domestic space—an ancestor theology of the threshold. Atlantic hoards in rivers and bogs suggest offerings to water powers or sworn destruction of weapons and wealth. No philosophers; ethics of honour and metal debt are inferred from diadems, blades, and deposition rites.
ESP.science: Argolic metallurgy, silver working, and fortification engineering mark specialised technical classes. Atlantic smiths cast, alloy, and recycle within pan-European scrap-bronze economies—recycling as industrial practice. Dryland farming and storage inside defended sites are survival science under hierarchical provisioning.
ESP.culture: El Argar organises labour, metal, and burial under house floors inside defended centres; Atlantic façades participate in pan-European bronze exchange and hoarding. Inequality is visible in diadems, weapon sets, and settlement hierarchy. Society is provincial—southeast courts and western warrior circuits—yet both belong to a metal age in which recycling, fortification, and dryland storage structure daily life.
ESP.description:
By the mid–second millennium BC southeast Iberia’s El Argar tradition experiments with early complex society: fortified hill settlements, marked inequality, intramural urn burials, and stark silver diadems. Farther west, Atlantic Bronze networks join wider European sword and scrap-bronze circuits. Visual politics splits by province—argaric goblets and fortress graves versus Atlantic warrior hoards.

Steppe-related ancestry is established yet diluted beside a durable Neolithic substrate; rough schematics near half EEF with substantial WHG and moderate steppe capture continuity-with-admixture, not a second British-style replacement. Culture names and metal fashions change faster than genes.

These regional ‘kingdoms’ of craft and coercion precede Celtic ethnonyms by centuries. Iberia’s Bronze Age is hierarchical provisioning, watery hoards, and metallurgical specialisation on a ternary already set in the Beaker centuries.

DEU.name: Tumulus Culture
DEU.literature: No native scripts in the Nordic zone; meaning is cut into rock and cast in bronze. Later Eddic myth is a distant Iron/Viking-Age reframing — handle as comparative poetry, not Bronze Age reportage. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.
DEU.art: Middle Bronze Tumulus weapon graves yield to Late Bronze Urnfield cremation cemeteries—urns, bronze swords, and situla art on the southern edge. Visual culture shifts from body-under-mound to ash-in-urn. Hillforts and hoards add landscape punctuation.
DEU.religion: Tumulus Culture: barrow cemeteries, weapon graves, and bronze hoards. Central European BA religion visible mainly as funerary and deposition rites.
DEU.ideas: Genetic continuity with CW-descended mixes under rapid cultural renaming. Urnfield networks may seed later Celtic linguistic zones—debated, but the idea of wide cremation communities is clear. Warrior fashion and bronze scrap economies integrate the Carpathian–Alpine arc.
DEU.philosophy: Cremation reframes the person as fire-transformed; urnfields are cities of the dead without biographies. Hoards suggest vows, trophies, or offerings to powers of water and earth. Worldview is ritual technology of fire and metal, not written ethics.
DEU.science: Advanced bronze casting (including early lost-wax flourishes), mining in the eastern Alps, and recycling economies are industrial science. Urnfield agronomy and fortification engineering organise surplus and defence. Weight systems and ingot trade imply quantitative exchange literacy.
DEU.culture: Tumulus elites display weapons under mounds; Urnfield communities gather cremation cemeteries as cities of ash. Hillforts organise surplus and defence; smiths and miners feed scrap circuits. Society is warrior-fashionable and metallurgically specialised on a genetically settled plain.
DEU.description:
By 1400 BC Central Europe moves through Middle Bronze Tumulus weapon graves toward Late Bronze Urnfield cremation cemeteries—urns, bronze swords, and situla art on the southern edge. Visual culture shifts from body-under-mound to ash-in-urn. Hillforts and hoards punctuate the landscape.

Genetic continuity with Corded-descended mixes underlies rapid cultural renaming. Urnfield networks may seed later Celtic linguistic zones—debated, yet the idea of wide cremation communities is clear. Warrior fashion and bronze scrap economies integrate the Carpathian–Alpine arc.

Advanced casting, eastern Alpine mining, and recycling economies make this an industrial Bronze Age. Culture change vastly outruns genetic replacement: the ternary set after Corded Ware mostly holds while rites of fire remake the dead.

ITA.name: Terramare
ITA.conflicts: Internal collapse debates; Apennine neighbors south.
ITA.literature: No native scripts in the Nordic zone; meaning is cut into rock and cast in bronze. Later Eddic myth is a distant Iron/Viking-Age reframing — handle as comparative poetry, not Bronze Age reportage. Italian cities teach prestige: from Roman monumentality to Renaissance brand management of beauty.
ITA.art: Terramare embanked villages of the Po plain—planned ditches, banks, and dense housing—are civic art in earth and timber; Apennine pottery and pastoral sites mark the mountains. Cremation and inhumation rites vary by facies. Visual identity is settlement geometry more than rock-art fleets.
ITA.religion: Terramare: settlement rituals, structured deposits, and cemetery practice in embanked villages — Po-plain civic-sacral order without Nordic rock-art cosmology.
ITA.ideas: Organised Po settlements imply collective labour and perhaps proto-urban control of floodplain wealth. Apennine mobility links coasts to uplands. Ancestry keeps Italian EEF weight with moderate BA steppe—foundation for later Italic/Etruscan genetic landscapes.
ITA.philosophy: Settlement rituals, structured deposits, and cemeteries suggest civic-sacral order without Nordic sun chariots. Water, ditch, and bank may themselves be charged boundaries. Ethics of communal embankment and pastoral seasonality stand in for written philosophy.

ITA.description:

Cremation and inhumation rites vary by facies. Visual identity is settlement geometry more than Nordic rock-art fleets.

GRC.name: Mycenaean palaces
GRC.summary: Palace states with Linear B Greek.
GRC.conflicts: Rivalry among palaces; Aegean–Anatolian conflicts culminating in LBA crises.
GRC.literature: No native scripts in the Nordic zone; meaning is cut into rock and cast in bronze. Later Eddic myth is a distant Iron/Viking-Age reframing — handle as comparative poetry, not Bronze Age reportage. Greek language and forms remain a reusable antiquity — quarried by every later age for prestige.
GRC.art: Mycenaean palaces, shaft and tholos tombs, gold masks, frescoes, and chamber tombs create Europe’s first palace visual regime; northern Balkans join Carpathian metal fashions. Linear B tablets are administrative marks, not epic manuscripts. Art is gold, megarons, and painted plaster.
GRC.religion: Mycenaean palaces: named gods appear in Linear B (e.g. Poseidon, Potnia); palace sacrifice, libation, and tholos/chamber tombs. First European written pantheon fragments.
GRC.ideas: Palace centres redistribute goods, sponsor warriors, and write early Greek—political theology of wanax and sanctuary. Genomes show moderate steppe on Aegean farmer bases—language attested, demography not CW-Denmark. Northern Balkan BA networks parallel Mycenaean without sharing palaces.
GRC.philosophy: Linear B records offerings to named gods (e.g. di-we / Zeus forms, Poseidon, female deities)—a real pantheon in accounting, not philosophy seminars. Sanctuary deposits and funerary gold stage honour and divine reciprocity. Thought is ritual and administrative; Homer is still ahead as epic memory.
GRC.science: Palace metrology, seal administration, chariot workshops, and Mediterranean shipping are bureaucratic sciences. Bronze armour, fresco chemistry, and ashlar masonry are specialised crafts. Northern Balkan metallurgy and amber routes link Aegean demand to Carpathian supply.
GRC.culture: Wanax-centred palaces organise workshops, warriors, and redistributive feasts; sanctuaries receive accounted offerings. Northern Balkan communities keep non-palace metal-age societies linked by trade. Belonging is palace catchment or regional metal network, not a single Balkan ethnos.
GRC.description:
By 1400 BC Mycenaean palace societies create Europe’s first palace visual regime in the Aegean: megarons, shaft and tholos tombs, gold masks, frescoes, and chamber tombs. Linear B tablets write early Greek as administrative marks—offerings, rations, inventories—not epic manuscripts. Northern Balkans join Carpathian metal fashions without sharing palaces.

Palace centres redistribute goods, sponsor warriors, and stage sanctuary reciprocity. Genomes show moderate steppe on Aegean farmer bases—language attested, demography not Corded-Denmark. Northern Balkan Bronze Age networks parallel Mycenaean demand through metal and amber routes.

Linear B records offerings to named gods (forms related to Zeus, Poseidon, and female deities)—a real pantheon in accounting. Thought is ritual and administrative; Homer lies ahead as epic memory of this world.

UKR.name: Srubnaya
UKR.literature: No native scripts in the Nordic zone; meaning is cut into rock and cast in bronze. Later Eddic myth is a distant Iron/Viking-Age reframing — handle as comparative poetry, not Bronze Age reportage. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: Timber-grave (Srubnaya) kurgans, bone and bronze weapon sets, and settlement traces keep a pastoral-steppe aesthetic; forest-steppe edges mix farmer motifs. Chariot-related imagery and horse gear echo Sintashta innovations farther east. Art is grave timber, weapon, and herd wealth.
UKR.religion: Srubnaya: timber-grave steppe rite under kurgans with weapons and animal offerings — continuing Pontic funerary religion into the Late Bronze Age.
UKR.ideas: Srubnaya and kin maintain steppe-rich ancestry on pathways often linked toward early Indo-Iranian—parallel to European BA diversification west. Fortified Sintashta-type experiments (Urals) show war-tech and metallurgy intensifying. Identity is pastoral confederacy more than Mycenaean palace.
UKR.philosophy: Kurgan and timber-grave rites continue ancestor–herd cosmologies; chariot burials farther east sacralise speed and war. Fire, horse, and sky motifs are reconstructed from Indo-Iranian comparisons with caution—not quoted steppe scripture. Ethics of guest, raid, and offering are inferred, not authored.
UKR.science: Sintashta–Petrovka chariots (spoked wheels, horse teams) and bronze arsenals are peak steppe engineering of the early 2nd millennium BC. Timber-grave communities manage herds, metallurgy, and forest-steppe farming edges. Long-distance horse and metal knowledge feeds both European and Asian Bronze Ages.
UKR.culture: Timber-grave pastoral groups and forest-steppe neighbours organise around herds, kurgans, and metal workshops. Sintashta-related fortified settlements farther east intensify warrior and chariot specialisation. Society is confederative and mobile, with farming edges softening pure steppe lifeways.
UKR.description:
By the mid–second millennium BC Srubnaya (Timber-grave) and related forest-steppe cultures keep a pastoral-steppe aesthetic of timber-lined graves under kurgans, bone and bronze weapon sets, and settlement traces. Forest-steppe edges mix farmer motifs. Chariot-related imagery and horse gear echo Sintashta innovations farther east in the Urals.

Srubnaya and kin maintain steppe-rich ancestry on pathways often linked—cautiously—toward early Indo-Iranian, parallel to European Bronze Age diversification west. Fortified Sintashta-type experiments show war-tech and metallurgy intensifying. Identity is pastoral confederacy more than Mycenaean palace.

Spoked-wheel chariots, horse teams, and bronze arsenals are peak steppe engineering of the early second millennium. Timber-grave communities manage herds, metallurgy, and forest-steppe farming edges. Long-distance horse and metal knowledge feeds both European and Asian Bronze Ages.

PRT.description:
By the mid–second millennium BC southeast Iberia’s El Argar tradition experiments with early complex society: fortified hill settlements, marked inequality, intramural urn burials, and stark silver diadems. Farther west, Atlantic Bronze networks join wider European sword and scrap-bronze circuits. Visual politics splits by province—argaric goblets and fortress graves versus Atlantic warrior hoards.

Steppe-related ancestry is established yet diluted beside a durable Neolithic substrate; rough schematics near half EEF with substantial WHG and moderate steppe capture continuity-with-admixture, not a second British-style replacement. Culture names and metal fashions change faster than genes.

These regional ‘kingdoms’ of craft and coercion precede Celtic ethnonyms by centuries. Iberia’s Bronze Age is hierarchical provisioning, watery hoards, and metallurgical specialisation on a ternary already set in the Beaker centuries.
PRT.culture: El Argar organises labour, metal, and burial under house floors inside defended centres; Atlantic façades participate in pan-European bronze exchange and hoarding. Inequality is visible in diadems, weapon sets, and settlement hierarchy. Society is provincial—southeast courts and western warrior circuits—yet both belong to a metal age in which recycling, fortification, and dryland storage structure daily life.
PRT.art: Hillfort silhouettes, intramural urns, silver diadems, and argaric pottery create a severe court style in the southeast; Atlantic carp’s-tongue swords and wet-place hoards shine farther west. Art is fortress, threshold grave, and deliberately destroyed wealth—metal as the sculptural medium of power.
PRT.ideas: Southeast Iberia tests controlled metal and coercion as early statecraft; Atlantic elites advertise belonging to European bronze clubs through swords and scrap economies. Steppe ancestry is present but not revolutionary; the idea of the age is craft hierarchy and provincial identity before later Celtic labels.
PRT.philosophy: Intramural burial under houses binds the dead to domestic space—an ancestor theology of the threshold. Atlantic hoards in rivers and bogs suggest offerings to water powers or sworn destruction of weapons and wealth. No philosophers; ethics of honour and metal debt are inferred from diadems, blades, and deposition rites.
PRT.science: Argolic metallurgy, silver working, and fortification engineering mark specialised technical classes. Atlantic smiths cast, alloy, and recycle within pan-European scrap-bronze economies—recycling as industrial practice. Dryland farming and storage inside defended sites are survival science under hierarchical provisioning.

IRL.description:
In the mid–second millennium BC post-Beaker Britain consolidates a barrow aristocracy under facies such as Wessex: gold lozenges, amber, bronze daggers, and later Deverel–Rimbury urnfields. Stonehenge’s Bronze Age reworkings keep the old sky theatre in elite service. Rock art is scarcer than in Scandinavia; prestige is portable gold and continental-style weaponry.

Ancestry remains the Beaker-set WHG–EEF–steppe ternary without another island-wide replacement. Chiefly exchange with Brittany, the Rhine, and Nordic zones advertises belonging to a European bronze club. Land, herds, and barrow cemeteries fix lineage claims in chalk country.

Southwest tin makes the islands a strategic node in bronze recipes across Europe—applied geography at continental scale on a gene pool already reset in the Beaker centuries.
IRL.culture: Barrow cemeteries, roundhouses, and emerging field systems organise agrarian and lineage life. Elites display continental metal and amber while smiths alloy local tin into bronze. Society is chiefly and funerary—mound skylines as claims—rather than palace bureaucracy. Belonging is cemetery, exchange partner, and control of metal routes.
IRL.art: Wessex rich graves stage gold lozenges, amber beads, and bronze daggers; later urnfields shift some communities toward cremation ceramics. Stonehenge’s remodelled settings keep solar architecture in elite orbit. Visual culture is portable glitter and weapon fashion more than Scandinavian rock fleets.
IRL.ideas: Cultural renaming (Wessex and successors) overlays genetic continuity. Elites think in terms of European bronze club membership—Rhine, Brittany, Nordic links—while chalk barrows fix local lineage. The idea of the age is aristocratic exchange without a second demographic apocalypse.
IRL.philosophy: Barrow cemeteries and watery hoards suggest ancestors and offerings structuring obligation. Solar and martial symbolism travels with continental metal styles more than with local scripture. Worldview is elite funerary theatre—gold, dagger, and mound—plus older henge memory still charged with power.
IRL.science: Tin from southwest Britain anchors alloy recipes across Europe. Smiths cast, recycle, and sheet-work bronze; field systems and roundhouses organise production. Seagoing exchange of metal and amber is measured commercial geography.

FRA.description:
By 1400 BC Bronze Age provinces overlie the third-millennium genetic settlement. Tumulus barrows, Atlantic bronze hoards, and later Urnfield cremation urns diversify funerary art. Swords, spears, and ornamented bronze advertise warrior fashion shared with Central Europe.

Ancestry is a stable ternary relative to Corded/Beaker formation; culture names change faster than genes. Atlantic and Tumulus networks pull elites into pan-European exchange. Toward Urnfield, cremation communities reimagine the dead as ash collectives—an idea of belonging through fire.

Monumentality shifts from megalith to mound and hoard. Metal becomes the sculptural medium of obligation, vow, and display across a corridor land between Channel and Mediterranean.
FRA.culture: Barrow aristocracies, hilltop occupations, and field systems organise production and defence. Atlantic hoards and Tumulus weapon graves stage warrior ethics; later urnfields gather cremation communities. Society is provincial yet networked—weights, alloys, and seasonal trade binding France into European bronze circuits.
FRA.art: Tumulus mounds, sword and spear sets, Atlantic hoards, and Urnfield ceramics diversify the funerary gallery. Visual culture moves from megalithic stone to metal deposition and ash urns—warrior fashion as shared Central European style.
FRA.ideas: Elites belong to exchange clubs that outrun local ancestry change. Cremation reimagines the person as fire-transformed community member. Ideas of honour travel with swords; ideas of offering travel with river and bog hoards.
FRA.philosophy: Hoards in rivers and bogs look like gifts to watery powers or ritual destruction of weapons. Cremation reorients the body–soul problem without texts. Sacred life is depositional and funerary—sun, metal, and mound—not academy philosophy.
FRA.science: Bronze casting, sheet-working, and long-distance scrap economies are industrial knowledge. Field systems and hilltops organise surplus and defence. Tin, copper, and amber routes make France a corridor science of weights, alloys, and seasonal trade.

POL.description:
By 1400 BC Central Europe moves through Middle Bronze Tumulus weapon graves toward Late Bronze Urnfield cremation cemeteries—urns, bronze swords, and situla art on the southern edge. Visual culture shifts from body-under-mound to ash-in-urn. Hillforts and hoards punctuate the landscape.

Genetic continuity with Corded-descended mixes underlies rapid cultural renaming. Urnfield networks may seed later Celtic linguistic zones—debated, yet the idea of wide cremation communities is clear. Warrior fashion and bronze scrap economies integrate the Carpathian–Alpine arc.

Advanced casting, eastern Alpine mining, and recycling economies make this an industrial Bronze Age. Culture change vastly outruns genetic replacement: the ternary set after Corded Ware mostly holds while rites of fire remake the dead.
POL.culture: Tumulus elites display weapons under mounds; Urnfield communities gather cremation cemeteries as cities of ash. Hillforts organise surplus and defence; smiths and miners feed scrap circuits. Society is warrior-fashionable and metallurgically specialised on a genetically settled plain.
POL.art: Weapon graves yield to urnfields; swords, situlae, and hoards become the sculptural media. Visual culture pivots from inhumation theatre to cremation ceramic and bronze ornament—fire as aesthetic as well as rite.
POL.ideas: Belonging shifts toward cremation collectives and pan-regional warrior styles. Ideas of Celtic linguistic seeding remain debated; clearer is the Urnfield thought-world of shared rites and scrap economies across the Alpine–Carpathian arc.
POL.philosophy: Cremation reframes the person as fire-transformed; urnfields are cities of the dead without biographies. Hoards suggest vows, trophies, or offerings to powers of water and earth. Worldview is ritual technology of fire and metal, not written ethics.
POL.science: Advanced bronze casting, including early lost-wax flourishes, eastern Alpine mining, and recycling economies are industrial science. Urnfield agronomy and fortification engineering organise surplus. Weight systems and ingot trade imply quantitative exchange literacy.

FIN.description:
From roughly 1700 to 500 BC the Nordic Bronze Age makes Scandinavia Europe’s great image culture of the metal age. Figurative rock art at Tanum, Bohuslän, and Østfold; the Trundholm sun chariot; oak-coffin costumes; lurs; and Viksø helmets stage ships, sun discs, warriors, and ploughs on coastal bedrock and in bog finds. Denmark’s dressed dead are prehistoric couture.

Imported metal founds a prestige economy—amber out, bronze in—binding chiefs to Únětice, Carpathian, and later Italian copper routes. Genetically the region is continuous with Battle Axe / Single Grave; this is cultural climax, not a third replacement. Rock-art fleets advertise maritime ideology and meeting places for exchange.

Sun-cult imagery and watery hoards stage a cosmology of light, voyage, and offering. Scandinavia’s science is network metallurgy: sourcing, alloying, and recycling foreign copper with local strategies, plus ship carpentry inferred from rock art and later boat finds.
FIN.culture: Longhouse farms, barrow labour, and chiefly exchange organise surplus around amber and bronze. Communities gather at rock-art panels and wet offering places. Society is maritime-prestige and agrarian—ships carved on stone, cloth and bronze on the dead—without Mycenaean palaces.
FIN.art: Figurative rock art, sun chariots, oak-coffin textiles, lurs, and horned helmets make the north Bronze Age Europe’s densest image world. Ships, discs, warriors, and ploughs cover coastal rock; portable bronzes and bog costumes complete the gallery.
FIN.ideas: Amber-for-bronze ideology binds northern chiefs into European metal clubs. Continuity with Single Grave ancestry means cultural fluorescence, not demic reboot. Maritime meeting places and sun symbolism articulate a northern theory of prestige and voyage.
FIN.philosophy: Sun-cult imagery (Trundholm; rock-art discs) and watery hoards stage cosmology of light, voyage, and offering. Processions and twin myths are guessed from paired figures and horns—reconstructed ritual, not named theology. Sacred knowledge is metal, ship, and sun performed on rock and in bog.
FIN.science: Network metallurgy—sourcing, alloying, recycling foreign copper—plus amber grading and route knowledge are commercial geography. Longhouse farms and barrow labour organise surplus. Ship carpentry is inferred from rock art and later boat finds as applied maritime science.

ALA.science: Network metallurgy—sourcing, alloying, recycling foreign copper—plus amber grading and route knowledge are commercial geography. Longhouse farms and barrow labour organise surplus. Ship carpentry is inferred from rock art and later boat finds as applied maritime science.

SMR.description:
By 1400 BC the Po plain’s Terramare embanked villages—planned ditches, banks, and dense housing—are civic art in earth and timber, while Apennine pottery and pastoral sites mark the mountains. Cremation and inhumation rites vary by facies. Visual identity is settlement geometry more than Nordic rock-art fleets.

Organised Po settlements imply collective labour and perhaps proto-urban control of floodplain wealth. Apennine mobility links coasts to uplands. Ancestry keeps Italian Early European Farmer weight with moderate Bronze Age steppe—foundation tones for later Italic and Etruscan genetic landscapes.

Hydraulic and embankment engineering, bronze workshops, and floodplain agronomy are Terramare sciences. Northern Italian copper later feeds Nordic networks—Italy as ore science for the amber north.
SMR.culture: Terramare communities organise ditch, bank, and house grid as communal labour; Apennine groups move seasonally between upland and lowland. Society is settlement-disciplined on the plain and pastoral-mobile in the mountains—two Bronze Age Italies sharing metal age inequality.
SMR.art: Embanked village plans, Apennine ceramics, and varied burial rites define visual identity. Art is civic earthwork and pottery facies more than sun chariots—geometry of living as display.
SMR.ideas: Collective embankment implies civic-sacral order and control of floodplain surplus. Apennine mobility ideas link vertical landscapes. Ancestry and later linguistic maps are still forming; the age’s idea is organised settlement before city-state names.
SMR.philosophy: Settlement rituals, structured deposits, and cemeteries suggest civic-sacral order without Nordic sun chariots. Water, ditch, and bank may themselves be charged boundaries. Ethics of communal embankment and pastoral seasonality stand in for written philosophy.
SMR.science: Hydraulic and embankment engineering, bronze workshops, and floodplain agronomy are Terramare sciences. Apennine herding calendars manage vertical mobility. Northern Italian copper feeds wider European—including Nordic—metal networks.

BGR.description:
By 1400 BC Mycenaean palace societies create Europe’s first palace visual regime in the Aegean: megarons, shaft and tholos tombs, gold masks, frescoes, and chamber tombs. Linear B tablets write early Greek as administrative marks—offerings, rations, inventories—not epic manuscripts. Northern Balkans join Carpathian metal fashions without sharing palaces.

Palace centres redistribute goods, sponsor warriors, and stage sanctuary reciprocity. Genomes show moderate steppe on Aegean farmer bases—language attested, demography not Corded-Denmark. Northern Balkan Bronze Age networks parallel Mycenaean demand through metal and amber routes.

Linear B records offerings to named gods (forms related to Zeus, Poseidon, and female deities)—a real pantheon in accounting. Thought is ritual and administrative; Homer lies ahead as epic memory of this world.
BGR.culture: Wanax-centred palaces organise workshops, warriors, and redistributive feasts; sanctuaries receive accounted offerings. Northern Balkan communities keep non-palace metal-age societies linked by trade. Belonging is palace catchment or regional metal network, not a single Balkan ethnos.
BGR.art: Gold masks, frescoed plaster, ashlar masonry, tholoi, and megarons define Aegean palace art; northern zones show Carpathian bronze fashions. Visual regime is gold and painted plaster in the south, weapon and hoard styles farther north.
BGR.ideas: Political theology of wanax and sanctuary meets northern metal confederacies. Early Greek is written for bureaucracy; epic ideology is later memory. Ideas of honour travel in gold and chariot gear as well as in tablets.
BGR.philosophy: Linear B offering lists name gods inside an accounting cosmos—reciprocity tabulated, not philosophised. Sanctuary deposits and funerary gold stage honour and divine debt. No philosophy seminars; ritual administration is the thought-world.
BGR.science: Palace metrology, seal administration, chariot workshops, and Mediterranean shipping are bureaucratic sciences. Bronze armour, fresco chemistry, and ashlar masonry are specialised crafts. Northern Balkan metallurgy and amber routes link Aegean demand to Carpathian supply.

BLR.description:
By the mid–second millennium BC Srubnaya (Timber-grave) and related forest-steppe cultures keep a pastoral-steppe aesthetic of timber-lined graves under kurgans, bone and bronze weapon sets, and settlement traces. Forest-steppe edges mix farmer motifs. Chariot-related imagery and horse gear echo Sintashta innovations farther east in the Urals.

Srubnaya and kin maintain steppe-rich ancestry on pathways often linked—cautiously—toward early Indo-Iranian, parallel to European Bronze Age diversification west. Fortified Sintashta-type experiments show war-tech and metallurgy intensifying. Identity is pastoral confederacy more than Mycenaean palace.

Spoked-wheel chariots, horse teams, and bronze arsenals are peak steppe engineering of the early second millennium. Timber-grave communities manage herds, metallurgy, and forest-steppe farming edges. Long-distance horse and metal knowledge feeds both European and Asian Bronze Ages.
BLR.culture: Timber-grave pastoral groups and forest-steppe neighbours organise around herds, kurgans, and metal workshops. Sintashta-related fortified settlements farther east intensify warrior and chariot specialisation. Society is confederative and mobile, with farming edges softening pure steppe lifeways.
BLR.art: Timber-lined graves, weapon sets, horse gear, and occasional chariot-related imagery define the gallery. Art is grave timber, bronze, and herd wealth—parallel to European Urnfield glitter without palace frescoes.
BLR.ideas: Steppe-rich continuity and possible Indo-Iranian linguistic pathways (debated in detail) frame eastern identity beside European ternary diversification. Ideas of war-tech and speed sacralise chariot horizons. Belonging is pastoral confederacy and metallurgical school.
BLR.philosophy: Kurgan and timber-grave rites continue ancestor–herd cosmologies; chariot burials farther east sacralise speed and war. Fire, horse, and sky motifs are reconstructed from Indo-Iranian comparisons with caution—not quoted steppe scripture. Ethics of guest, raid, and offering are inferred.
BLR.science: Sintashta–Petrovka chariots (spoked wheels, horse teams) and bronze arsenals are peak early-second-millennium steppe engineering. Timber-grave communities manage herds, metallurgy, and forest-steppe farming edges. Horse and metal knowledge radiates into European and Asian Bronze Ages.

periods.label: Iron, oppida, and first texts
periods.narrative: In the mid-first millennium BC iron tools and weapons spread; Hallstatt then La Tène define Celtic material Europe while Jastorf-related groups mark Germanic ethnogenesis. Classical Greek poleis write history; Etruscans and early Rome urbanize Italy; Scythian Iranian-speakers hold the steppe; Iberia mixes Iberian and Celtiberian speech. Genetics mostly continue Bronze Age mixes — ‘Celtic’ and ‘Germanic’ are linguistic-cultural labels, not new deep components.
periods.culturesNote: Hallstatt, La Tène, Jastorf, Classical Greek poleis, Etruscan/early Rome, Iberian/Celtiberian, Scythian — first dense linguistic attestation.

iberia.culture: Iberian coastal societies developed urbanising oppida, sanctuary terracottas, and literacy on lead and ceramic, with Mediterranean dress and banquet habits filtered through indigenous taste. Inland Celtiberian and related Celtic communities organised around hillforts, horse culture, and warrior funerary display; hospitality, cattle wealth, and reputation structured social capital. Northwestern castro zones lived in circular stone houses within fortified circuits facing the Atlantic. Daily life mixed intensive coastal agriculture and irrigation knowledge with meseta pastoral–cereal schedules. Social structure was elite and tribal-confederative rather than citizen-democratic; women appear in sculpture and burial with regionally variable visibility. Speech communities were the true map—Iberian, Celtic, Lusitanian, and northern isolates—making belonging linguistic as much as territorial. Markets and mercenary service tied households to wider Mediterranean demand.
iberia.description:
Iron Age Iberia was a language mosaic long before any ‘Spanish’ culture: non-Indo-European Iberian speech along Mediterranean coasts and south, Celtic and Celtiberian communities inland on the meseta, Lusitanian and related western groups toward the Atlantic, and Basque-line speech enduring in the north. Greek Emporion and Punic coastal pressure layered southern Mediterranean templates onto indigenous workshops without full Hellenisation. The visual split is sharp—Lady of Elche polychromy and Iberian scripts versus inland warrior stelae and La Tène-influenced weapons, with northwestern castros adding circular stone settlements and warrior statues.

Urbanising coasts and meseta confederations faced Carthage then Rome with different toolkits: literacy and silver on the façade, highland pastoral scheduling and castro masonry inland. Hillforts and oppida framed stone, iron, and horse gear as political display. Mercenary export and mining zones fed Mediterranean metal hunger while local pantheons and sanctuary votives kept religion plural—never a uniform Celtic church.

Iberian–Celtiberian rivalry and shifting alliances preceded the great wars that classical historians narrate. Identity was plural by necessity: bilingual frontiers, city and sanctuary politics on the coast, cattle and warrior reputation on the plateau. Coinage arrived as art and badge; inscribed lead plaques and ceramics braided script with craft.

By the later centuries BC the peninsula had become Rome’s and Carthage’s chessboard, yet the Iron Age achievement was already complete: a western European outlier of scripts, sculpture, and confederations that would not let Europe pretend it was ever only Latin.
iberia.ancestryNote: Schematic continuity with BA Iberia (~EEF-rich ternary). No separate “Iberian race” component in aDNA terms.
iberia.linguisticNote: Among Europe’s clearest Iron Age language mosaics: written Iberian alongside Celtic IE; Basque/Aquitanian is the long-lived non-IE western outlier.
iberia.art: Iberian art produced the Lady of Elche’s limestone polychromy, sculpted warriors, painted geometric pottery, and sanctuary votives—a Mediterranean-facing figural language distinct from La Tène scrolls. Celtiberian workshops fused La Tène weapon aesthetics with Iberian ceramic and stelae habits; fibulae and painted wares mark the inland eye. Castro northwest carved warrior statues and circular domestic architecture in stone. Greek and Punic coastal art entered indigenous workshops as filter and challenge. Coinage added portable political faces. Writing on plaques and vessels made script itself a visual craft. The peninsula’s gallery is plural by design: polychrome lady, warrior stele, castro statue, and iron scabbard sharing one geography without one style.
iberia.ideas: Non-IE Iberian, Celtic, and Lusitanian zones made identity a frontier negotiation. Coastal cities and sanctuaries managed Greek Emporion, Carthaginian, and later Roman pressure with urban tools; meseta confederations answered with hillfort autonomy and warrior leagues. Belonging was never a single Iron Age ‘Spain’—it was language community, oppidum, and confederation. Hospitality and cattle wealth organised inland honour; civic and sanctuary competition organised the coast. Mercenary service abroad exported Iberian military reputation into Mediterranean wars. Institutions included scripts and coin for some elites, oral law and raid custom for others. Political thought was practical pluralism under external empire hunger.
iberia.philosophy: No named philosophical schools wrote from Iron Age Iberia. Funerary sculpture, warrior stelae, and sanctuary votives encode honour, divine patronage, and afterlife care as practised theology. Cosmology was local and polytheistic—deity names appear in places without yielding a uniform pantheon list. Later Roman syncretism overlays interpretatio without documenting a prior dialectic literature. Ethics of courage, hospitality, and confederate loyalty appear through burial imagery and enemy ethnography. Thought is cult practice and honour code, not Academy curriculum. The Lady of Elche’s gaze is not a treatise, but it is a theory of personhood in stone.
iberia.science: Iberian script literacy, silver mining and metallurgy, wheel-made finewares, and coastal navigation are sciences of the trading façade. Castro masonry and circular planning show Atlantic hillfort engineering; meseta iron weapon manufacture and highland pastoral scheduling are inland strengths. Agricultural intensification—terraces, Mediterranean crops, irrigation knowledge—underwrote oppida and mercenary export. Urban fortification adapted to Hellenistic siege awareness on the coasts. Metrology lived in coin, metal weight, and amphora standards borrowed and localised. Medical detail is sparse; the technical signature is mine, masonry, script, and ship.
iberia.name: Iberians & Celtiberians

stories.text: In a workshop near the Mediterranean façade, artisans painted a limestone woman’s lips and jewels before she became votive or funerary presence. She was not a Greek import copy—she was Iberian personhood taught to stone.

stories.text: A scribe scratched Iberian signs into a lead plaque—names, gifts, or a curse—while a Celtiberian neighbour inland still trusted the sword’s genealogy more than the alphabet. One peninsula, two technologies of memory.

britain.culture: Irish Iron Age communities spoke early Gaelic dialects within regional kingdoms structured by cattle wealth, clientship, and assembly at royal sites. Settlement favoured ringed enclosures, open farms, and wetland trackways more than classical urban grids; daily life mixed dairying, tillage, and craft specialisation in metal and textile. Social rank was performed at feast and raid: who gave cattle, who received fosterage, who sat at inauguration mounds. Speech and law were oral; learned classes analogous to continental druids and bards are inferred more than documented for this exact horizon. Bog landscapes shaped movement and ritual—trackways of timber, deposits of valuables, bodies sometimes given to peat. Women and men appear in later literature with formalised status roles; archaeology keeps the quieter evidence of household and workshop. Belonging meant the túath you claimed, the assembly you attended, and the wetland paths your people maintained.
britain.description:
Iron Age Britain organised itself in tribal territories whose skylines were hillforts and whose houses were round: timber, thatch, and bank-and-ditch enclosures rather than classical stone temples. From Wessex chalk ridges to the eastern lowlands, communities negotiated alliance, cattle wealth, and raid without Roman towns to script the map. Continental La Tène style arrived in metalwork—mirrors, scabbards, torcs—without a Beaker-scale population replacement; ancestry stayed largely Bronze Age British while taste learned new curves.

Eastern chariot burials and great gold hoards such as Snettisham show regional elites staging funerary and votive theatre with horses, vehicles, and neck-rings. Hillfort engineering—multivallate ramparts, complex gates, quarry ditches—turned hills into political architecture visible for miles. Roundhouse settlements in their shadows kept the calorie and craft base: querns, salt, weaving, and bronze sheet-work for chiefs who paid in hospitality.

Classical ethnography (Poseidonius, later Caesar) folds Britain into the wider Celtic world of druids and oral law, yet the island’s accent is distinctive: Channel and North Sea boats, watery deposits in rivers and bogs, and a hillfort landscape denser than many continental zones. Belgic contacts in the southeast foreshadowed the political geography Rome would later try to annex. Before the Claudian conquest still lay generations of tribal negotiation—Rome imminent as rumour and trade good, not yet as province.

What survives is earthwork and metal more than text. Epic and law lived in memory; we overhear them through fascinated or hostile prose, while archaeology recovers the mirrors’ engraved backs and the ramparts’ labour calculus. Insular voices in a European chorus: Brittonic speech, continental fashion, and a sacred economy that preferred rivers and shafts to marble colonnades.
britain.linguisticNote: Insular Celtic stage; Latin arrives only with Rome.
britain.ancestryNote: BA ternary continuity; steppe typically substantial; “Celtic” ≠ new ancestry component.
britain.art: Irish Iron Age display concentrates on fine metalwork—gold collars and bronze ornaments—bog deposits, and the ceremonial topography of royal sites rather than marble temples or dense oppida sculpture. La Tène curvilinear taste arrives in selected objects; local workshops answer with Atlantic accents. Emain Macha’s great structures and Tara’s mounds are architecture as political theatre: earth, timber, and gathering space. Later Early Christian manuscripts and metalwork would inherit and transform these curves, but the Iron Age voice is portable shine and landscape monument, not figural freestanding stone. Beauty was worn, buried in peat, or walked as processional ground around inauguration places. Compared with Gaulish coin portraits or Greek pediments, Ireland’s gallery is quieter and wetter—gold, bronze, and ceremonial earth.
britain.ideas: Tribal territories negotiated alliance and raid without Roman municipal templates. Political geography was a patchwork of named peoples whose borders flexed with cattle wealth and marriage, not fixed provincial lines. Continental style and Belgic contacts arrived as fashion and faction without erasing Bronze Age demographic depth. Hillforts concentrated labour and defence; their occupancy pulsed—some crowded, some ceremonial, some abandoned—as politics shifted. Later Roman conquest would overlay roads and civitates onto this map without inventing it from nothing. Institutions were oral: assembly, clientship, and sanctuary deposit rather than written charter. Belonging meant the people you raided with, the hill you could see, and the river where offerings sank.
britain.philosophy: No contemporary philosophical texts survive from Iron Age Ireland. Ritual deposition in bogs and ceremonial activity at royal sites imply sacral kingship ideologies—rulers bound to land and otherworld powers—that medieval literature would elaborate and rewrite. Cosmology is practised as offering and inauguration, not as Academy metaphysics. Learned oral specialists almost certainly existed by analogy with Britain and Gaul, but Irish evidence for this century is archaeological inference more than named ethnography. Ethics of hospitality, cattle debt, and feud limitation appear later in law tracts; for the Iron Age they are plausible continuities, not quotable statutes. Worldview remains landscape ritual and social obligation—thought without Plato, wisdom without papyrus.
britain.science: Hillfort rampart engineering is applied geometry and labour organisation at landscape scale—ditches cut, banks raised, gates designed for control and display. Salt production, rotary querns, and mixed farming on heavy soils underwrote the calorie politics of tribal life. Fine bronze sheet-work and iron smithing show specialist chaînes opératoires serving elites. Channel and North Sea boat carpentry made the island a participant in Atlantic exchange; chariot construction in the east combined wheelwright and horse-breeding knowledge. Metrology appeared in metal weight, grain measure, and the surveyor’s judgement that laid out multivallate circuits. Medicine and calendrical lore remain largely mute; the visible sciences are earthwork, metallurgy, and seafaring.

stories.text: Clients drove cattle toward Tara’s ridges while smiths and poets claimed their places for the gathering. No Roman road marked the approach—only memory of which slope held judgment and which mound held inauguration.
stories.title: Procession to the Assembly Hill

stories.text: Oak planks laid across wet peat became a road for feet and wheels where solid ground failed. Travellers crossed a trembling world; sometimes metal or a body went into the dark water beside the path as payment to place.
stories.title: Trackway Over the Bog

stories.text: A collar of hammered gold left the neck of the living and entered the bog’s archive. Peat sealed shine from air; centuries later the same gleam would restart Ireland’s conversation with its Iron Age dead.
stories.title: Gold for the Wet Dark

stories.text: At Navan Fort great timber structures rose and burned in sequences that look like ceremony as much as domestic life. The royal site rehearsed power in wood and fire—architecture meant to be witnessed, then remembered.
stories.title: Emain’s Timber Ambition
